**A. The box has today's code.** The first line should end `The settle lane counts as alive while it runs; college flags carry their team`
(or be newer), and the second should print `has today's code`. If it prints nothing or
"Not a valid commit name", the box hasn't pulled yet: wait five minutes
and run both again.
```
git -C /srv/qellys log --oneline -1
git -C /srv/qellys merge-base --is-ancestor 05270b4b HEAD && echo "has today's code"
```

**B. Health check** (paste all of it):
```
uptime; free -m
ps -eo pid,ni,pcpu,pmem,etime,args --sort=-pcpu | head -8
for p in / /js/app.js /data/recommendations.json /data/record.json; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "$p %{http_code} %{size_download}B %{time_total}s\n" http://127.0.0.1:8000$p; done
journalctl -u qellys --since "2 hours ago" --no-pager | grep -iE "refresh|cycle|took|build|slip watch" | grep -v "/api/" | tail -15
```

**C. Is email on?** "Forgot password?" and the new last-leg email both
need it:
```
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/account/me; echo
```
`"reset_by_email": true` means it's on; go to D. `false` means step 26
below isn't done yet. It takes about ten minutes: a Resend account, its
key put on the box with `sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh QB_RESEND_KEY`, a

**D. Stripe** (step 37 says why). Three settings in Stripe's dashboard,
nothing to type on the box:
* Developers → Webhooks → your endpoint → **Send test webhook**. It
  should say `200`. If it's blocked, Bot Fight Mode is on; docs/DEPLOY.md
  says how to turn it off.
* Settings → Billing → **Customer portal**: "Update payment methods" and
  "Invoice history" switched on. That's how a locked customer pays.
* Settings → Billing → **Subscriptions and emails**: "Send emails when
  card payments fail" switched on.

Then two read-only checks. They print statuses, counts and times, never
an email. Open the site on a subscribed account first; the second line
should then print under 60 (seconds since Stripe was last asked):
```
cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys python3 -c "import time; from engine import accounts as A, billing as B; c=A.connect(); B.init(c); n=time.time(); print([tuple(r) for r in c.execute('SELECT status, COUNT(*), SUM(checked_at IS NOT NULL), ROUND(MAX(?-checked_at)/3600.0,1) FROM subscriptions GROUP BY status', (n,))])"
cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys python3 -c "import time; from engine import accounts as A, billing as B; c=A.connect(); B.init(c); print(c.execute('SELECT ROUND(?-MAX(checked_at)) FROM subscriptions', (time.time(),)).fetchone()[0])"
```
In the first, each tuple is (status, accounts, read from Stripe, hours
since the oldest read). Every status except `canceled` and `none` should
have the third number equal to the second, and the last under 6.

**E. The parlay checker's measurements** (read-only, a few minutes each;
paste back the tables). Steps 38, 39 and 41 say how to read them:
```
cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys python3 -m engine.proplivefit
cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys python3 -m engine.slipread nfl "Josh Allen" rush_att over 5.5 -130
cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys python3 -m engine.slipreadfit --sport nfl --seasons 2023 2024 2025
cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys python3 -m engine.slipreadfit --sport cfb --seasons 2024 2025 --limit 3000
```
* The first replays the live chance on three NFL seasons. If "blend"
  beats "ours" by much, say so; changing the model is your call.
* The second is our read on a prop no board carries. `"found": "read"`
  with a projection means it works.
* The last two replay that read on seasons already played. "ours" should
  beat "last8" on Brier (lower is better) in every market, and each
  calibration band should land near what it said.

minute; paste all of it). Nothing to run for the fix itself: the box pulls

```

systemctl show qellys -p ActiveState -p NRestarts -p ExecMainStartTimestamp -p MemoryCurrent
free -m; swapon --show; df -h /srv | tail -1
journalctl -k --since "2 days ago" --no-pager | grep -iE "oom-kill|out of memory|killed process" | tail -12
journalctl -u qellys --since "2 days ago" --no-pager | grep -iE "killed by signal|out of memory|database is locked|build failed|mlb charts|nba shots|charts:|watchdog|auto-update" | tail -30
python3 -c "import json,time; d=json.load(open('/srv/qellys/web/data/heartbeat.json')); print(round((time.time()-d['at_epoch'])/60), 'min since the last cycle;', d.get('swept'), '; cycle', d.get('cycle_s'), 's; running', d.get('commit'), ';', d.get('disk_free_gb'), 'GB free')"
for f in recommendations cfb mlb_recommendations nba wnba nhl ufc; do printf "%-20s %s\n" $f "$(stat -c %y /srv/qellys/web/data/$f.json 2>/dev/null | cut -c1-16)"; done
for u in "/api/players/search?q=allen&sport=nfl&scope=sport" "/api/recommendations" "/api/nba/recommendations"; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{size_download}B %{time_total}s  $u\n" "http://127.0.0.1:8000$u"; done
ps -eo pid,ni,rss,etime,args --sort=-rss | head -6
```
How to read it:
* The kernel lines (`oom-kill`, `Killed process ... python3`) are the
  memory wall. Before the fix they would name a python child near a
  gigabyte, from late on the 13th on. None after the fix landed is the
  fix working.
* The qellys lines: `killed by signal 9 ... out of memory` is a chores
  child the kernel stopped; `mlb charts` and `nba shots` lines are the
  backfills, which still read 400 and 300 games a night, now eight at a
  time. Paste any `database is locked` or `build failed` line.
* The heartbeat should say a few minutes since the last cycle and `ran`,
  and every board's time should be within the last hour. Past an hour old
  the page takes that board's picks off (the stale bar at the top says
  so) until the next build lands.
* Search should answer `200` with a few hundred bytes in well under a
  second. A `502` or `000` is the app not answering.
* In `ps`, the web server (`launch.py --bind`) is the one at NI 0; builds
  and chores run at NI 10, and each of them now also marks itself first
  for the kernel to stop (oom_score_adj 500), so if memory runs out again
  a child goes, not the site.
* From the next push on, `autoupdate.json` can say `the restart waits for
  the board sweep in progress (N min in; waited M of 45 min)`: the new
  page is already served, and the box restarts into the new code when
  that sweep ends, 45 minutes at most. That is the new normal, not a
  fault; `cat /srv/qellys/data/cache/sweep.json` shows the sweep it is
  waiting on.

**CO. The price rule reaches posted picks** (step 146).

Your CN paste read 247 board picks, 0 at the price. The cause:

- A pick counts as posted once it has been on a previous build, and that
  is nearly every pick by Saturday evening.
- The first cut skipped posted picks.
- The board also takes a posted pick's number back from the list on every
  build. So the rule could touch a pick on its first build only, then
  lose it.

The fix:

- A posted pick keeps its line, price and book as before. Its chance is
  today's on every build, and the price now judges that chance too.
- The list shows the same number (your one-bet-one-chance rule).
- The board now carries its own counts: picks checked, picks with no book
  quote, picks with under three books at the line, picks with a field,
  picks above it, and picks moved. A zero now says why it is zero.

Run this after the box has pulled and the next NFL build has run (about
half an hour). The first line should name `The price rule reaches posted
picks`, and the file time should be later than that commit:

**CQ. The game report on every NFL game page** (step 148).
Your "I want a full layed out detailed explanation for every nfl game just
like how the report is. Obv keep out the prop picks". Every NFL game page
now opens on a written report, in the research reports' order:

- The short version.
- Game facts, then the market: the line and what it implies, where it
  opened, the prediction markets and their money, and the simulator.
- How the units rank, both offenses against the other defense.
- How each team plays: run rate, play action, the target tree, the
  coverage and the blitz.
- Injuries and what they open.
- Who's guarding who: a verdict on every key player, the soft corner, and
  where each defense leaks and holds.
- The trenches, the red zone, coaching and the schedule.
- How the game could go, players to watch, weather.
- What to confirm before kickoff.

Every number is the board's own. A section with nothing behind it is left
out, and no line, price or chance on a player appears anywhere in it.
With the report on the page, the matchup scan and the game plan's
narrative steps step aside, so nothing is said twice. The replay chart
moves inside the report. The game plan keeps its plays. The report is
paid; a reader without the subscription sees what it holds and the
usual matchup scan.

It does not slow the site down. The report's page code loads only when
a game page opens, the way the Toolbox does, and if it ever fails to
load, the page shows the old matchup scan and full game plan instead. The
wiring that has to stay in the main file is 0.6 KB, so its size limit
went from 496 to 497 KB (the reason is written in the test).

The Paris game was read as a dome. nflverse gives a game abroad the home
team's stadium until it is played. Stade de France (Steelers at Saints,
Sunday 9:30 AM ET) read "dome" because the Superdome is one, so no
forecast was pulled and the report said "a fixed dome". Open-air grounds
abroad (London, Paris, Munich, Berlin, Mexico City, São Paulo, Rio,
Dublin, Melbourne) now read outdoors and get their own city's forecast.
A stadium whose roof can close, like Madrid or Frankfurt, keeps the
schedule's word. The report also leaves out the surface for a game
abroad, because that is the home team's too.

**CR. Everything in the report, a report for every league, what changed,
copy and share** (step 149). Your "I want you too do all of it besides

- **A, the NFL report reads the history.** Under every key player's card:
  his season, his last three games, a trend when he is running hot or
  cold, and his red-zone work. The practice report: how each listed man
  practised and how often players listed that way have played. The role
  changes the detector sees, as a breakout watch. When the two teams last
  met, with the lines they closed at. Each team's turnover margin and
  tempo. The kicking air: the air's density and the wind along the field.
  The coaches' calls: how often each goes for it on fourth and short, two
  point tries, how often it throws two scores up and two scores down, and
  its pass rate over what the situation calls for.
- **B, a report for every league.** College games get the same report in
  college's terms (short names, the AP rank, a neutral site, a conference
  game, college's own unit stats). MLB: the pitching matchup as a table,

  of the tape with ranks and tonight's expected goals, the goalies
  (confirmed or not, save rate, goals saved above expected), the injury
  report. NBA and WNBA: rest and travel, who carries each team over his
  last ten, where each defence gives up the most and the fewest, the
  injury report. The run line and the puck line are said by name, and no
  team totals are read off them.

  **What changed** log under the short version: the line moving half a
  point, a man ruled out, the forecast turning, a starter scratched, a
  goalie confirmed, the lineups out, each stamped Eastern time. Small
  wobbles are not written; a slow drift is, once it adds up. Two buttons
  over every report: **Copy the report** (the whole thing as text) and
  **Share this game** (only the game, kickoff, line and link, so nothing
  paid goes out in a forwarded message).

**CT. NBA opening night: no lines, no live, a stale Pick of the Day**
(step 151). Your 7:04 PM screenshot: the 76ers @ Knicks card read "lines
post closer to tip-off", Top Picks was empty and the Pick of the Day read
"decided 04:17 UTC, when 0 of the slate had not started". You also said the
games weren't showing live. Three causes found in the code, all fixed:

- **The NBA build was cut off after three minutes.** The launcher kills a
  build that runs past 180 seconds unless that build gets a longer limit.
  MLB, the NFL and college got 600 seconds. The NBA, WNBA and NHL never
  did. Tonight is the first night the NBA board priced real props. A build
  killed every cycle leaves the board file at the last build that finished:
  no lines, no props, and live scores frozen at that build. All three now
  get 600 seconds.
- **The NBA had no cheap way to buy game lines.** Its only paid pull was
  the props pull, 19 credits a game, on the NBA's small share of the day.
  A night the pacer declined it had no moneyline, spread or total at all.
  The NBA and WNBA now have the NFL's and college's 3-credit tier: the
  whole slate's moneyline, spread and total in one request, on its own
  clock. It is bought only for games that haven't started, and every build
  reads the saved copy for free.
- **The Pick of the Day kept a "no bet" from Monday night.** At 12:17 AM
  Eastern the board was still on Monday's empty slate (the slate rolls at
  5 AM). That decline saw zero games, and the tie rule kept it all day.
  Now a decline that saw nothing never holds, and a card from a different
  slate date is never carried.

**CV. The month's odds plan: 100k credits, NFL first** (step 153). Your
"we have 100k credit per month for figure out how too budget in all the
sports that are currently active while keeping NFL at number one
priority". The pacer now runs on a monthly plan (docs/ODDS_PLAN.md has
all of it):

- **NFL funded first, in full.** Then college. Then the NBA, NHL, MLB and
  UFC split what's left at the same percentage, so a short month trims
  each of them a little instead of shutting the last one off. Extra room
  goes to the NFL first, but only after every league's normal cadence is
  paid for.
- **Every league gets a daily ceiling** sized to its real cadence: NBA and
  NHL three prop pulls a game day (noon, the pre-game run, 6pm ET), college
  eight on Saturday, the NFL its full Sunday. Before this, the NBA got
  about 2% of a weekday, which was one pull. That's the opening-night board
  with no lines.
- **November at 100,000:** NFL 42,020 and college 13,940, both in full. NBA
  16,667, NHL 9,001, MLB 426 and UFC 445, each at 86% of its target. Held
  back: 12,000 for closing lines, 5,000 buffer, 500 reserve.
- **Cheaper with it:** game lines no longer refresh every 15 minutes on days
  with no game within 36 hours (NFL Tuesdays and Fridays were about 290
  credits each). The live line polls every 10 minutes instead of 5. UFC is
  metered at its real one credit a fight.

**DD. Is our receiving curve too cautious on receivers like Burden?**
(step 161). No, so nothing changes. I rebuilt 2021 through this week from
the same public data the box stores, refitted the curve the way the box
does (the fit came out the same as the box's), and held out each season
in turn. Then, by how many yards each receiver was projected, I compared
what the curve claimed for bets like Burden's (over about three quarters
of his projection) with what actually happened:

- Receivers projected 45–60 yards: the curve said 58–59%; they landed
  55–62%, depending on how much you trust a hot streak.
- Projected 4–5.5 catches: the curve said 62–64%; they landed 59–64%.
- The plain curve behind the 72% I first gave you said 66–69% for the
  same bets. It was 10 points too high.

So the board's lower number on Burden was the honest one, and history
says the books' −260 (69% after the vig) was a steep price for a bet like
that. He hit a 60-something-percent bet; one game can't say more than
that. If anything
our curve is a bit narrow, not too cautious: real games have more duds
and more big days than it allows, and fixing that would lower these
bets, not raise them. I didn't change it: the box fits it on recent-game
averages but prices off the full projection, so a width tuned here could
make the board worse.

**DE. The bigger lines on every Most Likely pick** (step 162). Your "If we
know a player can do well we should be recommending the higher line bc
obv it would have hit." You chose to keep each pick the likeliest line
and show the bigger ones under it:

- Every player pick on Most Likely has a "Bigger lines" fold under it,
  closed so the phone card stays the same size. Open it for up to three
  bigger lines further out on the same side (50+, 60+, 70+ above a 40+
  pick; lower lines under an under). Each shows its best price across the
  books, our chance, and the price it's worth betting at.
- A line whose price beats our chance by 2% or more (the Pick of the
  Day's own bar) is marked "priced better than its chance" and is always
  listed, even past the first three.
- Left off: long shots (under 20%), lines where our chance and the book's
  own price are more than 10 points apart, and books you can't bet.
- They are never picks: not staked, not journaled. The pick and its
  record don't change. Every sport's board gets them wherever books post
  alternate lines.

Why the pick stays the low line, for the record. Receivers projected
50–60 yards since 2021 (1,080 games) went 40+ in 64% of them, 50+ in
52%, 60+ in 42%, 70+ in 32% and 80+ in 26%. A higher line pays more
because it misses more. It's the better bet only when its price beats its
chance, which is what the mark says.

**DG. Are our carry projections right?** (step 164). Your "yes do the
carry projection check", after Swift carried 22 times on our 15. I replayed
every running back's game in 2025 and 2026 from week 3 (1,625 games), each
projected only from the weeks before it, the way the board builds it:

- No bias to fix. Lead backs land 0.4 carries under projection on average,
  inside the noise, and the projection beats a plain average of a back's
  last three games (3.3 carries off a game against 3.4).
- Nothing left in the spread: lead backs on favourites and underdogs land
  where we put them, so the game-script step is the right size.
- The misses are game flow. A lead back whose team loses by a score or
  more gets 3.4 fewer carries; one whose team wins big, 1.2 more. Swift's
  22 (Bears won by 6) is that, and no number made before kickoff can know.
- The biggest misses are backups starting for a hurt lead back. The live
  board's injury step sees those; the replay can't.

D, built:

- **The referee before kickoff.** Every NFL game report's "Before
  kickoff" names the referee once a source has him: named by hand first,
  then ESPN's game summary, then Football Zebras' weekly assignments
  post (credited). Beside the name are his games since 2024 and the
  league's: penalties a game (the league runs 12.9), how often his games
  went over the closing total, how often home teams covered. The line
  ends with what we measured on 7,340 games: a referee's record adds
  nothing the closing line doesn't already have, so it's context. The
  numbers refit every Tuesday. The first fit is the first command below,
  so tomorrow's reports have them.
- **Grades.** PFF's terms limit its grades to personal, non-commercial
  use, so a page members pay for can't show them; using them would need
  a licence from PFF. Instead, each key player's card in the report has
  **Our grade**: 0–100 against his position this season, from the free
  Next Gen Stats and PFR charting the site already reads. Receivers:
  yards a target, separation, yards after the catch over expected,
  drops. Backs: yards over expected, after contact, broken tackles. QBs:
  completion rate over expected, yards an attempt, bad throws,
  interceptions. Each corner gets a coverage grade. Every part is shown
  with its rank, and the report says once that the grade is ours and
  part of no number. Luther Burden III, through week 6: 68, against 72
  wide receivers.
- **Public betting percentages.** The pages that print these (Action
  Network, VSiN, the books' own) don't offer them for reuse. SharpAPI
  sells them: DraftKings' and Circa's share of the bets and of the money,
  every five minutes. Its docs disagree on whether splits come with the
  free plan or need Pro ($229 a month). Built and **off until you set a
  key**: once set, the report's market section says, for example, "72%
  of the bets and 58% of the money on KC to cover", with Circa's money
  beside it, as context the line already prices. It's paid-only, and
  every reading is kept so fading the public can be measured on our own
  record. To try a free key (sign up at sharpapi.io; the key is typed at
  the prompt, never pasted into a file):


Every fold and flip. Measured first: 42 screen shapes × 10 pages, from the
first Galaxy Fold's 280px cover to a 1920 desktop. Nothing ran off the
screen; the work was making each shape feel built for, the way the Duo's
own apps do (Notes and Messages in two columns when open, MLB's game above
the stats when half folded):

- **Fold, Pixel Fold and OnePlus Open inner screens** get the open Duo's
  desktop view (the sidebar beside the page) instead of the phone's.

  on its side, a Surface Duo, a TriFold, a tablet on its side): tap a
  pick and it opens on the right while Most Likely stays on the left; tap
  another and the right side changes; fold the phone and the pick fills
  the screen.
- **Folded like a book**, the two sides split exactly at the hinge.
- **Flex Mode**, folded like a laptop (a Flip on the table): the page stays
  in the top half and the bottom half is big buttons.
- **Flip and Razr cover screens:** slim bars and icons only, picks first.
  **The narrowest covers** show each pick on two rows, so a name is never
  one word per line.

The hinge comes from the standard fold APIs: Chrome and Edge have them on
Galaxy and Pixel foldables. On your Duo, Safari 27.1 has them behind two
switches. To try the half-folded layouts there, turn on both "Device
Posture API" and "Viewport Segments API" in Settings → Apps → Safari →
Advanced → Feature Flags. Without them, the Duo still gets the open and
folded layouts by shape. On the phone: open Most Likely on the Duo turned
sideways, tap a pick, then fold it.

licensed programme to facilitate wagering, and those buttons open a
sportsbook's bet slip filled in. Either the app build drops them (the
website keeps them) or you apply to the programme, which needs licences.

native feature first (push alerts when a pick settles is the strongest).
US iOS apps may now link to the Stripe checkout (since May 2025).

**DW. The live pages, caught up with the game** (step 180). Your "about
a 45-second delay between what actually happens on the TV compared to
... our app", "the play-by-play, the score, all of it is very delayed".

- **Why it was late.** Measured on the live site that afternoon: the box
  rewrote each game's file every 16.5 seconds (it slept 12, then worked
  4.5), but the score and clock under it were kept for 20 seconds, so
  they only moved on every other write, about every 33 seconds. Then the
  live game page asked for news every 12 seconds, and the Live tab
  answered from a copy kept 30 seconds and only asked again every 30.
  Added up, our own part could reach most of a minute.
- **On the box.** The score loops (NFL, college, NBA, WNBA, NHL and MLB)
  now sleep 5 seconds between passes while a game is on, and every cache
  under them is shorter than that, so each pass reads ESPN (and MLB's
  feed) fresh: the scoreboard, each game's plays, baseball's pitches and
  hockey's rink. A pass fetches up to four games' plays at once instead
  of one after another, so a full Sunday slate doesn't slow the pass. A
  fresh file about every 8 to 10 seconds while a game is on. Nothing
  changes when no game is on, and none of it costs odds credits.
- **On the page.** The live game page asks every 5 seconds and the Live
  tab every 5 seconds while a game is in progress. When nothing has
  changed the server answers "not modified" with no download, and the
  page doesn't redraw, so it doesn't jump under your thumb. The live game
  page had also been polling twice as often as it meant to (two timers
  running side by side); it runs one now.
- **What's left.** Our part is now about 8 seconds typical and under 20
  at worst. ESPN's own feed is what we read, so the site can't run ahead
  of ESPN's gamecast; and a streamed broadcast often runs behind live
  itself.
- **The Record, one more fold.** On the live NFL record the verdict still
  repeated two things the same screen already said: the "Combined with
  the Most Likely board" line under the Combined card at the top, and the
  Most Likely sentence ("We said 62%, they hit 62% ...") above the Most
  Likely section that leads with it. Each now prints once; the verdict
  keeps its copy when the other one isn't on the page (a window cut to
  the last N days, or no Most Likely rows).

around** (step 181). Your "an app that is better than ESPN ... live chats
on each game for the play-by-plays", "The other app ... is called Reel"
(it's Real, realapp.com), and "make the website free, but the only free

give away any picks or props", with your four answers that day.

- **A chat in every game.** Every live game page (football, college,
  baseball, basketball, hockey) has a Chat button; it opens the game's
  room over the page with the score pinned on top. Anyone can read it.
  Posting, reacting and voting need a free account: a username, an email
  and a password, no card. A message can carry the bet you're on, typed
  by you (player, market, side, line, price, book) and drawn as a ticket.
  The rules show once, and so does a pill when new messages land below

- **Every play has its own thread, like Real.** Each play in the
  play-by-play has a speech-bubble button with its comment count; tapping
  it opens that play's thread. Big plays (scores, turnovers, home runs,

  after that) and three seconds between messages; the profanity filter
  the feed uses; blocking hides someone in every room; three reports hide
  a message until you look at it (the same moderation door as the feed);
  you can hide any message. Rooms keep 14 days.

**DZ. Referral codes: $6.25 off for both sides** (step 183). Your "users,
when they have a paid account, they should be given a referral code ...
the new user would get 25% off 1 month, and then the person that referred
them would get 25% off their next month."

- **Why $6.25 and not "25%".** A quarter of the $25 month is $6.25, and
  both sides get it as that amount on every plan. The three plans are one
  Stripe product, so a 25%-off coupon on the yearly plan would take 25%
  off $225 ($56.25) for a referral meant to cost $6.25.
- **The member's side.** Every paying member gets a code (Settings →
  Membership → Invite friends) with a link that carries it
  (`qellysbook.com/?ref=CODE`), Share and Copy buttons, and how it's gone:
  joined, paid, credited. When a friend's membership goes active (their
  first real payment; a trial doesn't count), $6.25 goes on the member's
  Stripe balance, and Stripe takes it off their next invoice. Several
  friends stack, with no limit. If the member isn't paying at that moment,
  the credit waits until they are.
- **The new member's side.** The code rides in on the link, or goes in the
  sign-up's optional "Friend's referral code" box, or into Invite friends
  later before their first plan. Their checkout then carries a $6.25
  coupon (Stripe makes it the first time it's needed), on top of the
  3-day trial when the plan has one. The plans page tells them it's
  coming.
- **What it refuses.** Your own code, a second code on one account, and a
  code after an account has ever subscribed. Stripe idempotency keys mean
  a repeated webhook can't pay the same friend twice. One person with two
  email addresses can't be stopped without keeping card details, which
  the Privacy Policy says we don't do, and it doesn't pay: the second
  account spends $18.75 to earn $6.25.
- **The legal pages caught up.** The Terms gained §5.10 (referral credits:
  no cash value, one per account, can be ended for new referrals). The
  Privacy Policy now names everything an account can hold. It had been
  missing the Feed, friends and messages, phone alerts, the two emails
  and the game chat; now they're all listed, with who sees each and how
  long it's kept. Deleting an account now also removes its chat messages,
  its own alert rows and its referrals. "Download my data" includes its
  chat messages and referral code. A test now fails if a new table
  holding someone's data ships without the policy naming it.

Nothing to install, and no new keys. The Stripe secret key that's already
set makes the coupon and the credits. Read-only, any time:

```
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://qellysbook.com/api/account/referral
```

**EC. Sign up with a phone number, like Real** (step 186). Your "you can
either make an account with an email or a phone number. So we should add
that option as well."

- **What it does.** Sign-up gets "Use your phone number instead":
  username, mobile number, then "Text me a code", the code, and Create
  account (with the referral box and the 21+ box like the email form).
  The sign-in card gets "Sign in with your phone number". A phone account
  has no password; it signs in by a texted code each time. Settings shows
  the number instead of an email.
- **It's off until you switch it on.** It needs a Twilio account with a
  Verify service. Twilio texts and checks the code, so the code never
  touches our server. Until the three values below are set, nobody sees
  the phone option.
- **Cost, and the fences on it.** Twilio Verify charges per successful
  verification plus the carrier's text fee, about 5 to 6 cents a sign-in
  in the US (check Twilio's pricing page for today's number). An open
  "text this number" button is how SMS-pumping fraud runs up a bill, so
  it only texts US and Canadian numbers, at most 3 codes to one number
  and 6 from one address an hour, and Twilio's own Fraud Guard sits
  behind that.
- **Privacy.** The policy now says a phone account keeps its number for
  signing in and nothing else, and that Twilio receives the number to
  text the code. Nothing is ever emailed to a phone account.

To switch it on: in Twilio's console make a Verify service (Verify →
Services → Create, any name), then put the three values on the box. Each
is typed at the prompt, never pasted into a file. Then restart:

```
cd /srv/qellys && sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID
cd /srv/qellys && sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN
cd /srv/qellys && sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh TWILIO_VERIFY_SID
sudo systemctl restart qellys
```

Read-only, any time:

```
curl -s https://qellysbook.com/api/account/me | grep -o '"phone_signup": [a-z]*'
```

It prints `"phone_signup": false` until the three values are set and the
site restarted, and `"phone_signup": true` after. Then on your phone, in a
private tab: sign up with "Use your phone number instead" and your own
number.

**Which value is which** (2026-10-26: the Account SID went into the Verify
slot too). The Account SID starts with `AC` and sits on the console's home
page with the Auth Token beside it. The Verify SID starts with `VA`: in
the console, Verify → Services → the service you made → **Service SID**.
A value of the wrong shape now keeps the phone option off rather than
showing a button that fails, and this names any value that is missing or
the wrong shape (it never prints a value):

```
cd /srv/qellys && sudo python3 -m engine.smsverify --check
```

To put the right one in (it replaces the old value), then restart:

```
cd /srv/qellys && sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh TWILIO_VERIFY_SID
sudo systemctl restart qellys
```

sign-up carries on; the phone option stays hidden until you set it up.

**It needs a paid Twilio account** (2026-10-27: a free trial shows only
the Account SID, the Auth Token and an API key, no Verify service). A
trial only texts codes to numbers its owner verified, five at most, and
Twilio offers the Verify service once the account is upgraded (a card, a
starting balance and a business profile Twilio approves). Until then the
phone option stays hidden and email sign-up carries on; the check above
says where the `VA…` value comes from. The API key is not needed: the
site signs its requests with the Account SID and the Auth Token.

(step 197). Your two reports:

- **"The buttons to get to the game chat glitch out and throw errors."**
  Two causes, both fixed. Step 196's members strip on Live named its loader
  `mbLoad`, which is My Bets' own loader's name; once the chat loaded, it
  replaced My Bets' — so opening the chat threw an error and drew half a
  sheet, and My Bets broke with it. And the chat card under the scoreboard

**FA. Start A or B?** (step 209). The question every manager asks every
week, "who do I start?", had no tool: each player's week was its own row.
Fantasy → This week now opens on a "Start A or B?" card. Type two to four
names (or a defense), or tap them from your roster once your league is
linked, and pick PPR, half or standard. It answers:

- **The call**: who to start, and how often he outscores each of the
  others (from the same projection and measured spread the league desk
  uses for your win chance).
- **The clock**: a questionable player is decided about 90 minutes before
  his own kickoff, when his team names its inactives, and everyone locks
  at his own kickoff. If the questionable one plays first, it says "Wait
  on him: active, start him; out, start the other." If he plays after the
  other, it says the other locks first, so the call is on his chance to
  play, and to keep a later-game bench player ready.
- **Floor and ceiling** when the points are close: who is the safer start
  (favoured this week? take him) and who has the bigger week in him (the
  underdog? take him). With your league linked it says which you are.

Free accounts get all of that; members also see each player's stat line,
touchdown chance and the reason behind his number. Ask answers "Should I
start X or Y?" with the same call.

Fantasy once, so your league desk loads: that is how the site learns which
Sleeper league is yours. Every fifteen minutes the box reads the lineup you

list names the replacement. Quiet hours (11pm to 9am Eastern) hold it to
the morning. The alert names the player and his designation (both public)
and never a projection.

your Sleeper user ID (to read the lineup you set). Turning it off deletes
them within fifteen minutes; deleting your account deletes them at once.

  rebound, 1.5 an assist, 2 a steal or a block, −0.5 a turnover; hockey 8.5
  a goal, 5 an assist, 1.5 a shot on goal, 1.3 a blocked shot. Bonuses
  (double-doubles, hat tricks) are not counted, and goalies are left out:
  their wins and goals against are not projected.
- **Each part** is the board's own projection; a stat the board does not
  price is the player's season average (steadied by last season's early
  on) and drawn dim. A player listed out is left out.
- **Free and paid:** the points are free; the stat line under them is the
  members', like the football week.

ESPN's player photos (the NBA's, the WNBA's, college's, the UFC's, and the
NFL's whenever nflverse has none) are wider than they are tall, and the
site asked ESPN's image resizer for squares. The resizer stretches a photo
to the size it is asked for instead of cropping it, so every face it sent
back was squeezed to about three quarters of its width, in every frame.
Now each photo is asked for in its own shape, and the round and square
frames crop it, so faces look right everywhere. MLB's photos come from
MLB's own server and were already cropped properly. The box's photo check
(photocheck.py) asks for the same sizes the page does.

**GJ. Karma: levels and badges for watching and talking** (step 244).
Your message: "diving back to the Real app there's a feature at hand where
they give you karma for viewing live games and talking and chatting … a
level up feature and you can get badges … see what other apps do like that
as well then implement features like that."

What Real does, from its own help pages: karma for each live game you open
while it's on, for the day's first comment and reaction, and for polls
called right; badges by amount (karma reached, live games watched, upvotes
on your comments, polls won); perks at karma milestones; daily, weekly,
monthly and season leaderboards with trophies; a daily streak. What the
others add: Twitch pays points for every five minutes watched and fills a
Hype Train when a chat goes off together; Duolingo has three daily quests,
a streak that one missed day freezes instead of breaking, and a weekly
league; Reddit's karma is the upvotes your words get; Discord's level bots
pay a message only once a minute, so spam levels nobody.

What's built, for every account, free ones too:

* Karma for watching (+10 for each live game you open while it's on, +2
  every five minutes watched, +5 for being there when a big play posts),
  talking (+10 for the day's first chat message, +2 a message after, one a
  minute; +1 for each person who reacts to yours; +5 the first time a day
  you react), the free games (+5 for voting who wins and +10 when your side
  wins, +5 for each Call it call and trivia answer right, +25 for five calls
  right in a row), showing up (+5 a day, three daily quests at +10 each and
  +20 for all three, bonuses at 3, 7, 14, 30 … 365 days in a row, with one
  missed day forgiven after seven), and friends (+15 when a friend joins
  your watch party, +5 for joining one, +5 for each of your first ten teams
  or players followed, +100 when a friend you invited becomes a member).
  Each kind has a daily limit, the same thing never pays twice, and a
  message hidden for everyone gives back what it earned.
* Levels, quick at first and slower later (level 10 is about a month of
  most nights; level 40 is a long road), with a tier every few levels:
  Rookie, Starter, Pro, All-Star, MVP, Hall of Famer, Legend. Level 3
  unlocks a flair emoji worn beside your name in the chats, level 10 makes
  your level badge shine, level 20 puts a glow round your picture.
* Sixteen badges in tiers from Bronze up (live games watched, chat
  messages, reactions earned, Call it right and in a row, trivia, winners
  picked, days in a row, leagues watched, big plays seen live, watch
  parties, friends brought in, weeks in the top ten, karma), plus Founding
  fan (an account made this year) and Night owl.
* A weekly karma ladder (and an all-time one); the week's top ten take a
  trophy and its karma on Monday. "Show me on the karma ladders" takes a
  name off them.
* The room's heat in every game chat: when three or more people are going
  back and forth, a meter fills through five levels, and everyone in it
  earns karma as it climbs.
* Where it shows: your level and flair beside your name in every chat; a
  strip on the Live tab with your level, the way to the next and the day's
  quests; a Karma tab on your profile page with everything; the level and
  best badges on every profile; a "+10" note when something earns it and a
  celebration when you level up.
* Never for money or bets: nothing pays for a bet logged, tracked or
  placed, a sportsbook opened, a parlay built or a plan bought, and karma
  buys nothing. The Privacy Policy names the new tables; an account's
  karma is exported and deleted with it.
* Everything since the chat opened counts: the first page to show karma
  works through the chats' last two weeks, every Call it call, the trivia
  answers, the votes, the watch parties, the follows and the friends who
  became members, by the same rules and limits.

**HN. NBA Most Likely stops leaning under** (step 274; your words: "almost
ever nba most likely bet is an under bet so that seems wrong and we need
to work on that and calibrate that more"). You were right, and it was a
bug in the minutes, not the market. Every NBA projection is minutes times
a per-minute rate, and the minutes start from a weighted average of his
recent games. Tonight's blowout risk and back-to-back were then taken off
that average, but the average already held his own blowouts and
back-to-backs, so they were counted twice, and only ever downward. A
starter on an even team read about 2% light; one on a team favoured most
nights (the Thunder, the Celtics) about 7% light. Most Likely picks the
likeliest number near −250, where a few percent of a player's average is
several points of chance, so the under won nearly every seat.

Now each haircut is measured against what his own last twenty games
carried (their final margins and their rest, read off the results we
store): a bigger spread than his usual still costs minutes, an extra
day's rest still adds, but on average the projection sits on his own
level, which is what the replay the board is calibrated on assumes. The
scoring-environment adjustment got the same treatment: tonight's total is
read against the league's real recent average instead of a fixed 225.

graded NBA Most Likely picks by side (how often each hit against how
often we said); and whether the minutes base runs light this early in
the season, when a player's last twenty games are mostly last season's
final weeks. That last one decides the next change.

**HP. Every NBA alternate line meets the market** (step 276; "Ok keep
going"). The alternate lines (the "15+ points, 20+ points" ladders) are
often quoted one way only, over. A line quoted both ways was always pulled
toward its own price before Most Likely ranked it; a one-way line carried
the model's raw number. So with the model running a little low, every over
on those ladders read below the market's view and missed the 55% floor,
which handed the unders more seats; running high, those overs would have
taken seats on numbers nothing had checked. Now a one-way line is checked
against the main line: its price, vig out, is read as the player's
average, that average prices the rung, and the model is pulled toward it
at the same weight as every other line. A rung where the two are far
apart is dropped, as a main line would be.

The report had a bug of its own, caught before you ran it: it read the
public copy of the board, which has the picks taken out, so it would have
said there were no NBA picks. It reads the full copy now, and adds one
line: how many of tonight's alternate lines are one way.

**HQ. The NBA board checks itself against the sharp book** (step 277;
"think like a pro sports better ... use the data and resources we have").
Pinnacle is the book the betting world treats as the market's best guess:
it takes big bets from sharp players and moves its number when they hit
it, so its price with the vig taken out is the best single estimate of a
prop's real chance. The NFL board already prices props against it first.
The NBA board pulled Pinnacle's prices in the same odds call and threw
them away, so its "market" was the best over and the best under across
the other books: a pair no single book offers, set by whichever book is
slowest to move.

Now, when Pinnacle prices a prop, its number is the market: the side, the
model check and the edge are all read against it (a Pinnacle line a point
or two away is converted through the same curve the model uses), while
the price you take is still the best one at a book you can bet. The same
on any alternate line Pinnacle prices both ways. The card says so
("Market: Pinnacle's price, vig out — 52% over (the other books' best
prices say 49%)"). Where Pinnacle has no price, nothing changes.

Nothing to set, and no extra odds credits: Pinnacle was already in the

props Pinnacle priced tonight and how far the other books sat from it:

**HW. Your members' own activity, what each one is worth together, and
"while you were away"** (step 283; you: "we can be recording what users do
on the app, how long they spend on it, and we can base notifications off
that"). The research and the full list are docs/RETENTION.md §6. In short:

- **What it keeps, per member, a row a day:** time with the site in front
  of them, which pages and leagues, what hour, how many visits and how many
  an alert opened. Never clicks, typing, location, device or other apps.
  Kept 120 days, deleted with the account, in their export — and **only for
  a member who says yes** (Settings → Your activity, or the unticked box on
  the "Make it yours" card on their second visit; your second paper:
  "nothing fires before consent"). Each yes and no is in the consent log
  with the policy's date; no deletes everything kept.
- **What it does with it:** stages (new, power, regular, casual, lapsing,
  dormant, gone — "lapsing" measured against each member's own rhythm, so a
  Sunday-only fan isn't "drifting" on Friday); a proper "still around?"
  model (BG/BB, the textbook one) fitted on your own members and kept only
  if it beats the stages on members it never saw; your report with
  **revenue at risk**, the power-user curve, cohorts, churn and lifetime
  value; "While you were away", one alert a week at most at the member's
  own usual hour (their team's game today, else what's new since they
  left, else their league's slate), stopping after three unanswered; and
  fewer "picks up" / "last night" alerts to phones that never open them.

  narrower than about 1,520 and 1,440 pixels (both are on the page

- **Under the Duo's clock:** not possible for a web page, and the limit is
  Apple's. WebKit's notes for Safari 27.1 say web content on the iPhone
  Duo does not extend behind the system's side controls, and that Safari
  fills that space with the page's background colour. Your screenshot
  showed exactly that: the strip under your clock was the site's own
  colour (12, 11, 9), painted by iOS, and the page ended at its edge, 910
  of the screen's 1,000 points. The App Store app built in Xcode for iOS
  27.1 can: iOS hands it the strip, and the shell in deploy/ios passes it
  to the page (`contentInset: never`). That build needs a Mac with Xcode
  (deploy/ios/README.md), and the Apple Developer Program ($99 a year) for
  TestFlight and the App Store. With the sidebar back on the open Duo
  there is no bar beside the clock any more.

- **A NO BET day names the board's best bet.** Measured first, from the

  and across the leagues it named a pick on about 10 of the last 14 days.
  Your NBA card said NO BET while the NBA board staked 66 bets. Now, on a
  day the Pick of the Day sits out but the board has staked bets, the card
  says NO PICK TODAY and names the board's own strongest staked bet still
  to play: today's games first, then the biggest stake, then the edge.
  It's never the lean the day's bar turned down. Members only, paid like
  the card. A day with nothing staked still says NO BET.
- **How often it names one, on the record.** The card's record line now
  ends "a pick on 5 of the last 9 slates", and the Record page's Pick of

  never today. `potd_report.py --sitout` prints the table on the box.
- **The playoff race** (college football → Playoff race in the menu):
  - the bracket if it started today: the AP Top 25 until the committee's
    first ranking on November 3, then the committee's, with today's
    conference leaders as the champions;
  - every contender's chance to make the twelve, earn a bye, win its
    conference, win it all and win out, and each game it has left at our
    price;
  - this week's games that swing the field, each team's chance either way;
  - the conference tables.
  It uses the 2026 rules: the four Power Four champions and the
  highest-ranked Group of Six team get in automatically, and Notre Dame
  does in the top 12. It's built on every college build, off the same
  ratings the board prices with. The committee's own ranking can't be
  modelled. Our stand-in is written on the page: a team's rating, plus 8
  points for every win above an elite team's record against the same
  schedule, plus 4 for a title.
- **The NBA Cup** (NBA → NBA Cup in the menu): the six groups with point
  differential and points scored, the wild card race, how a tie is broken
  (head-to-head, then differential with overtime counting zero, then
  points), our chance for every team to advance, reach the final and win
  the Cup, and each group game left at our price and margin. Group play
  starts tomorrow, October 30. It's built on every NBA build.

  load the first time they open, which paid for all of this; the budget
  went from 388 to 386 KB.

```
python3 - <<'PY'
import json, urllib.error, urllib.parse, urllib.request
def get(path, **q):
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(f"http://127.0.0.1:8000{path}?{urllib.parse.urlencode(q)}", timeout=90) as r:
            return r.status, json.load(r)
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        return e.code, {}
for sport, team in (("nfl", "GB"), ("cfb", "Alabama"), ("nba", "BOS"), ("wnba", "NY"), ("nhl", "BOS"), ("mlb", "LAD")):
    st, d = get("/api/team", sport=sport, team=team, only="schedule")
    if d.get("resolved"):
        st, d = get("/api/team", sport=sport, team=d["resolved"][0]["team"], only="schedule")
    played = [g for g in ((d.get("schedule") or {}).get("games") or []) if g.get("final")]
    if not played:
        print(sport, team, "- no finals on the box for this team"); continue
    g = played[-1]
    st, doc = get("/api/game", league=sport, date=str(g.get("date") or g.get("period") or "")[:10], home=g["home"], away=g["away"], game_id=g.get("game_id") or "")
    lv = doc.get("live") or {}
    print(sport, g["away"], "@", g["home"], g.get("date"), "->", st, doc.get("event_id"), lv.get("state"), lv.get("away_score"), "-", lv.get("home_score"), "| plays", len(doc.get("plays") or []), "| drives", len(doc.get("drives") or []), "| box", bool(doc.get("box")))
PY
```

  before Sunday came. Now it buys the one game (about 50).

Under pressure card picks each game's favourite, so its favourite and underdog rates counted every road favourite as

him. The reports never said it in one place. Now each NFL report's injury section has a "Who steps up" part for a

(while the player out played in one of the team's last three games, whatever list he is on: Nacua and Adams went
on injured reserve on 22 November, which our numbers count as out): the share to fill, who took
the targets or carries in this season's games without them (each teammate's number a game then against with
them), which picks our numbers raise for it and by how much, and a read on each teammate named, graded after the
game on his targets (carries, for a back) against his own average. Those reads are their own group, "Who steps
up", on the report's summary, on Report Picks' totals and on the Record. A read is made only where a step up was
measured: the out player's own position, and a tight end once a third of the targets are gone. Measured the same
day and not added to the numbers: the tight end in that case caught 12% more (± 7%, 155 games, three seasons of
four), just short of our bar, so the report says it and nothing is priced on it; two receivers ahead of a player
out at once (×1.31 ± .23, 24 games) is too thin; the fourth and fifth receivers already carry it in their own form
(×0.96 to ×1.17); a back gets no more targets when receivers sit. Every journaled pick now keeps the teammate lift
it was priced with (`bets.mate_mult`), and the Record's Calibration tab says how those picks have done by book,
raised for a teammate out and lowered for one back, from 25 November on. The heartbeat's NFL board counts the
teams, the reads and the moved picks (`stepup`).

**AEE. Picks "bolder than the books" go on paper by their own record, and short weeks were measured** (step
922; 24 November). Nothing to run. You asked for more that changes which bets get picked. The board's own record,

overs hit 63.3% where we said 63.5%, and without the bold picks the NFL board hits 58.2% against 59.0% claimed. A
bold pick 15 or more points over was already on paper (since 15 November), but one 10 to 15 over still posted, and
the correction that pulls picks toward their price cannot go below the price, while the NFL's bold overs hit below
theirs. So the paper hold (engine/paperhold, your rule of 15 November: record, don't post, until they run honest)
now tests "every league's bold picks" as a kind of its own, on the same bar as every other kind, and holds them
when they run hot; they come back by themselves once 30 held since run within five points of what we said. Held
bold picks keep being journaled in the bold book, so the record keeps measuring them. The heartbeat's paper-hold
line names the kind when it is on. Also measured today, and nothing changed because nothing cleared the bar:
short weeks. Since 2006, games with both teams on short rest went 135 to 132 to the under against the closing
total (the score landed 0.3 points over it), and on 2022 to 2025 players on short rest produced what their own
form said (passing and receivers' targets a few percent above, rushing a couple below, none two standard errors
out). So Thanksgiving week's totals and props carry no rest adjustment.

67.8%, and those under 65% hit 60.6% where we showed 57.0%). Nearly every one was an alternate-line rung far from
the main line: a back over 0.5 catches, a quarterback over 3.5 rushing yards, a kicker over 0.5 field goals or
under 10.5 kicking points, shown at 80% to 99.9% while its own price said 55% to 70%. The cap (step AAV, decision
17: at most ten points over the price) went live on 21 November, but week 12's Sunday picks were posted from 17 to
20 November, and a posted pick keeps the chance it went up at (engine/likelyboard.harmonize), so they kept their
pre-cap chances. Week 13 is the first week posted under the cap. Before it, picks this far over their price hit 47%
(65 of 137), below their own price's chance as well as ours, so the cap may still show them too high; that is

**AEM. Every college basketball game gets a report, and your three decisions** (step 929; 24 November). Nothing
to run. Your answers that evening: "Decisions: A, yes more B, we always want every sport posting props and bets and
game reports at all times for every games so we learn and dial in and calibrate and all that shit too make our picks
better. C, like u said not a problem."

- **B, reports for every game.** That evening every league with games wrote a report for every one of them (the NFL 16
  of 16, college football 2 of 2, the NBA 3 of 3, the NHL 1 of 1) except college basketball, which wrote one for the 5
  games it prices: 7 reports for 87 games. Now every college basketball game still to tip gets one. A game we price
  players for reads as before. Every other game's report reads the two teams (the tale of the tape and its key
  matchups) and the betting market, and its facts say "Players: not read for this game" and why. Its key matchups
  are graded on the box score once the game is final, as every report's are (How our reports did), so every game
  now adds to what our reads are measured on. A game already under way when first seen gets no report: written after
  the tip, it would not be a pregame call. The heartbeat counts these reports (`reports_teams_only`).
- **B, the NFL cap.** Kept, and those picks stay posted and graded; none goes to paper. The 1 December check still
  measures week 13, and I'll bring you the numbers.
- **C.** No licensed scores feed; ESPN's free feed stays.
- **A, what more college games cost.** By the odds plan's own price table (a model, not yet the API's measured bill):
  college basketball spends about 315 credits a game day now (three pulls of 5 games at 13 credits a game, plus the
  game lines and the live line), about 9,800 over a 31-day month. 10 games a pull would be about 15,800 a month
  (6,000 more); 15 games about 21,900 (12,100 more). Every game of a night like this one's 87 would be about 3,500
  credits for that night alone, more than the plan's whole daily average (100,000 a month is 3,333 a day).
  December's plan funds every league's own target and leaves about 1,800 credits over, which go to the NFL's extra
  pulls, so more college basketball games in December mean taking credits from another league or a bigger odds
  plan. College football prices 12 games a pull; on this Saturday's rivalry slate, 20 a pull would cost about 900
  credits more that day, and after Saturday (the conference title games, then the bowls) no college football day
  is likely to reach 12 games, so its cap stops mattering.
- **What the API really bills.** Our table charges 13 credits for a college basketball game whether or not the books
  posted a player prop on it. The heartbeat now carries the API's own bill for each league's game-by-game calls over
  the last day (`odds_bill`: the calls, the credits billed, our estimate, and how many calls billed each amount). If
  a game with no props bills less than the table says, more college games cost less than the numbers above, and the
  next step is sized from that. Nothing to run: I read it off the heartbeat.

**AIE. The game report learns from your Bears at Lions research** (step 1023; 27 November; nothing to run). You
sent the research you bet Thanksgiving on, which won, and said: "learn from these reports and structure better and
research better for these games". I read it beside our CHI@DET report, section by section.

- **Most of it the report already does.** The market and each team's implied points, who is out and who plays
  instead (the corner who steps in), the units, who covers whom, the red-zone counts, the game scripts with what
  each ticket needs, and the parlay cards with their joint chance, fair price, take-at price and backups. Our
  CHI@DET report went 5 of 6 on its picks and 3 of 3 on its two-leg parlays.
- **New: the touchdown board as one table.** Your board put every scorer on one row: the chance, the fair price,
  the price to take, and the books side by side ("Gibbs −270 at FD/DK, −250 at BetMGM"). The report said each
  scorer in a sentence with one price and one book, so the books could not be compared at a glance. The Red zone
  section now ends with a table of both teams' scorers (up to 10), ranked by our chance: our chance, that chance as
  a fair price, the best price any book posts and where, then FanDuel's and DraftKings' prices (a dash where that
  book posts none). A best price shorter than −250 says "(past −250)", the limit our picks keep. The prices are the
  ones the books had up when the build read them. The sentences above the table stay: they say why, and a finished
  game grades them.
- **New: how tickets that share a leg play together.** Your research: "Swift is on both tickets, so they win
  together. Both win 11% of the time, at least one wins 37%". When two or more of a game's two-leg, three-leg or
  touchdown-pair tickets share one leg, the Parlays section now says how often all of them cash, how often at least
  one does, and that a game without the shared leg loses every one. It treats each ticket's other legs as unrelated
  once the shared leg is in, as the cards' own chances do. Tickets that share two or more legs get no line: that
  arithmetic is different, and a wrong number is worse than none.
- **Measured, then shipped: the backfield-partner split** ("Swift scored in only 2 of the 5 games both were
  active"; "7 of his 10 rushing TDs came in the 4 games without Monangai"). Our touchdown number for a back reads
  the back's recent games whole: its share of the team's work, its red-zone touches and its touchdowns. When the
  partner missed some of those games and plays tonight, all three count games the back had the backfield alone.
  The site already did this for a back's yards and catches (the teammate-back step) and carries (step AHX), but
  never for touchdowns.
  Measured before anything moved:
  - **On play-by-play, 2017-2026:** in 1,420 games where a back's partner (the team's other back with the most
    carries, 20 or more) had missed some of the back's last six games and then played, the back got 86% of the
    red-zone touches its recent share said. With the partner there throughout: 101%. Counted over only the games
    both played: 99%.
  - **Through our own touchdown model, 2022-2025, each season held out:** in those 695 games the backs scored 26.6%
    of the time, and our number said 30.4%. Read over the games both played, it says 28.1%. It was better in three
    of the four seasons, which is the bar the other teammate steps had to clear. The more games the partner had
    missed, the higher our number ran: 3.1 points with one game missed, 5.3 with three or more.
  - **What changed:** an NFL back whose top teammate back is on tonight's slate, isn't ruled out, and missed one or
    more of the back's last six games now has its touchdown chance read over its most recent six games with the
    partner there (at least two of them, or nothing changes). That covers its share, its red-zone touches and this
    season's touchdowns; last season's games stay as they were. The row says so first in its reasons ("Backfield
    partner back: ... so the chance is read over the 5 games both played"). Most Likely, the touchdown picks, the
    game report's scorers and the fantasy chances all read the same number. College isn't measured, so it is left
    alone.
  - **The other way round did not pass.** When the partner is ruled out tonight, our number for the back who plays
    runs low: in 656 such games those backs scored 34.6% and our number said 30.4%. Reading the back's games without
    the partner (where there were two or more) moved it to 31.7%, but its accuracy got worse overall and was better
    in only one of the four seasons. That is the same answer the teammate-absence step got for touchdowns before
    ("too noisy to price"), so it stays shown on the row and not priced.

**AIB. Our reads' record says what an ordinary game does** (step 1020; 26 November; nothing to run). Your Bears at
Lions screenshot read "breakout candidates beat their average 56 of 108 times (52%)". That looks like a coin flip,
and it is not one. I measured it the way the record grades a read: the read's first stat (catches for receivers and
tight ends, rushing yards for backs, passing yards for quarterbacks) against the player's previous games, at most
10, at least 2. The data is public weekly stats for every key player in the 2017-2025 regular seasons, 25,403
games. A key player beats that average in **42%** of ordinary games and falls short in **57%**, and every season
sat between 40% and 44%. The stats are skewed, so the average sits above most games. So:

- breakout candidates (52%) are about ten points better than an ordinary game, and fades (68%) about eleven;
- the record line under Players to watch now says the ordinary game beside ours ("For comparison, a key player in
  an ordinary game beats that average 42% of the time and falls short of it 57% (measured over the 2017–2025
  seasons)"), and so does How our reports did on the Report Picks page (football only; the other leagues are not
  measured yet, so they say nothing of the kind);
- **the angles group is the weak one.** The free record has the angles (a defense's leak pointed at a player) at
  50 of 117 (43%), no better than an ordinary game's 42%. They are explanations and never move a number, but as
  calls they show no lift yet. Worth deciding whether to keep grading them as calls or rework what makes one;
  I have not changed them.

**AIA. A parlay leg or pick against the report's own read says so** (step 1019; 26 November; nothing to run). You:
"keep going harder and working better on the game reports". Bears at Lions' tickets are on the free record, and one
of them took Amon-Ra St. Brown's catches under 7.5 (it won, 7 catches), in the same report that called St. Brown a
good spot and named St. Brown for a big day. The same kind of mixed message your screenshots were about. What I
found, and what changed:

- **Both were ours, and both stay.** A read never moves a number (the scan measured no lift over our model), and the
  Most Likely list already picks the read's side whenever a number on that side clears its bars. So an under on a
  good spot means no over cleared. The Most Likely card already said "matchup read leans the other way" (your
  October rule: "keep 3 with the warning"), but the parlay leg built from it dropped that warning, and so did the
  report's own picks card. Dropping such legs would cost tickets our numbers back, with nothing measured to say they
  lose.
- **Now a leg against its player's read says so on its ticket,** with our projection and which side of the line it
  sits on, in the form "<player> under <line> receptions goes against this report's good spot for <name>: our
  number is <projection> receptions, under the line even so". Where a leg carries no projection, it gives our chance
  instead. A fade (tough matchup, avoid) with an over leg reads the same way. A mixed read leans nowhere, so it says
  nothing. Touchdowns ride their own research and are left out.
- **The report's picks card says it first** when one of its picks goes against that player's read ("This pick goes
  against this report's good spot for St. Brown: ..."), before the reasons.
- **Names keep their particle:** "St. Brown" and "Van Noy", not "Brown" and "Noy" (a first name like Van Jefferson's is
  left alone). This also fixes the plays-or-sits section's title.
- **"No edge either way" says the matchup, not our numbers.** It read "our numbers lean neither way on these
  matchups", which a touchdown pick on the same player contradicts (the pick is our projection's). It now reads "the
  matchup leans neither way for these players ... a pick on any of them comes from our projection, not the matchup".
- **One more count fixed:** the heartbeat's touchdown-pairs short count (`td_short`) read 12 with all 12 games still
  waiting to post, as the two-leg count did; it now leaves a waiting game out too.

in a good spot but then u go to the breakout candidates and who could have a big day and they are no where too be

  the game around them (the points the lines expect, in the board's highest total), not from the Bears' defense.
  Players to watch put those on one list with the good matchups, gave each team only its single best seat, and let
  the stronger cases fill the rest, so at most one Lion could be named there, below the Bears' matchups. The
  big-day line had three seats: two Bears and Jahmyr Gibbs.

  player on the matchup cards with a good read is on one list or the other. Each team's best two are seated before
  the rest fill in. A key player whose read leans neither way is named under "No edge either way", so being left
  off the lists is never mistaken for a fade.

  "the Lions' Jahmyr Gibbs (running back) and Amon-Ra St. Brown (wide receiver) — the lines expect the Lions to

**AHX. The backs step up too: a backup's carries are lifted, and the next back up is read** (step 1016; 26
November; nothing to run). You: "do the same for running backs too". What a back had:

- **His carries were never in the step.** The teammate step lifted a back's rushing yards behind a starter just
  ruled out (×1.66), his catches and his receiving yards, but the fit had never measured carries. So the board
  priced a backup's carries at his own form while raising his yards by two thirds. Measured now on the same four
  seasons (2022-2025) and the same rule as every other cell (two standard errors from 1.0, three seasons of four):

  | the case | carries, snap-ranked (what the board uses) | target-ranked |
  |---|---|---|
  | the back ahead of him just ruled out | ×1.72 (± .12, 99 games, up in every season) | ×1.74 |
  | the back ahead already out | ×1.33 (± .06, 227 games, every season) | ×1.32 |
  | a back below him just out | ×1.07 (3 seasons of 4) | ×1.07 |
  | a back below him already out | ×1.07 (3 seasons of 4) | short of the rule, not applied |

  A teammate back coming back is read for carries too (the deflation test passes, as it does for the yards). The
  test that re-runs the fit on the real box scores and requires our tables to match it passes with them.
- **The next back up had no read.** The scan reads a back with a quarter of his team's carries this season. For
  example (the test's numbers, not a real game), behind a lead back with 60%, a backup with 22% had no read unless a
  book priced him. With a lead back's share sitting, a back's share is now read as his share of the carries left
  (22% becomes 55%), and the read says it.
- **The short version** already says who took the carries in the games without him (step AHW's sentence), and now
  which of our numbers it raises, in the test's example: "our numbers raise Blake Corum's carries ×1.72 for it".

**AHW. When receivers sit, the report names who steps up, reads the next men up, and our numbers lift the room**
(step 1015; 26 November; nothing to run). You, after Packers at Rams: "when there is alot of players out we dont
reccomend any props for the backups ... and dont say anything about them or how there usage could step up". What
the report had: a "Who steps up" block, at the bottom of the injury section. What it lacked:

  receivers by season target share, 12% or more. Konata Mumpfield had 8.7% of the Rams' targets with Puka Nacua
  playing, so he got no read unless a book priced him. With a fresh share sitting, a receiver's share is now read
  as his share of the targets left (Mumpfield 14%), and every read on that team says it ("With Puka Nacua out, 36%
  of LA's targets sit tonight: Konata Mumpfield has taken 9% of them this season, 14% of what is left").
- **Nothing in the short version.** It said who was out and nothing else. It now says, right after: "Who steps up
  for the Rams: without Puka Nacua (36% of the targets this season), in the 3 games this season without Puka
  Nacua, the targets went to Tyler Higbee (7.5 targets a game, 39.5 yards a game; 4 a game otherwise), Konata
  Mumpfield (4.7 targets a game, 62 yards a game; 2.2 a game otherwise) and Kyren Williams (...)". That is the real
  Rams week-12 read, off nflverse's own file.
- **The rest of the room was not in our numbers.** I measured it before touching anything (roomfit.py, ten
  seasons, 2016-2025, each season held out in turn). When a fifth or more of a team's targets sits, the receivers
  left beat our number more often than the same players do in normal games: about 5 to 7 points more for every rank
  at 20-35%, and 9 to 14 points more for the third man on down at 35% or more. As a flat bump on everyone it cut
  no error, because who takes the work changes game to game. It does close the over/under gap for the fourth
  receiver left and after, so only those cells ship (engine/room):
  - 20-35% of the targets out: catches ×1.16, receiving yards ×1.24 (the gap from 6.4 to 3.2 points and from 5.9
    to 3.0, closer in 7 and 8 seasons of 10);
  - 35% or more out: catches ×1.32, yards ×1.42 (from 8.9 to 5.9 and from 9.8 to 3.4, in 8 and 9 of 10).

  The top three left are lifted by the teammate step where it was measured (a receiver behind a man out at his
  position), and not otherwise: their own room numbers came and went by season. The lift rides the same card as
  the teammate step, so the pick's "why" says it, the injury block says which measurement moved each pick, and
  the journal keeps it. The Record's "Who steps up" section counts the room's picks on their own line ("raised for
  the room left"), so whether it wins is on the record from its first graded pick. For the Rams before week 12, Colby Parkinson, Blake Corum
  and Davis Allen take ×1.32 catches and ×1.42 yards; Mumpfield keeps the teammate step's ×1.10. A team throws about
  4% less in those games (×0.96), so this is the room's share of the work, not more passing.
- **Every league's short version says it.** College football says it from its own "Who steps up" block (who
  took the catches in the games the starter had no catch on record), and basketball from its "What the absences
  change" section ("Who steps up for the Heat: in the 6 games Tyler Herro missed this season, Bam Adebayo took 28%
  of the points (23% with Tyler Herro playing) ..."), only where that section has enough missed games to say it.
- **Breakout candidates stay measured.** A breakout still needs a starter's share (18% or more of the targets) and
  two counted reasons. A backup with 9% of the targets now has a read, a counted teammate-out reason where our
  numbers move, and the step-up lines, but not the breakout label. Whether his prop is a pick is the board's call
  on the lifted number against the book's line.

**AHV. College football's stat lines count for the right school, and a night game is filed once** (step 1014; 26
November; two commands, RUN_NEXT 00t). The nightly count (step AFG, heartbeat `cfb_copies`) found 25,028 college stat rows on 25
November that copied a game already on file, eleven days after the 14 November cleanup removed 130,078. The biggest
kind, 17,401 rows, was one game a day apart under the same two teams and the same ESPN number: A'Marion Peterson's
UTSA at Texas on 19 and 20 September. The writer:

- **The mirror dated a game by its UTC day.** One of the two college schedule feeds (the cfbfastR mirror) cut the
  date off the UTC kickoff stamp, so a Saturday night game landed on Sunday, a day after the scoreboard's row of the
  same game. Only the mirror's row names the ESPN number the nightly play file joins its stat lines through, so the
  play file filed every night game again under Sunday, beside the Saturday rows the cleanup kept. It now dates a game
  on its Eastern day, as the scoreboard does.
- **The join takes the earliest day.** Until the old Sunday rows go, the ESPN number now joins the game's Saturday
  row when the pair has one a day or less older. A rematch weeks later is still its own game.
- **The box-score backfill reads each game once.** `ingest.py cfb` read one summary for every games row (twice for a
  night game) and none for a game under an away@home key, which the nightly rekey gives every row. It now reads each
  ESPN number once and files it on the game's earliest day.

  again under its away@home key the next, after the nightly rekey renamed the game's row: Adam Hrynciw's Air Force
  game against UTEP on 20 November sat there twice. The copy is now always filed under the ESPN number.

  November. It still leaves the same name on the two teams of one game (3,325) and on two unrelated games (1,692),
  because those can be two different players.
- **The nightly count says what is new.** `cfb_copies.since` counts the copies of games played since 14 November,
  which can only have been filed since, and `latest` gives each kind's newest example. After the cleanup runs it
  should read close to nothing. `markets` and `zeros` say what is left on the other side of a game.
- **A play counts for the side with the ball. This is the big one.** The count's "other side" kind (3,325 rows)
  named A'Marion Peterson (UTSA) under South Florida, the team he played on 8 October, in the play file's own row.
  I downloaded the mirror's 2026 file and read that game's plays. The feed files a sack, a pass broken up, an
  interception and some plain incompletions once, on a row whose school is the defence, and that row names the
  offence's passer and receiver: Owen McCown's incompletion to Peterson, both UTSA, says South Florida. By each
  name's school on the season's roster, 10,297 of the 197,178 rows that name a player name only the other side's
  players, and 4 mix the two. We read each such play as the defence's, opening a line for the passer and the
  receiver under the wrong school. A stat row's key is the game, the player and the market, with no school, so the
  phantom line and the real one wrote the same row and the last one stood. Run through our own parser, the table
  kept 8,165 of 2026's 9,271 touchdowns, 61,923 of 87,963 pass attempts, 48,340 of 53,342 receptions and 580,595 of
  642,163 receiving yards. Peterson's three touchdowns in that game were stored as 0, and McCown's 31 attempts and
  22 completions as 5 and 0. Last season lost 280 of 6,370 touchdowns and 21,706 pass attempts; 2023 lost 225
  touchdowns. Every college read that counts these was short: the touchdown board's base rates, a passer's attempts,
  a receiver's catches, and what a defence allows. A play now counts for the school its players are on, by the
  roster (`cfbstats.play_side`), in the stat lines and the carry, route and passing charts. A line one ESPN id still
  splits across both schools is joined, and two players of one name stay apart. Re-run on the 2026 file: no line
  under both schools, 26,964 phantom rows gone. This season's rows are rewritten on the next nightly pull. The nightly
  also reads the four seasons before it again, one a night and the newest first, against the games rows already
  stored, so each changed row is rewritten in place (`cfb_copies.reread` on the heartbeat says which are done).

**AGN. The role chart reads the player's own rows, not the league's** (step 982; 25 November; nothing to run).
This is what made Kucherov's role chart take 22.6 s and Soto's 32.8 s. The chart asks the database for the

no statistics for SQLite to plan with, and for that shape of question it chose to walk the table in its own stored
order: every row the league has, to find one player's seasons, and every row of the league's season, to find one
player's games. The more seasons and players a league has stored, the longer it took, which is why baseball was
the worst. Both reads now go straight to the player's own rows by the indexes made for that (the same fix other
parts of the site already use). On 2.6 million hockey rows here the whole chart went from 217 ms to 1 ms, with the
same chart. The other player-page reads I checked already take the player's own rows.
