**AEU. Basketball's team ratings checked against the closing line** (step 937; 25 November). Nothing to run.
Every game report shows our team ratings' own chance beside the price's, marked unproven. The NFL's, college
football's and baseball's are checked against their closing lines every night; basketball's never were. The nightly
check now does college basketball and the NBA too: for every game with a stored price from before the tip, it
rebuilds our ratings from only the games played before that day, the way the report read them, and measures how
much of their disagreement with the closing line held up. The heartbeat shows each one's games, slope and error,
and for the spread how often the ratings' side covered (`chores.settle.phases.last_learned.verdicts`, under "game
lines", `measured`). Nothing changes on any board until a measurement holds: 400 games and a tight enough error,
the bar every league meets. When one holds, the report's "Unproven" line says what was measured. Basketball totals
are not measured, because nothing of ours projects one.

**AET. College basketball's game reports read the college ratings** (step 936; 25 November). Nothing to run. A
college game report's "Our team ratings alone" line, and the slip checker's read of a college ticket, used each
team's plain average margin with last season's beside it: not adjusted for who a team played, so a mid-major that
beat five small schools by twenty read as a top team, and never measured. The Race page already fits the college
ratings that fix that (adjusted for every opponent, measured on four seasons of results: 15,945 games). Each time
the race fits them it now keeps them in a small file, and the reports and the slip checker read that file (up to 36
hours old). The line now says what the ratings were fitted on and that they have not been measured against the
price yet. Where no fit is kept, or a school has not played yet, the old average margins stand.

**AEO–AER, measured on Tuesday night** (24 November, 7:57 PM ET; nothing to run). The college basketball build on

credits to about 660, and January's from about 5,500 to about 4,400. Ten games a pull would be 91% funded in

**AEN. College football's Saturday prices more games for the same credits** (step 930; 24 November). Nothing to

kickoff a game is bought at every pull, as before, and every price is bought again before it passes the six hours a
price stays bettable. Each pull still buys 12 games at most. A cached build now shows every game's last paid price,
not only the top 12's.

- **What it should do, by a simulation of a Saturday** (not yet a measured one): 60 games in four waves, 12 games a

**AEO. Three slow reads of the game logs now read only the season they need** (step 931; 24 November). Nothing to

history file has no statistics for SQLite to plan with, and for these three reads it picked an index with no season
in it, so it walked every stored season's rows to keep one season's. Now each read walks only the season it asks

three reads ran 11, 9 and 2.7 times faster. The box's real times show on the heartbeat after the deploy (the
`logcache` read times and the board's stage times). Each of the three is read once more in full after the deploy,
because its code changed.

**AEP. The comps read this season's rows alone on a game night** (step 932; 24 November). Nothing to run. The

to 11.8 seconds each at 6:46 PM that evening, about 40 seconds of a 416-second build. Each season's part is now kept
on its own, with each player's last ten games carried into the next season, so a night's rows re-read this season
alone and the seasons before come from their kept copies. The comps come out the same, every one, in the same order
(tested against the old whole-history read). On the test history this season's part read in 0.021 seconds where the

**AEQ. The freshness check finds the newest day of stats in a few seeks** (step 933; 24 November). Nothing to run.

**ACZ. A breakout candidate is never one our own pick bets against** (step 891; 23 November). Nothing to run. You

number takes Under 25.5 points (−130, 61%) — so neither way"), and it is off the breakout and fade lists and the
short version. The pick itself stays as it was. Every league whose reports carry our picks on their reads (the NFL,
college football, the NBA, the WNBA, college basketball and baseball) goes through the same step; hockey's reads
never carried them.

**Decision 20, answered: college football's injuries** (23 November; answered the same day). Our college injury feed
is ESPN's college board. On Monday afternoon it listed 1 college football injury and no college basketball ones,
against the NFL's 797, because schools owe ESPN nothing. College football teams do publish availability reports for
conference games now, through their conferences: the Big Ten requires four a week for 2026, and the SEC, ACC and Big
12 publish theirs too; the College Football Playoff posts its teams' reports for playoff games. There is no single
feed: each conference posts its own page in its own format. Reading them would put a missing quarterback or running
back into college picks and reports the way the NFL's inactives are. Those sites can't be reached from where I
build, so I would write a reader for each conference, run it on the box, and check it against a Saturday's published
reports before it changes any pick. Your answer: "decision 20 is a yes if it helps and get us more up to date info
for the users". Being built from step ADA.

**ACY. Every league says "spot" when the opponent didn't decide it** (step 890; 23 November). Nothing to run. Last
step made a football verdict that the defense had no say in read "Tough spot" or "Favorable spot" instead of "Tough
matchup". The NBA's, the WNBA's, college basketball's, hockey's and baseball's reads still said "Tough matchup" when
only the schedule, a blowout spread, the points the lines expect or the player's own role put it there. They now
follow the same rule: a verdict that nothing about the opponent carried (its defense, the goalie, the starting
pitcher and his hand against the hitter, how many power plays it gives up) says "Good spot" or "Tough spot" ("Avoid"
keeps its word) on the report cards, the Players to watch lists and the picks' cards. A verdict the opponent did
carry still says "matchup". Which way each verdict leans and every pick stay as they were; only the word changes.

**ACX. The NBA's chances say what its picks win** (step 889; 23 November). Nothing to run. Your answer to decision
19: "do whatever you think. All I want is picks that win the most on there, and we need to be truthful about our
shit." Built as proposed. In the NBA, and in hockey only if its own record shows the same, a Most Likely pick where
our number and the price both put its side above 50% now shows the chance picks like it have actually won, worked
out from the graded record for its maker (the list, the matchup picks, the bold picks), overs and unders together,
once a maker has 200 such graded picks. One fit with the same weight on both numbers matches both sides of the NBA's
list: at each side's average numbers it gives 65.8% for the overs and 63.8% for the unders, where they won 65.4% and
64.2%. That can put a chance above both numbers, and it can lower one where agreeing picks at that level won less
than we said. It goes on only after it beats the number the site shows today on games the fit never saw (five splits
by game, the bottom of its 95% range above zero), the same bar as every other correction; until then nothing
changes, and it comes off by itself the first time it stops passing. Whether and when it goes on is the record's
call, and it may take more graded games: on made-up records the NBA's size (3,450 picks over 468 games) where
agreeing picks won 2 to 3 points more than the higher of the two numbers, it passed in 3 of 8 tries, and on ones
where the picks won their own number it passed in none. Previewed on the public receipts of every graded NBA pick
through 22 November (3,450, rebuilt the way the box reads them; the correction we have scores the same there as on
the box), it predicted games it never saw better than the number the site shows, and by more than the correction we
have (a gain of 0.0026 against 0.0019), but the bottom of its range is still just under zero (−0.0003), so it does
not go on today. About a hundred NBA picks are graded a day, and the record is asked again each time. Hockey's falls
further short (−0.0013), so hockey stays as it is. It is refitted with the rest of the board's learning, at most
every three hours once new picks are graded. The card says why, in the form "Most Likely list picks where our number
and the price agree have hit X% of N where we said Y% and the price (its cut taken out) Z%, so this shows W%". The
honest chance sets the tier a pick earns and its place in the order; the list keeps the same picks, and parlay legs
stay held to the book's own chance as before. While building it I found that a pick the record raises toward its
price (your yes to 8 on 21 November) was read as one the record had caught over-claiming, so an NBA pick just raised
would be held off the board whenever the matchup read leaned the other way. A raised pick is never held for that
now. The Record page's "Where Most Likely wins and loses" shows what agreeing picks have won and whether the
correction is on. Switch: `QB_RECORD_AGREE=off`.

**ACW. A matchup verdict never argues with the numbers beside it** (step 888; 23 November). Nothing to run. You saw
it on tonight's Bengals at Commanders report: the Bengals give up 76 receiving yards and 6.2 catches a game to tight
ends, 2nd-most in the league, and the report still called the Commanders' tight end a tough matchup. Rebuilt from
this season's box scores, here is what happened. A receiver's or tight end's verdict counts how many passing yards
the defense allows overall, because that is the number that has predicted their games. Re-tested this morning on
2022 to 2025, each season held out, it improved predictions of tight ends' yards and catches (+0.15% and +0.40%),
while what a defense allowed to tight ends themselves made them slightly worse (-0.12% and -0.17%); receivers came
out the same way. The Bengals are 15th in passing yards allowed, dead middle, so the defense had no vote, and the
verdict leaned tough on the forecast 9 mph wind alone, which takes about 3% off receiving yards. Three changes. (1)
A verdict that points against what the defense gives up to the player's own position, in the top or bottom quarter
of the league, now reads "Neutral — mixed": it names both numbers, leans neither way, and makes no matchup pick or
"hard day" headline. (2) A verdict the defense had no say in is called a spot, "Tough spot" or "Favorable spot",
with its reason first, instead of "UNFAVORABLE" under "vs CIN's coverage"; the defense's own number is said on the
card. (3) Under "Where the defense is weakest" the report now says which number our receiver and tight end
projections read and why. Tonight the Commanders' tight end reads mixed. The numbers themselves are this season's,
through last week.

**ACV. A season's averages read the games that have each number** (step 887; 23 November). Nothing to run. The
Monday-morning check of the WNBA's nightly re-read found A'ja Wilson's 2026 line reading 3PT "0.9-0.8" and 3P% 113.2
over 48 games. The re-read fills a season newest first, forty game days a night, and her September and October games
now carry every column. Her older games still carry only what was kept then: points, rebounds, assists and made
threes, with no attempts, steals, blocks or turnovers. The page divided every column by all 48 games, so made threes
came from every game and attempts from a few. Now every league's season lines, game-log averages and headline
numbers divide each number by the games that have it, and a percentage or a made-attempted reads only the games with
both. A column no game has both halves of shows a dash, not a wrong number. A season whose games all carry every
column reads exactly as before. Until the re-read reaches her May to August games, those averages come from the
games read so far.

**ACQ. A tab you just tapped stays readable** (step 882; 22 November). Nothing to run. On a phone, the sub-tab you
had just tapped (Report Picks' SGPX parlays or Record, and every other row of sub-tabs) turned a faint grey with

**ACP. Sunday night's inactives, and the board asked fresh** (step 881; 22 November). Nothing to run. The watcher's
first whole window, Vikings at 49ers. The Vikings' five inactives carry ESPN's filing stamp of 7:00 PM ET and the

whole list (six or seven). So the board is the complete list but slow, and the question is whether ESPN's board
itself is slow or only a copy of it on the way. The watcher now also asks the board's own page with an address of

**Decision 19, answered: NBA chances that say less than they win** (22 November; answered 23 November). The NBA's
Most Likely picks win more often than they say. Over 3,371 graded picks the board said 61.2% and won 64.2%. The
list's overs said 61.3% and won 65.5% (1,375 picks); its unders said 61.8% and won 64.3% (1,711). Both gaps are past
chance (the Record's "beats its claim"). The chance the site actually shows, after the record's own correction,
tells the same story: 61.6% shown and 64.8% won over 3,085 picks, and on the picks shown at 45 to 60%, 57.2% shown
and 62.4% won (1,311). The NFL's (62.3% shown, 61.9% won), college's and hockey's shown chances match their results.
Your yes to (8) on 21 November lets the record raise an NBA pick toward its price, never past it, and that can't
reach these picks. On the unders the price says less than we do (59.4%), so there is nothing to raise toward. On the
overs the price (63.0%) is still under what they won, and that raise, tried on held-out games, gained too little to
pass the bar. Why it happens: the NBA's numbers are tuned toward 50% by a fit on 25,000 to 29,000 past games a
market, most of them priced against each player's recent average as a stand-in line, not a sportsbook's. Football
had the same problem and now tunes against real lines. Simply un-tuning the NBA would be wrong, though: the NBA's
Edge bets, where we disagree with the price, said 51.2% and won 48.3% (451 bets), so the model is already too sure
there. When our number and the price agree on a side, the pick wins more than either says; when they disagree, it
wins less than ours says. The fix I would make on a yes: let the record put a Most Likely pick's chance above both
our number and the price when the two agree, by as much as held-out games prove and never more, on the same bar as
every other correction. NBA first, and hockey only if its own record shows the same. It would change the chance
shown, the tier a pick earns and the order of the list, not which picks are on the board. Your answer, 23 November:
"do whatever you think. All I want is picks that win the most on there, and we need to be truthful about our shit."
Built as step ACX.

**ACO. SGPX for college football** (step 880; 22 November). Nothing to run. You want every league run the way the
NFL runs, and a college Saturday is the NFL's Sunday many times over. College football now gets SGPX tickets too:
