the day's windows, built, posted, kept, followed live and counted on the Record the way the NFL's are. College picks
post 90 minutes before kickoff with no inactives to wait for, so a college window posts once every game in it has
reached that time. On a day ticket, a later game's legs are the ones that game would post as built at that moment,
and the card says "picked before its game posted" where the NFL's says "picked before its inactives". A window or a
day with more than six games now counts them on its opening line instead of listing every one. They start with this
week's college games. Switch: `QB_SGPX=off` turns off every league's. A signed-out visitor's Report Picks showed a
locked SGPX tab in every league, the NBA's and hockey's included, which make none; it now shows only in the NFL and
college.

**ACN. SGPX tickets are followed live** (step 879; 22 November). Nothing to run. The Live tab follows each game
report's tickets leg by leg; an SGPX ticket spans games, so it had no game to sit under. Every posted SGPX ticket, a
window's or the day's, is now followed once any of its games is under way: one "SGPX parlays" card on the Live tab,
each leg with its own game and its number so far, and the ticket alive, down to its last leg, won or lost, the way
the report parlays read.

**ACM. Day-wide SGPX, one book first, and SGPX on Today's picks** (step 878; 22 November). Nothing to run. You said
yes to day-wide SGPX. A day with two kickoff windows or more (a Sunday, or Thanksgiving's three games) now also gets
three player-prop and three touchdown day tickets, each with legs from at least two windows. They post with the
day's first window, once its games have posted their picks and before its first kickoff, and never change. A later
game has not posted by then, so its legs are the ones it would post as built at that moment, picked before its
inactives were out. Each such ticket says so on its card, each such leg is marked, and a leg on a player who ends up
not playing is void, as a book voids it. They count on the Record as their own kinds (SGPX day parlays, SGPX day
touchdown parlays), so the record will say whether the early legs cost anything. Every SGPX ticket, window or day,
now ranks the ones a single sportsbook prices at every leg's number first, since an SGPX is one bet at one book, and
its card names that book and its prices. On Report Picks, Today's picks now lists every posted SGPX ticket in rows
beside the game report picks, like the likeliest tickets above them; a tap opens the SGPX tab, where each is drawn
whole. Best Parlays, the same switch's ranked page, has an SGPX tab too, one book's whole tickets first and then our
chance. A night game alone in its window now shows the day's tickets on its report.

**ACL. The chemistry measurement runs on the box every Wednesday, with two new tests** (step 877; 22 November).
Nothing to run. ABZ's measurement (`python3 chemfit.py`) needs the box's ten seasons of play-by-play, so it only ran
when someone ran it by hand. It now runs with the Wednesday refit, and its last line, every test's verdict, shows on
the heartbeat's weekly jobs, so its answers can be read off the site. Two tests join A, B, C and S. R asks whether a
returning starter's old target shares with a club (ACJ) predict his receivers' shares now, better than their own
recent shares. Z asks whether a new starter's own split of his red-zone targets between wide receivers, tight ends
and backs carries over the way his whole split does (test B, the lean ABZ ships): that is the touchdown props'
question. Neither moves a number until it passes the bar the others were held to.

**ACK. A receiver or back with a club he played for is read against his games there too** (step 876; 22 November).
Nothing to run. The same as ACJ for every other man with a prop in an NFL game: a wide receiver, tight end or back
whose club now is one he played for before playing somewhere else (four games there or more) gets a line on his
game's report, off the box's game logs: his games for them, the seasons, and his catches and receiving yards a game
there, or his carries and rushing yards. Three such lines a game at most, the most games there first. Words only,
like ACJ: nothing prices them until it is measured.

**ACJ. A quarterback back with a club he played for is read against his games there** (step 875; 22 November). One
optional command (00r). You asked for this with Kirk Cousins back with the Vikings; tonight he starts for them in
Kyler Murray's place. The quarterback history the box builds off the play-by-play (the one ABZ's lean reads) now
keeps each starter's games club by club: his attempts, completions, yards and touchdowns there, and the receivers he
threw to there. When a new starter is back with a club he started for before starting somewhere else (four starts
there or more), the quarterback line on his game's report says his starts there, his yards and touchdowns a game,
and, of the receivers on the club now, what share of his targets each drew then. It moves no number yet. ABZ
measured that one receiver's share with one quarterback predicts nothing beyond his share of the offense, and
whether a returning starter's old games there do is a separate question, to be measured on every season the box
holds before any pick uses it. The box rebuilds that history once tonight in its nightly run, so Monday's builds are
the first that can say it; command 00r does it now, for tonight's Vikings game. The same for receivers and backs
back with a former club is next.

**ACI. SGPX parlays: our best picks from different games in one ticket** (step 874; 22 November). Nothing to run.
You asked for same game parlay X tickets: the top picks of separate NFL games combined, one kind for player props
and one for touchdowns, like Derrick Henry with Jahmyr Gibbs and Amon-Ra St. Brown. Each kickoff window gets three
of each: games that kick off within 45 minutes of the first share a window (a Sunday's 1 PM games; its 4:05 and 4:25
games). A ticket has three legs from at least two games, at most two from one game. The legs are the ones each
game's own report posted: the player props of its three-leg and two-leg parlays, and the scorers of its touchdown
pairs. Legs from different games are counted as unrelated, so their chances multiply. Two legs from one game are
counted the way that game's own parlays count them, and a pair our rules keep apart (two pass catchers from one team
on a touchdown ticket) makes no ticket. The likeliest tickets post first, each leg on two tickets at most. Because
each game's picks wait for its inactives, a window's tickets post once every game in it has posted, before the first
kickoff, and then never change. A window of one game (a Thursday, Sunday or Monday night game) has none. They are on
each game's report as an "SGPX parlays" section after its own parlays, on Report Picks as their own "SGPX parlays"
tab, and on the Record as their own blocks, graded at the price each card says to take it at (`sudo
./deploy/setenv.sh QB_SGPX off` turns them off). The first window with more than one game is next Sunday's early
games.

**ACH. The NFL's inactives are read fresher, and ESPN's other feeds are timed against the board** (step 873; 22
November). Nothing to run. You asked for a faster inactives source than ESPN's injury board. On Sunday the 4:25
games' lists reached our picks 25 to 42 minutes after they came out: ESPN's board filed each club's men 1 to 21
minutes after the lists came out, our copy of the board was up to 10 minutes old, and the NFL board is rebuilt once
a sweep, about every 10 minutes. Three changes. First, from 100 minutes before an NFL kickoff to 5 minutes after it,
the box reads the injury board again once its copy is a minute old, not ten (`sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh
QB_INACTIVES_FRESH off` puts it back to ten). Second, after each other board's build, the sweep checks whether a
waiting NFL game is now due to post (its post time passed with both teams' lists on the board, or its deadline
passed) and rebuilds the NFL board then, instead of at the next sweep, at most once every 5 minutes
(`QB_NFL_DUE_BUILD off` stops that). Third, a watcher on the box reads ESPN's other feeds for each game in that
window: the game's summary from two hosts, its gamecast, and both clubs' game rosters. It notes when each feed first
shows each man inactive, and how far ahead of or behind the board that was. None of those feeds has been looked at
during an inactives window (this sandbox cannot reach ESPN), so the watcher finds the marks by key, whatever the
page's shape, and notes where in each page it found them. It changes no pick. Its counts and times are at
/data/inactives_watch.json, with no names, and `python3 -m engine.inactiveswatch` prints them on the box. Tonight's
Vikings at 49ers and Monday's Bengals at Commanders are its first two games. If a feed proves faster than the board,
the picks switch to it in a later step (`QB_INACTIVES_WATCH off` stops the watcher).

**ACG. A three-leg ticket has one name everywhere** (step 872; 22 November). Nothing to run. Looking at the new
settled cards on the live Record page: the same ticket was "Parlay 1" there, in its game's own report and on the
Live tab, but "Three-leg parlay 1" on Report Picks' Today tab. Every page now calls it "Three-leg parlay 1", beside
"Two-leg parlay 1" and "Touchdown pair 1", and Report Picks' lists say "Three-leg parlays" over them. Reports
already written keep the name they were written with.

**ACF. A game the NFL moved takes ESPN's kickoff time** (step 871; 22 November). Nothing to run. Today's board had
the Steelers at the Eagles at 4:25 PM and the Jaguars at the Giants at 1 PM; ESPN's live scoreboard had them the
other way round, and the Steelers' game was in its first quarter while the board still showed it as a 4:25 game. The
season schedule the build reads had not caught the swap. Everything timed off the kickoff used the wrong times: the
Steelers' and Eagles' 1 PM inactives were not counted as their game's list, the game's picks and parlays were held
to post at 3:10 PM, after it had kicked off, and the Jaguars-Giants picks were due before that game's inactives.
Now, whenever the build reads live scores, a game that ESPN's scoreboard lists ten minutes or more from the
schedule's time on the same day takes ESPN's time right away, before the forecast, the inactives and the post times
are worked out. A time still to be decided, and a move to another day, are left alone and noted in the build's
output. And a game whose picks and parlays have already posted keeps them whatever its start now reads: when the
Jaguars-Giants kickoff moves from 1 PM to 4:25, the picks it posted for 1 PM stay up rather than coming down until a
new post time. Today's two games cannot be re-timed after the fact; from the next build on, a moved game is timed
right.

**ACE. The WNBA's re-read starts with this season** (step 870; 22 November). Nothing to run. Checking A'ja Wilson's
page on the live site: only her newest 2026 game shows steals, blocks and turnovers, because the nightly re-read of
the WNBA's older box scores (step ABO) has not had its first night yet. It was set to go oldest first, forty game
days a night, which would have reached 2026 only after 2024 and 2025, about ten nights from now. It now goes newest
first, so tonight's run fills the latest forty game days of 2026 and the rest of the season follows over the next
few nights.

**ACD. Baseball's team pages open again** (step 869; 22 November). Nothing to run. Every baseball team page gave up
before it answered: the Yankees' and the Mariners' at 90 seconds, the Dodgers' with an error at 55, while hockey's
answered in about four seconds and basketball's in one. The cause: a baseball stat line is filed under the player
and the day, so the page found a team's lines by reading every game day of its season, and each day held every
team's lines. One team's page read nearly the whole league's season, and did it twice (the roster and the stat
tables). Now the season is read once for every team together, and that read is kept until a baseball stat line
changes (all winter, it never does). The nightly run makes that read, so a reader's first team page is served from
it straight away. Hockey and basketball team pages are read as before.

**ACC. A settled parlay reads like your screenshot** (step 868; 22 November). Nothing to run. You sent a betting
app's "Recently Settled" list and said you want to scroll through the game report data and see each leg green if it
won, red if it lost, and the whole parlay green if it won. Every place that lists a finished game's report tickets
now draws them that way: the game's own report, Report Picks (the Today tab's finished games, and every finished
game under "How our reports did"), and the Record's newest tickets. Each ticket shows its name, then "Won · 3 wins"
or "Lost · 2 wins, 1 loss", and on the right the units it won or lost at the price its card said to take it at, with
that price under them. Each leg sits in its own box with a green or red border and a check or an X. The box says the
bet ("Over 249.5 · Joe Burrow Passing Yards"), then what the player did, the two teams with their logos and the
final score, and the day ("409 · PIT 18 – 38 CIN · Final 11/15"). The whole ticket is outlined and tinted green when
it won and red when it lost, and says so in words too. On the report, what the card said before the game (our
chance, the script, each leg's why) is one tap under the ticket, under "How we built it". A finished game's own
picks get the same boxes on Report Picks, and on the report each pick card gets a green or red outline. For the
Record's newest tickets, the box now looks up each game's final score and day in the game history (an NFL ticket by
its week).

**ACB. An NFL game's picks and parlays wait for both teams' inactives** (step 867; 22 November). Nothing to run.
What today showed: the inactives come out 90 minutes before kickoff, and ESPN's board files them a team at a time.
For the 1 PM games a team's first inactive reached the board 1 to 14 minutes after 11:30 AM ET, its last up to 21
minutes after, and Carolina's none by noon; the board our builds read is up to ten minutes old. So the 1 PM picks,
posted at 11:45, saw only a few teams' lists. Now an NFL game posts at 75 minutes before kickoff only if both teams'
lists are already on the board; otherwise it waits and posts on the first build after they are, or at 50 minutes
before kickoff at the latest. While it waits, its report and its parlays say "Our picks for this game post once both
teams' inactives are in, at 12:10 PM at the latest" (in the reader's zone). A build that could not read ESPN's board
posts at 75 minutes as before, and the other leagues are unchanged. Today's 4 PM and night games are the first it
reaches if it is live by then.

**ACA. A questionable player not on his club's inactives list plays, and his own props are priced** (step 866; 22
November). Nothing to run. You said: "we need to be having that information on hand and using that data to our
advantage." What today's inactives showed: ESPN's board filed the Ravens' seven inactives as "Out" with the note
"inactive" at 11:32 AM ET, two minutes after the lists came out, and our builds read "Out" as out, so an inactive
player was already handled. The other half was not: a questionable player who is active stays "Questionable" on the
board until kickoff (Mayfield still did, after his game's injury list had dropped him), and the site holds a
questionable player's own props, so his props never priced, inactives or not. Now, once a club's list is on the
board for its game (at least three players filed inactive since 100 minutes before kickoff; a list left from an
earlier game does not count), every player it still lists questionable, doubtful or a game-time decision who is not
on it is active: his own props are priced, no teammate is priced as if he sat, and his game's report says "active:
not on the Ravens' inactives list (was questionable)". ESPN also files some active players one at a time ("Mayfield
(foot/thumb) is listed as active Sunday at Detroit, Scott Smith of the Buccaneers' official site reports" at 11:36
AM ET, with no Buccaneers inactives on the board), and our builds read an "Active" row as a cleared-to-play notice
that changes nothing, so the club's Friday "Questionable" stood; an "Active" filing inside a player's game window
now clears him by himself. A club whose list is not on the board yet, and a player with no such filing, stay as they
were. NFL only; college posts no list. Off without a deploy: `sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh QB_ACTIVE_AFTER_INACTIVES
off`.

**ABZ. Quarterback and receiver chemistry, measured: a new starter's own lean moves his targets, a pair's
"chemistry" does not** (step 865; 22 November). Nothing to run. You asked to measure "the chemistry between
quarterbacks and their wide receivers and their tight ends ... one quarterback may prefer to throw more to a certain
wide receiver or tight end ... or they may prefer to throw to tight ends more compared to wide receivers in
general". I measured it on nflverse's play-by-play, every regular-season pass 2017 to 2026 (about 170,000 targets),
each setting chosen on 2021-2023 and judged on seasons it never saw. One receiver with one quarterback: his share of
the targets with this week's starter, against his share over all his recent games, predicted his targets worse at
every setting (the two shares sit 1.3 points apart at the median), and so did his catch rate and yards a target with
that quarterback; a receiver's role is set by the offense, not by who throws to him, so it is in no number. A new
starter's own split between wide receivers, tight ends and backs is real: moved a fifth of the way from the team's
recent split toward his career split, it improved six of the seven unseen seasons (199 games; 2017 +11.7%, 2018
+12.1%, 2019 -0.6%, 2020 +6.5%, 2024 +1.8%, 2025 +2.3%, 2026 +0.7%). Its size is not pinned down: the fit seasons'
own best, a blend of 0.35, fails on the unseen seasons, so the fifth is the one-standard-error rule's pick, and
every blend from a tenth to a fifth passes. Now, when a team's starter is out or benched, each receiver's catches
and receiving yards move by how much his position's share moves that fifth of the way, capped at 15% either way,
after the measured downgrade step; the board, Most Likely, the Edge picks, the report's picks and the if-he-sits
version all read it, and the report says it ("Kyle Trask has thrown 40% of his targets to tight ends ... the tight
ends' targets +7%"). The career splits are built by the Wednesday fitters, so it starts with this Wednesday's run.
`python3 chemfit.py` measures it again. Off without a deploy: `sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh QB_QB_LEAN off`.

**ABY. A listed player's newest word, everywhere the site lists him** (step 864; 22 November). Nothing to run. You
said: "Baker Mayfield's foot/right thumb is slated to play in Sunday's game against Detroit Lions, Ian Rapoport of
NFL Network reports. But he's still labeled as questionable on ESPN ... we need to be ... reporting it in our game
reports and every other spot where we report injuries." Where it stood: his game's report said it in its "If he
plays, and if he sits" section (step ABS) and the player page showed the blurb in full; the Injuries page showed it
only on a hover, and every report's injury lines said "questionable" and nothing more. Now the Injuries page says it
under his status, green or red by its lean ("expected to play Sun, per Ian Rapoport of NFL Network"), and every
league's report says it on the player's injury line ("Baker Mayfield (QB) — questionable; the newest word: expected
to play, per Ian Rapoport of NFL Network"), on its practice-report line too. One reader serves the page, the reports
and the live watch, and it reads a blurb for the game it names, counted from when it was posted: "McVay said
Saturday that Williams ... is expected to play Wednesday" is Wednesday's game, a Sunday blurb naming Saturday is
about a game already played, and a blurb about the rest of a game under way or about someone else is no word. Using
it to our advantage in the picks themselves (a questionable player's own props are held until the lineup) waits on
what the inactives showed today.

**ABX. Every WNBA club has its whole team page** (step 863; 22 November). Nothing to run. Checking the live team
pages: the Indiana Fever's had its name, roster and depth chart; the Las Vegas Aces' read "LV" with no name, no
roster and no depth chart, and so did the Valkyries', the Sparks', the Liberty's and the Mystics'. The WNBA's stored
games keep ESPN's codes (LV, GS, LA, NY, WSH) while its names and rosters use the league's (LVA, GSV, LAS, NYL,
WAS), so the five clubs whose codes differ lost everything keyed the other way, and searching "LVA" found no team at
all. Now a club's code in either spelling is the same club on its team page: its full name, its roster and depth
chart, and the search finds it from either code or its name. The NBA's search finds "GS" and "NY" too.

**ABW. The Injuries page says the NBA's own word too** (step 862; 22 November). Nothing to run. Step ABU put the
league's word for the game into the NBA's game reports; the Injuries page still said only ESPN's "Day-To-Day". Now a
day-to-day player whose blurb gives the word for today's or tomorrow's game shows it under his status ("questionable
for Sun"); a blurb about another day's game shows nothing extra, and one that names no day counts only when it was
filed in the last day.

**ABV. The night keeps the basketball history to its leagues' own games** (step 861; 22 November). Nothing to run.
Checking the live player pages against ESPN's: Caitlin Clark's 2026 season still counted the All-Star Game (it read
"IND/SPO") and exhibitions against "COOP" and Nigeria's national team; A'ja Wilson's every season since 2021 counted
an All-Star side (USA, WIL, CLA, SPO); Jalen Brunson's 2024-25 and 2023-24 counted the NBA's (STRIPES, KEN). Those
games sat in the pages' averages and in the boards' form and hit rates. The nightly has refused such games since 17
November, and the two commands that take out what it stored before (RUN_NEXT 00j) were never run on the box. The
night runs them now: once a week it takes out every stored game with a side that is no club of its league (a side
with more than six stored games is a club the tables do not list yet, and it is said in the log and left alone), and
it moves each stored season's preseason games to the preseason tables, forty scoreboard days a night until every
season is done. The first night should clear them. One more difference from ESPN's pages, in every league but
baseball, the NFL's included: a season's row counts its playoff games with the regular season (Josh Allen's 2024
reads 19 games), where ESPN shows the regular season and the postseason apart. Not changed here; it is a decision
for you, since the NFL page does it too.

**ABU. The NBA's own word under ESPN's "Day-To-Day"** (step 860; 22 November). Nothing to run. ESPN files an NBA
player who is probable, questionable or doubtful all as "Day-To-Day", and the blurb under it keeps the league's own
word. This morning: "Siakam (hip) is listed as questionable for Sunday's game against New York", "Cunningham (knee)
is probable to play Sunday in Atlanta", "Antetokounmpo (groin) is listed as questionable for Sunday's game against
Oklahoma City". The NBA's game reports said "day-to-day" for every one of them, though probable nearly always plays
and doubtful nearly never does. Now the report's Injuries list and its "Still to be decided" line say the league's
word for that game ("Pascal Siakam (IND) — questionable, hip"), read only off a blurb about that game: one about
another day's game, the rest of a game under way, or giving two words is passed by, and ESPN's status stands. The
game page's "Since this report was written" card says a new word too ("day-to-day (hip), now listed questionable for
the game"). Nothing moves a number: the board still holds a day-to-day player's own props until the lineup, as
before.

**ABT. A listed player's newest word reaches his game's page** (step 859; 22 November). Nothing to run. You said:
"we need to do better on reporting on injuries, figuring out which players are in or out for all sports, for all
game reports." What I found, on this morning's live injury file: ESPN's listed status was never behind its own news.
Every "ruled out" blurb on a player not listed out was about a game already played or the rest of one under way
(eight NBA players read "Day-To-Day" with a blurb about Friday's or Saturday's game). What the status misses is the
morning lean: at 7:24 AM ET Baker Mayfield was still "Questionable" and his blurb said "slated to play in Sunday's
game against the Lions, Ian Rapoport of NFL Network reports"; Ladd McConkey's and Carnell Tate's said the same
within the quarter hour. The report watch, which reads the injury board every five minutes, kept only designations,
so none of that reached a game's page. Now a listed player whose blurb changes and leans one way is an update of its
own, on the game's "Since this report was written" card and in the next build's report: "Baker Mayfield (TB)
questionable (foot strain), now expected to play, per Ian Rapoport of NFL Network", marked green; a lean the other
way is marked red and names any of the report's bets on him. It reads conservatively: a blurb about another day's
game, about the rest of a game under way, or one that leans both ways (about someone else) is no word. Every
league's game reports get it. Nothing here moves a number; the board still reads the designation. The first look
after the deploy only remembers each blurb, so the first words show from the next new blurb on.

**ABS. A questionable starting quarterback gets both versions of his game's report** (step 858; 22 November).
Nothing to run. You said: "today for the Lions game, it's not confirmed if Baker Mayfield is playing or not yet. So
we should have a game report ready for if Baker Mayfield is in and one if he's not in." What the site did: a starter
listed out or doubtful was already priced as out (his backup starts, and his receivers' numbers drop by what we
measured behind a backup: about 9% fewer catches and 10% fewer yards, 2022 to 2025). A starter listed questionable,
or a game-time decision, changed nothing: the game was priced as if he plays and the report answered only that side.
Now, for every team whose starting quarterback is questionable or a game-time decision, the build prices that team's
props a second time, through the same pricing, with the backup the site would start in his place; and the game's
report opens a section right under our picks, "If he plays, and if he sits": his status, when the inactives come out
and when our picks post (after them, from whichever version holds then), the injury report's newest word on him with
when it was posted (this morning's on Mayfield: "slated to play in Sunday's game against the Lions, Ian Rapoport of
NFL Network reports"), who starts if he sits and what that has done, and every number that moves, both ways ("Mike
Evans over 4.5 receptions: 64% if he plays, 58% if he sits"). NFL and college football both build it; college's
backup effect is measured from college games and is flat until its fit saves one, so a college game says who would
start and that nothing moves yet. It shows on the next build after the deploy, so today's 1 PM games, whose picks
post at 11:45 AM ET right after the inactives, are settled by the inactives themselves.

**ABR. The Picks pages share one switch: Most Likely, Report Picks, Best Parlays** (step 857; 22 November). Nothing
to run. You said: the Picks button "will take you to the most likely picks page, and then there'll be an option in
that picks page to switch to the game report picks and parlays". The Picks button at the bottom still opens Most
Likely. Most Likely, Report Picks and Best Parlays now each open on the same three-way switch under the league
chips, the page you are on filled in gold, and the bottom Picks button stays lit on all three, so they read as one
place. A league with no game reports (UFC) shows no switch. The "Best Parlays" button that sat at the top of Report
Picks since yesterday is gone, because the switch right above it does the same thing and a second button to the same
page on one screen is clutter.

**ABQ. A game report's picks post once, with its parlays, and never change** (step 856; 22 November). Nothing to
run. You said: "not throwing a million different picks into one game report and keep switching picks ... like the
issue we had last night for NBA ... figure out the timeline for that." Why it happened: every build (every 7 to 10
minutes) chose a report's picks afresh, and the record journals a pick the first time any version of the report
shows it, so a game piled up picks through the day (Saturday night's seven NBA reports put 50 graded single picks on
the record) and you saw different picks each time you looked. The timeline now: a game's picks post at the same
moment as its parlays, 75 minutes before an NFL kickoff (right after the inactives) and 90 minutes before every
other league's games. Before that the report shows all of its analysis and says when its picks post, and nothing in
it counts. At the post time its card (at most 4 picks, 6 on a featured game) and the picks on its matchup reads post
once, built from the newest injury news, lineups and lines, and they stay exactly as posted until the game starts;
the report's other sections keep updating. Report Picks says when a waiting game's picks post. So each game posts
one set of picks, and those are the ones the Record counts. It applies from its deploy on. One correction to what I
wrote you earlier today in passing: the Record's "Earlier picks" row is every report pick from before 20 November,
not picks a report replaced, so it says nothing about switching. Off without a deploy: `sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh
QB_REPORT_PICKS_POST off`.

**ABO. The WNBA's player pages get every box-score column, by the night** (step 855; 22 November). Nothing to run.
Every WNBA player page showed four columns (minutes, points, rebounds, assists) where the NBA's show fifteen. The
reason is old data, not the page: the box-score reader learned steals, blocks and turnovers on 13 October and field
goals, free throws and offensive rebounds on 20 October, after the WNBA season had ended, so every WNBA game on file
has only the first few. RUN_NEXT 00i had the one-off command to read 2026 again; instead of you running it, the
nightly run now reads every stored WNBA day from 2024 to 2026 that has no steals on file again, forty days a night,
oldest first, each day twice at most, and says in its log how many are left; once none is left it does nothing. The
pages fill in as the nights go. The WNBA still has no shot chart (the NBA's and college basketball's come from their
own shot tables); that is a bigger piece, for before the WNBA season starts in May.

**ABN. Hockey's and college basketball's Record pages read like the NFL's** (step 854; 22 November). Nothing to run.
You said: "the record pages to match each other. Not numbers wise but visual wise." Hockey and college basketball
stake nothing yet (their edge picks wait on paper and their Most Likely picks are tracked for their hit rate), so
their Record leads with the Most Likely record: hockey's top card read 1958-1024 over 2,982 graded picks. Everything
under that card read the empty staked record instead: the 90, 30 and 7-day buttons were greyed out with "Not enough
settled days for a window yet", the verdict card said "0-0-0 ... Too early to call. 0 graded picks", the running
profit chart, the books and the splits were folded away as "too early to read (0 of the 30 settled bets the record
needs)", and the running chart drew nothing. Now every one of those reads the record the page leads with: the window
buttons work (hockey's 90-day one says the record covers 39 days so far, as the NFL's says of its own), the verdict
shows that record with its own claimed-versus-landed chart, and the panels unfold as the NFL's do. College
basketball has 13 graded picks, so its page still says "too early", now with its real count (13 of 30) instead of 0.
Leagues with a staked record (NFL, college football, NBA, baseball) read exactly as before; the profit calendar
keeps its own Edge and Most Likely switch.

**ABM. Baseball's game page and play files work like every other league's** (step 853; 22 November). Nothing to run;
baseball is in its offseason, so this shows in the spring. Step ABL fixed finished games that kept reading LIVE in
every league the main live loop serves; baseball's play files come from a loop of their own that had the same gap,
and it now writes a game that has just ended once more, as final, the same way. Its page also looked a game up on
the scoreboard strip by a field baseball's rows do not have (they carry baseball's own game number), so a baseball
page never picked up the strip's Final, the fix every other league got on 25 October for a file frozen at its last
live write; it finds baseball's games by their own number now.

**ABL. A finished game reads Final on its page, in every league** (step 852; 22 November). Nothing to run. You said:
"We want all the live pages to match each other ... NFL is kind of like the one we want to go off of ... how it gets
data." Opened this morning, the Knicks' 97-96 win over the Trail Blazers still read LIVE, "End of 4th Quarter" and
"updated 10 hr ago", and a college basketball game's page the same, where the NFL's finished games read Final and
the day they were played. The cause: the live loop wrote a game's play file only while the game was live, so the
pass that first saw it final wrote nothing, and the file kept its last live copy until it was deleted a day and a
half later (hockey's read Final only because its rink pass writes the score onto the file). Fixed three ways: (1)
the loop now writes a game that has just ended once more, as final, with its last plays, a few games a pass after
the live ones; its card on the Live tab is left alone. (2) A page that opens a file still saying live, more than
three hours old, of a game the scoreboard no longer has live, reads the game from the archive instead (the same
place the NFL's past games come from), which builds it final; that covers the games that ended before this change.
(3) Every final's header now says the day it was played, in your own time zone, where the live-loop finals said
"updated 10 hr ago". One more difference fixed with it: a past game's page (the archive) drew no network, where the
live loop's finals said "NBA TV"; the archive now reads the network from ESPN's game summary. I could not reach ESPN
from my sandbox to see that summary's exact shape, so I will check an NFL game's archive page on the live site after
the deploy.

**ABK. Every league's player page reads like the NFL's** (step 851; 22 November). Nothing to run. You said: "We want
every single sports player pages to match each other and like have it match ESPN ... NFL is kind of like the one we
want to go off of." I drew one player's page in each league side by side from the live site's own player data (Josh
Allen, Jeremiah Smith, Jalen Brunson, Caitlin Clark, Connor McDavid, Aaron Judge and a college guard). The layout
was the same; what differed came from each league's data, and is fixed: (1) the header's height and weight were each
feed's spelling, 6'5" and 237 lb on the NFL's and the NHL's, 6' 2" and 190 lbs on the basketball leagues'; every
page says 6'2" and 190 lb now. (2) College football's and baseball's headers had no height, weight or age, and
college basketball's no age: their feeds sent the size and the parsers dropped it. College football's roster now
keeps ESPN's height, weight, class and hometown, baseball's MLB's height, weight and hometown (its per-team fallback
asks for the birth date too), and college basketball's its class; a college player shows his class ("Junior") where
a pro shows his age, as ESPN does. These fill in when the rosters next rebuild. (3) College football's previous game
said Ohio State "15-9": the games table holds some college games twice (a known problem the standings already
filter), and the player page counted every copy, plus one copy dated 1993; it counts each game once now (7-4), and a
game dated outside its own season is dropped, from Ohio State's schedule too. (4) The WNBA's box scores name five
clubs by ESPN's codes (GS, LA, LV, NY, WSH) where our team list has its own, so Caitlin Clark's last opponent read
"LV" with no name or colours; both codes read the club now. (5) A basketball rate rode the season's small boxes as a
count, "81 free throw percentage"; rates stay out of them. Still different, and data rather than the page: the
WNBA's stats tables carry 4 columns (minutes, points, rebounds, assists) where the NBA's carry 15, because the
WNBA's box scores are stored with fewer stats, and the WNBA has no shot chart.

**ABJ. A game short of its parlays says why in one plain sentence** (step 850; 22 November). Nothing to run. A game
report that posts fewer than three of a kind says why under them, and it read "... make no more two that fit
together without a conflict and reach 30% by our numbers with no leg on more than 2 of the game's parlays". It reads
now: "2 of 3: the 7 legs at 60% or better in this game's priced props make no other two-leg ticket without a
conflict that reaches 30% by our numbers, with no leg on more than 2 of the game's parlays" (and with no ticket at
all, "make no three-leg ticket ..."). Every league's notes read the same way.

**ABI. A game page never prints "NaN°F"** (step 849; 22 November). Nothing to run. Checking the NFL game reports in
a browser for step ABH, the game page's header read "NaN°F · NaNmph · kickoff forecast" for a game with no weather
on file: the header printed whatever numbers the game carried, where the game cards on the board already said
"Outdoor · weather not pulled". A game the weather pull never reached, or reached without a temperature, says that
in the header too now, and a wind it lacks is left out. A sweep of every league's demo board and its first game
pages found no other "NaN", "undefined" or "null" in the text.

**ABH. A game's report says exactly what the board posts** (step 848; 22 November). Nothing to run. You said, the
Sunday morning: "I see parlays posted now on the game reports for nfl but those shouldn't be there by what u said."
You were right. Each game report writes its own copy of the game's parlays (its parlays section, its card's parlay
line and its short version) the moment its picks rebuild them, and the post time (step ABD) and the lock (step ABB)
were applied to the board only after every report was written. So the board, Report Picks and Best Parlays held
Sunday's NFL parlays until 75 minutes before each kickoff while every NFL report printed a fresh set; and since the
lock went in on the 21st, a game that had posted showed on its report page each build's newest set, not the locked
one Report Picks, Best Parlays and the Record use (the Record always counted the locked set). Now each report
applies both to its game before it writes a word: before the post time its parlays section says only when they post
(in the reader's own zone on the page) and its card names no ticket; after it, the report shows the posted set
exactly as posted. Every league's report goes through the same step.

**ABG. An NBA leg rides at most two of a game's six parlays** (step 847; 22 November). Nothing to run. Your answer
to decision 18: "Yes limit it". Each list already held a leg to two tickets, so one NBA leg could ride four of a
game's six parlays, two three-leg and two two-leg. On the NBA's tickets graded at their start (17 to 21 November), 8
legs rode four tickets each; 4 of those 8 lost and took 16 tickets with them, and 53 of the 64 tickets lost had a
losing leg on another ticket too. Now an NBA leg rides at most two of a game's three-leg and two-leg tickets
together. The three-leg tickets are chosen first, as before, and the two-leg ones around them (around the ones the
game posted, once it has posted); a posted game's open places fill to the same cap, and what it posted stands as
posted. It leaves how often a ticket hits as it was and stops one miss sinking most of a game's parlays. Replayed on
those graded tickets, 20 of the 45 two-leg ones would have stood as they were (11 of them won) and 25 would have
been rebuilt from picks with room left (10 of those had won). A game with few strong legs posts fewer two-leg
tickets, and its report says the cap is why ("with no leg on more than 2 of the game's parlays"). Every other league
is unchanged. Off without a deploy: `sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh QB_GAME_LEG_CAP off`.

**ABF. A game's post time reads in your own zone, with its day** (step 846; 21 November). Nothing to run. Since step
ABD a game's parlays post shortly before it starts, and its report and Report Picks said when in Eastern time ("post
at Sun 11:45 AM ET") while every start on the site reads in the reader's own zone (your answer to decision 13). The
page now says it the same way, from the game's post time ("post at Sun 8:45 AM" in Los Angeles), and Best Parlays,
which said only the clock of the next post, gives its day too when that is not today where the reader is, so a
Saturday evening's "the next at 11:45 AM" reads "the next at Sun, Nov 22 · 11:45 AM".

**ABE. The heartbeat counts the NFL's capped picks, and why the NBA's Top two-leg parlays lost** (step 845; 21
November). Nothing to run. The NFL board now says its cap (step AAV: a pick shown at no more than its own price's
chance plus ten points) is on even on a build where it moved nothing, and the heartbeat counts what it moved
(`price_ceiling.capped`, and of those already posted, `capped_posted`); on the day's boards it moved none, since the
standing paper hold (step BK) already keeps NFL picks 15 points or more over their price off the board, so the cap
only acts between 10 and 15 points over. The Record's NBA two-leg tiers (Top 1 of 11 where we said 52%, Strong 18 of
27 where we said 47%) are tickets from games of 17 to 21 November, 42 of the 45 before 21 November's NBA fixes; 20
November's slate alone went 8 of 26. Before those fixes a ticket's price check passed only where we rated its legs
together above the book's own price, and step AAM found legs we rated above the book overrated; Safe two-leg tickets
went 12 of 34 (we said 50%) and Balanced 9 of 11 (we said 43%), as step AAR found. Since then an NBA leg counts at
no more than the book's chance, the price check says nothing for the NBA (step ABA), and Safe and Balanced stand on
the chances alone, so nothing further changes. Watched, too few to act on: NBA tickets with one leg from outside the
report's picks went 1 of 12 since 20 November (college's went 7 of 13).

**ABD. A game's parlays post late, when the news is in, and then never change** (step 844; 21 November). Nothing to
run. You said, the same evening: "Clearly the parlays posted the latest are doing the best ... I just want whatever
parlays are on the record page doing good. We are reporting we are doing good on all the game reports yet I'm not
doing good when I put the pick in." Measured on the public record of every finished game since 16 November, the set
each report carried at the start (its latest) against the versions it posted earlier and replaced: three-leg parlays
hit 41 of 113 (36%) against 89 of 343 (26%), the NBA's 23% against 15% and college football's 58% against 30%;
two-leg 47 of 88 (53%) against 45 of 90 (50%); touchdown and goal-scorer pairs 14 of 79 (18%) against 4 of 55 (7%);
and their legs about ten points apart (the NBA's 67% against 57%, college's 83% against 66%). The latest set knew
the day's injury news, lineups and line moves; the Record counted it, and a member who bet in the morning bet an
earlier one. Step ABB's lock alone would have frozen the earlier one. Now a game's parlays stay off the board until
90 minutes before it starts (75 for the NFL, just after its inactives), are built then from the newest numbers, post
once, and never change; the boards rebuild every 8 to 30 minutes, so every game posts in time. Before then the
game's report and Report Picks say when its parlays post, Best Parlays says how many games are waiting and when the
next posts, and the heartbeat counts them (`parlay_waiting`). What a member bets is now the latest set and exactly
the one the Record counts. Tomorrow's NFL parlays, posted days ahead, came down until their post time (11:45 AM ET
for the 1:00 PM games). Off without a deploy: `sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh QB_PARLAY_POST_LATE off`.

**ABC. Report Picks opens Best Parlays from the top of the day** (step 843; 21 November). Nothing to run. You said,
the same evening: "I want the game report parlays too have its own page like the most likely picks where it ranks
and lays out the parlays best to worst". That page is Best Parlays (built this morning, step AAL): every parlay the
reports posted, ranked across the league's games the way Most Likely ranks a pick (Top parlays, Strong, Worth a
look, then our chance), with a Two-leg and a Three-leg switch, and the touchdown pairs on their own tab. Report
Picks, where you read the reports' parlays game by game, never pointed to it. Now the first thing on its Today's
picks tab is a button, Best Parlays: every report parlay, two-leg and three-leg, ranked best to worst. It is still
in the menu too, right under Report Picks.

**ABB. A posted parlay never changes, and the Record shows every parlay we posted** (step 842; 21 November). Nothing
to run. You found it on the 76ers at Bucks report: the parlays you bet earlier in the day were gone, others stood in
their place, and the Record counts only the set a report carried when its game started, so your losing tickets were
nowhere and the winning ones were counted. The cause: since 20 November a posted ticket was posted again only while
the newest build would still make it. A pick that left the report's card, a leg the newest numbers no longer backed,
injury news, or a rule changed during the day (three went in on the 21st) replaced it, and a line the books moved
was shown at the new number. What changed, in every league: once a game posts a parlay, every later build posts it
again exactly as it was (the same players, lines, prices and chances) until the game starts. A build only fills a
place the game never filled, and never with a leg already on two of its parlays. Which book has the whole ticket is
still read fresh, so a leg no book lists any more still says so. For the past, nothing posted is hidden: each
league's parlay cards on the Record add a line for every parlay we posted, the ones replaced before their game too
(with how many hit and the units), and each finished game's list adds a fold, Posted earlier, replaced before the
game, with each one marked; neither is counted in the game's own tallies. The counted record stays one set a game,
and from now on that set is the one posted, since it can't change. How big the gap was: the NBA's three-leg record
counts 55 graded tickets and left out 281 replaced versions; hockey's 43 and 343; the NFL's 3 and 317. Off without a
deploy: `sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh QB_PARLAY_LOCK off`.

**ABA. Best Parlays' Top tier fills again in the NFL, college football and the NBA** (step 841; 21 November).
Nothing to run. Found on the heartbeat: the 3:20 PM ET boards ranked no NFL, college or NBA player-prop parlay as a
Top parlay (NFL two-leg 4 Strong and 25 Worth a look, three-leg 1 and 22; hockey had 9 and 4 Top). One of the page's
checks asks whether a book's same-game price (the legs' own prices multiplied, less its cut) pays our fair price
plus 5%. Since step AAM each leg in those three leagues counts at no more than the book's own chance, so our fair
price is the book's own less its hold, and no ticket can pass but by a strong link between its legs: a check every
ticket fails ranks nothing and pushes every ticket down a tier. The same side effect step AAR mended for the Safe
and Balanced labels. In those leagues that check now says nothing (as an unknown always has), so a ticket every
other check backs is a Top parlay again; the ticket's own note that a book's same-game price likely pays less than
it needs still shows. Hockey, whose legs keep our own number, is as it was. Which parlays are built does not change,
only their tiers.

**AAZ. Hockey's live game page draws the win chance line, as every sport's does** (step 840; 21 November). Nothing
to run. You asked for every page to match. Read side by side on today's live games (college football, college
basketball, hockey) and the Record page for each league, the Record pages already match: the same sections in the
same order and the same cards, and what differs is what each league has (hockey and college basketball fold the
sections that have too few settled bets). One card on the live game pages differed. The line of each side's win
chance through the game is drawn from the chance the feed gives after each play, which ESPN gives in football and
basketball and not in hockey, so a hockey game showed only our number now, as two bars titled "Win probability",
where the others showed the line titled "Win chance". The live build now gives each hockey play our own chance after
it (the same score-and-clock reading the bars show; a hockey play's clock counts up through its period), and the
page draws the same line from it, labeled as ours; the bars stand down, and while the game is on the line ends on
the scoreboard's reading, since the feed's plays can trail the score by a play or two. It costs about 26 ms for a
whole game's plays the first time and a lookup after. College football's page drew no field for a moment today only
because the ball had no spot after a touchdown, which the NFL's does too. Also measured today, with nothing built:
the football bet types that keep missing (college passing-yards overs, college rushing- and receiving-yards unders,
NFL rushing attempts both ways) have nearly left the board since the NFL's 60% bar (15 November) and college's bar
and price hold (20 and 21 November), 0 to 5 of each since 15 November, and college's passing overs slumped on two
Saturdays (7 and 14 November) when every college passing over missed and the books' prices missed it too, so a rule
would chase noise. And the NBA's report parlays with a prop one play decides (now off parlays, step AAM) went 4 of
15 (two-leg) and 2 of 19 (three-leg), where the rest went 16 of 27 and 10 of 30.

**AAY. Football kickoff times read in your own time zone** (step 839; 21 November). Nothing to run. Your answer to
decision 13 ("yes"). The NFL's board carries a kickoff as the game's Eastern day and an Eastern clock ("2026-11-22",
"13:00"), so every NFL time on the site read "1:00 PM ET", even for a member who picked another zone in Settings,
while every other league's start read in the reader's zone. The day and the clock together are now read as one
moment (Eastern is five hours behind UTC in winter and four in summer) and shown in the reader's zone wherever a
game's start appears: the game cards and game pages, the empty board's and the Live tab's next-kickoff line, a
player's upcoming game, the NFL inactives note (90 minutes before kickoff) and the parlay grader's legs, which now
show college football's start too (they showed none). The next-kickoff line also picks the earliest game by its real
time now: on a Thursday it named Sunday's 1:00 PM, because the text "13:00" sorts before "20:15". For a reader on
Eastern time only the "ET" goes. The reports' own written text ("kicks off Sun 1:00 PM ET") still says Eastern,
since it is written once for every reader. Checked in a test under Los Angeles and London time, winter and summer,
and on the Sunday summer time starts.

**AAX. The Record grades Best Parlays by tier** (step 838; 21 November). Nothing to run. Your answer to decision 15
("yes"). Best Parlays ranks each game's tickets in three tiers by how their checks agree (Top parlays: every check
agrees; Strong: all but one; Worth a look: two or more against) and drops a game once it starts. Now, when a game
starts, each ticket the record counts (the set its report carried at the start) keeps the tier those same checks
give it, and each league's parlay cards on the Record say how each tier has done ("By Best Parlays tier: Top parlays
3 of 8 hit (we gave 41%) · Strong ..."). Games from before the page went up today are tiered the same way from the
starting sets the archive keeps (from 16 November), on tonight's archive pass, and the line says so. Tickets on
paper and tickets with a leg no book listed any more were never on the page and have no tier. Your answer to
decision 14 needed no change: the free Record's league tabs already list every finished game with each report pick
and parlay marked hit or missed, under How our reports did (checked signed out on the live site); my note saying it
was members-only was wrong.

**AAW. College football's Thursday-night games are featured** (step 837; 21 November). Nothing to run. Your answer
to decision 11 ("yes"). A featured game, until now the NFL's alone (Lions games, Thursday nights, Monday nights),
gets a deeper report card (six picks where others get four), a badge at the top of its report with how games like it
have done, and a record of its own on Report Picks and the Record. A college game kicking off at 6 PM Eastern or
later on a Thursday is now featured the same way; Friday nights and Thursday afternoons are not, and college has no
Lions or Monday kind. Its record counts the finished Thursday-night games already archived. Nothing about how the
picks are made changes.

**AAV. The NFL's quarterback pass attempts are benched from stakes, and its Most Likely picks far above their price
are shown at most ten points over it** (step 836; 21 November). Nothing to run. Your answers to decisions 16 ("bench
them") and 17 ("cap them"). Pass attempts: on the public record they lost on both sides. The Edge board's picks went
21-26 (-4.0 units); the Most Likely overs hit 45 of 85 (53%) at prices that needed 64%, the unders 20 of 38 (53%) at
55%; as parlay legs the overs hit 20 of 41 (step AAQ had already taken them off parlays). The market goes on the
bench the way completions did on 18 November: its Edge picks carry no stake ("Tracked · no stake") and neither side
rides a parlay. It comes off by itself once 60 of its picks graded since the bench have made money. The cap: NFL
Most Likely picks shown more than ten points above their own price's chance (the book's cut taken out) hit 65 of 137
(47%) where we said 79%, and 23 of 42 since 1 November where we said 89%; every other NFL pick hit 60% where we said
62% (2,159 picks). The books' field only holds a pick that three books price on both sides at its number, so these,
mostly alternate lines one book prices, kept their own chances. Now an NFL prop is shown at no more than its price's
chance plus ten points, its note says why, and it moves down the board to where that puts it; a pick already posted
says it was restated. Off without a deploy: `sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh QB_NFL_CAP off`.

**AAU. The parlay record keeps each leg's own line's chance; the learned correction moves onto it only when its
record says so** (step 835; 21 November). Nothing to run. You asked for this follow-up to step AAT. Every parlay leg
is journaled with the book's fair chance beside ours, and on a Most Likely pick on an alternate line that was its
main line's, so the record's legs read well under their own prices: the NBA's 53% (three-leg) and 56% (two-leg)
where their newest legs were priced near 63% and 65% once the book's cut is taken out, hockey's 58% and 59% near 65%
and 66%, the NFL's 59% and 55% near 63%, college's 53% and 51% near 58% and 61%. The learned correction (how far
each league's legs are pulled toward the book's chance; hockey's pulls 20%) was fitted against those numbers. What
changed: each leg is now journaled with its own line's chance too, in a column of its own, and the record's leg
figures report it where it is kept. The correction compares the two anchors on its own record: once 60 graded legs
carry both, the newest 30% of them are scored with each anchor's fit learned on the legs before them, and the own
line's is taken only when it scores better; until then, and whenever it does not, every league's correction is
exactly what it was. The heartbeat's `leg_fit` says which anchor each league reads. Measured first on the public
record of settled Most Likely picks (a stand-in for the legs, with the main line's chance taken as the own line's
less 10 points, which is rough): hockey's and the NBA's newest legs scored best with no pull at all against either
anchor (0.6236 and 0.6406, the pulls a hair worse), so neither league's numbers should move far; the NFL's scored
far better pulled all the way to their own line's chance (0.649, against 0.661 toward the main line's and 0.733 with
none), which the book cap of step AAM already does; college's came out about even (0.678 and 0.675).

**AAT. Each leg and card pick is held to its own line's chance, not its main line's** (step 834; 21 November).
Nothing to run. A fix to steps AAM and AAO, found on the heartbeat. The NFL's board built at 2:25 PM ET kept 3 of
its reports' 48 picks as parlay legs, where that morning's had kept 19, and posted 5 two-leg and 1 three-leg ticket,
where it had posted 34 and 26: ten of its twelve games had fewer than three legs to build from. The cause: a Most
Likely pick on an alternate line carries two fair chances, its own line's (`implied_prob`) and its main line's
(`fair_prob`, kept for the board's credibility bar), and both new rules read the main line's. So Nabers 5+
receptions at -250 was held to the -110 main line's 50% and was no leg, and the report cards read every such pick as
twenty points over the book and moved it behind, so touchdown picks took their places (touchdown picks ride only the
touchdown pairs). The evidence for both rules was measured on each pick's own price, so the code was wrong, not the
rules. Each leg now carries its own line's chance (`fair_line`) and both rules read it; a rung with no two-way price
of its own is read at its price less the book's cut. The parlay journal's own `fair` field, which the learned
correction reads, is left as it was; that it carries the main line's on a rung is a separate question, written down
for later.

**AAS. The Live tab follows the game reports' own picks** (step 833; 21 November). Nothing to run. You asked to see
the game report bets and parlays on the Live page the way the Most Likely and Edge bets are, live. The reports'
parlays already were: "Our report parlays, live" near the top of the tab follows every posted ticket leg by leg (at
1:56 PM ET it was following 62 tickets in 8 games, 7 of them live). The reports' own picks were not: they journal to
a book of their own and the tracker behind the Edge and Most Likely panels never read it, so a report's picks went
quiet at kickoff. Now they have their own panel, Open game report picks, under Open Most Likely bets, drawn with the
same rows: the number so far, the progress bar, what it still needs, cleared or busted, the live chance where there
is one, and where the report posted it (Our picks, Matchup read, Breakout candidate, Fade). A finished game's picks
fold under it until the overnight settle, as the others do. Each game's own page lists them too, as Game report
picks on its picks rail above its report's tickets. A report's card pick is a Most Likely pick as well, so it shows
in both panels, once in each; it is counted once in each book on the Record. Members only, as the reports are
(`live_report` is a paid key). Because the rows are a member's, the public heartbeat counts them for each league
(`live_report`: how many picks, and how many of their games are under way), so anyone can see the tracker found
them.

**AAR. The NBA's tickets keep their classes under the book cap** (step 832; 21 November). Nothing to run. Step AAM
put each NBA leg at the lower of our chance and the book's fair one, which sits under the price's own break-even by
the book's cut, so an NBA leg could almost never grade Green, and a ticket's Safe and Balanced classes need Green
legs: nearly every NBA ticket would have read Pop or Long shot, and on Best Parlays almost no NBA two-leg ticket
could be a Top parlay. Its classes now stand on the chances alone, as football's always have (football's numbers
were tied to their prices before AAM). The record agrees with dropping the Green half there: before AAM the NBA's
two-leg Safe tickets, every leg Green on our own number, went 3 of 18 where we said 51%, its Balanced 11 of 14 (said
48%), because Green on our number marked the legs we rated over the book, the ones AAM found overrated. A pick's own
Green, Yellow or Red label is unchanged, and hockey's tickets, whose legs are not capped, still read it. Switching
the cap off (`QB_BOOK_AGREES=off`) brings the NBA's Green half back with it.

**AAQ. A quarterback's pass-attempt over rides no ticket** (step 831; 21 November). Nothing to run. On the record of
every settled Most Likely pick, an NFL quarterback's pass-attempt over that we and the book both rated 60% or better
hit 44% in the first 60% of days (9 legs) and 50% since (32), where we said 64%: 20 of 41, at prices that needed
69%. Every other NFL leg rated as high hit 68% early and 65% since (1,038). The book cap of step AAM cannot catch
it, because the book rated it as high as we did. Its sister market, completions, hit 55% of 56 and was benched on 18
November. College's pass-attempt overs went the same way as picks (13 of 26, where its others hit 58%). So in
football a pass-attempt over is now kept off every ticket and goes behind the other bets on a report's card; it
stays a pick on the board, and the census counts it under our rules. This is no bench: its picks keep their stakes;
whether to bench them as completions were is your call. Switch: `QB_VOLUME_LEGS=off`.

**AAP. Football's touchdown pairs take two scorers at our touchdown rule first** (step 830; 21 November). Nothing to
run. A game report's two-leg touchdown pairs (NFL and college) were ranked on their research, and our 40% rule (a
scorer we rate 40% or better) was only the pair card's words. On the record of every settled Most Likely touchdown
pick, a college scorer at 40% or better scored 51% of the time in the first 60% of days and 53% since (279 picks),
one under it 41% and 36% (211): two at the rule land together about 27% of the time, two under it about 15%. The
NFL's: 46% and 58% at the rule (192), 44% and 36% under it (151). So a pair whose two scorers are both at the rule
now ranks ahead of one that is not, and a game's scorers at the rule are tried first; inside each side the research
still orders them, and a pair with a stand-in scorer still goes last. A shorter-priced scorer pays less, so this
lifts how often a pair lands, not its price. Hockey's pairs rank on our chance as before. Switch:
`QB_TD_RULE_FIRST=off`.

**AAO. A report's card puts the picks the record backs first** (step 829; 21 November). Nothing to run. Each game
report's card ranks its best picks (four, six on a featured game), and those are the picks the record grades and the
parlays are built from first. The same record as step AAM says two kinds of pick do much worse than the rest: an NFL
pick whose chance sits more than 10 points above the book's own fair chance hit 45% (92 picks, where we said 75%)
and 53% since (45, where we said 87%), while every other NFL pick hit 58% both times; and an NBA prop one play
settles (over 1.5 rebounds, over 0.5 threes, under 0.5 blocks) hit 62% as a single and lost 7.6% at its prices,
where every other NBA pick hit 65% and made 3.3%. On a report's card those now go behind every other bet (reads
still last), so a game shows them only when it has nothing better; nothing is taken off the board. College
football's far-over picks hit what its others did (57% and 55%), so its card is left as it was. Switch:
`QB_CARD_DOUBT=off`.

**AAN. The two cleanups, and fantasy points back on football's game page** (step 828; 21 November). Nothing to run.
The game page's code still carried two things nothing drew any more. The box score's old tables (football split into
passing, rushing and receiving, every other league one table), drawn only by baseball's old Player stats tab, went:
since step AAK every league's box score is the one game page's own card. And football's drive tracker card (the
drive drawn on a field play by play, with its Replay button) went from the shared live-game code: since the one game
page the drive in progress is its drive view, and the whole game's drive chart and the drive on the photograph,
which draw the same field, stay. In all 337 lines of code and styles went and 26 came in. One thing came back: the
fantasy points you asked for on 27 October (the game's top fantasy scorers so far, PPR and half-PPR, off its box
score) were drawn only inside those old tables, so they quietly left the NFL and college game pages when the page
was redesigned. They are a card again, on the Stats tab under the box scores ("Fantasy points so far"). Checked on a
made-up live NFL game at phone width.

**AAM. A parlay leg needs the book to agree** (step 827; 21 November). Nothing to run. You asked to dial in the
three-leg parlays and to look at all the data. I read every settled Most Likely pick the site's public record holds,
the pool the parlay legs come from: 2,639 NFL picks since 10 September, 3,240 NBA since 20 October, 2,871 hockey
since 6 October, and college football's. Two things stood out. First, where our chance sits well above the book's
own, our number is wrong, not early: NFL legs we rated 60% or better at prices of -100 to -130 hit 40% (78 legs,
where we said 75%), and at -130 to -160 they hit 51%; from about -160 and shorter they hit close to what we said.
College football is the same, the NBA milder. So in the NFL, college football and the NBA a player-prop leg now
counts at the lower of our chance and the book's fair chance (the board's own fair chance for it, else the price
with an average 4.5% hold taken out). A leg reaches the 60% floor only when the market rates it that likely too, and
a ticket's chance is built on numbers the market stands behind. Checked the honest way, rule chosen on the earlier
weeks and then read on the newest 30% of days: NFL legs at the floor hit 66.4% instead of 62.9% early and 62.9%
instead of 62.0% late, and the legs it removes hit 49% and 50%; NBA 69.3% instead of 66.8% and 67.1% instead of
66.3%, removed legs 57% and 59%; college football 65.2% instead of 61.2% and 60.6% instead of 58.6%, removed legs
56% and 55% where we said 71%. Ranked by the lower number, the top fifth of each NFL day's legs hit 66% against 60%.
A ticket whose legs were held down says so on its card ("Each leg counts at the lower of our chance and the book's:
Malik Nabers 68% (ours 72%)"). Your own Nabers, Skattebo and Daniels ticket is the example: at its prices the books
say 68%, 64% and 64%, so it now prices at 28%, not the 33% we said. Hockey is left alone: the legs this would remove
there hit 65% early and 60% late, and hockey's tickets are beating their numbers (22 of 43 three-leg tickets hit
where we said 38%). Second, in the NBA three props a single play settles (over 1.5 or 0.5 rebounds, over 0.5 threes,
under 0.5 blocks) hit 62% of the 337 we rated 60% or better, against 68% for every other leg, and the books price
them as high as we do, so the first rule does not catch them; on the parlays' own record the NBA's blocks legs hit
10 of 20 where we said 72%. They stay on the board as single picks and ride no ticket, and the heartbeat's
report-pick count files them under "our rule". Expect fewer NFL and college tickets on some games (your answer to
decision 1: fewer rather than forced) and NBA tickets without bench rebounds or zero-block legs. Switches:
`QB_BOOK_AGREES=off`, `QB_ONE_PLAY_LEGS=off`.

**AAL. Every report parlay ranked best to worst, on its own page** (step 826; 21 November). Nothing to run. You
asked for each sport's best two-leg and three-leg parlays ranked the way the Most Likely picks are, best to worst,
on a separate page, with the player-prop parlays and the touchdown parlays in sections of their own. The new **Best
Parlays** page sits in the menu right under Report Picks (on the phone, in the menu's Picks group), and an old
#parlays link now opens it. It shows the league on the sport row: every parlay that league's game reports posted,
ranked across all of its games. Two sections, each its own tab: **Player prop parlays**, with a Two-leg / Three-leg
switch (each size ranked on its own), and **Touchdown parlays** (Goal-scorer parlays in hockey; a league with no
scorer pairs shows only the first). The ranking works the way Most Likely ranks a pick: each ticket goes through a
set of checks, its tier comes from how many it fails, and our chance of the whole ticket orders it inside the tier.
**Top parlays** pass every check, **Strong** fail one, **Worth a look** fail two or more. A player-prop parlay's
checks: its class (a two-leg ticket Safe or Balanced; a three-leg ticket Pop or better, 25% or better together), one
sportsbook has every leg at its number, every leg is the report's own pick (no fill leg), a book's same-game price
can plausibly pay what the ticket needs, and it does not need the game to go a different way from the game's other
tickets. A touchdown pair's: each scorer at our 40% touchdown rule (in hockey, the pair at 25% together), no
stand-in scorer, and the same together check; inside a tier, football's pairs go by their research score first, then
our chance. Each card shows its place, the game and kickoff, our chance, the tier and class, each leg with its
price, book and our chance, the price to take it at and the fair price, the one book that has it whole, and which
checks are against it. Its Bet it button puts the whole ticket on a book's slip (the same button every report parlay
has, so touchdown pairs get it too), and another button opens the game and its report. Chips above each section
filter by tier, with counts; a tier shows 20 cards, then a Show all button. A game that has started drops off the
list (the page is for picking), and so does a ticket with a leg no book lists any more; a line at the bottom counts
both. Members only, as the reports' parlays are: a visitor without a plan sees the lock, and the plans page says
what the page holds. The server makes the ranking when each board builds and again after the reports post their own
tickets, so the page ranks exactly the tickets the reports show. If the ranking ever fails, the page says so rather
than looking like a quiet day. The public heartbeat counts it per league, numbers only: each kind's tickets by tier
(`ranked_tiers`), the tickets left off, and the kind of error if it failed. The page's two files are served whole
until the Caddy reinstall already waiting under Commands waiting for you (00k) is run; the same command now serves
them trimmed too. Checked here on a made-up NFL board, at phone width and on a 1280px desktop, both sections, and by
two new browser tests: the ranking on both tabs, and a card's Bet it putting a three-leg ticket on one slip.

**AAK. Baseball's live game page is the one game page too** (step 825; 21 November). Nothing to run. Step AAI left

score in view (with the outs and the count), the ⋯ menu, Standings, the Stats tab's odds, game facts and umpire

opening day.

**AAJ. Your nine answers, built** (step 824; 21 November). Nothing to run. (1) A game short of three three-leg
parlays posts fewer; no touchdown leg comes back to fill it. The site already worked that way since step AAH, so

whole is now chosen ahead of one no single book has. A same-game parlay is placed at one book, so a ticket without

posted ticket stays until a leg breaks. This matters most in college: Saturday morning's board had 30 of its 65
tickets with no one book. Switch: `QB_ONE_BOOK_FIRST=off`. (4) No college basketball prop is priced off a ladder
alone: no change. (5) In the NFL and college football, the matchup scan's read on a pass catcher (good, breakout,
tough, avoid) no longer counts toward his catches or receiving yards reaching Top, and no longer ranks him. It still
shows on the card and in the report, where it explains the pick. What counts there now is the projection's own
matchup step, the defence-vs-position effect that was measured to hold, when it moved his number 3% or more toward
the pick. A back's and a quarterback's reads count as before, and Ask's slip grader reads it the same way. Switch:
`QB_COVERAGE_READ=on` puts the old way back. (6) v3.1's parlay rules already covered college football but one: no
pass-catcher legs behind a new starting quarterback too green to rate. College's quarterback-change card never
counted the replacement's passes, so that rule never fired there. It counts them now, from college's own game logs
(this season and last), and a replacement under 50 passes marks the card as the NFL's does: a catch or
receiving-yards pick behind him tops out at Worth a look and is no parlay leg. The card no longer says "too few to
rate" about a replacement with more passes than that. (7) College football's picks ask 60%, as the NFL's do. A prop
or game line under 60% on the number the page shows is held back and says so ("the college board asks 60%");
touchdowns keep the shared bar. Switch: `QB_CFB_TIGHT=off`, which also lifts college's held receiving-yards unders.
(8) In the NBA and the NHL the record's correction may now raise a chance, where it only ever lowered one. A pick
priced above our number can rise toward the price's own chance, never past it; a pick we rate above its price still
only comes down. It is fitted and checked on held-out games by the same bar as before, so it takes effect after the
next nightly board-learning run (about 4 AM Eastern) if that check passes. Switch: `QB_RECORD_RAISES=off`. (9)
Saturday's college slate is bought from Friday. College already bought tomorrow's games the day before, but only on
a day with no college game that night, and Fridays nearly always have one: at 5 AM today no college report had a
parlay, and at 9:20 AM 33 of the 58 games still had no prop priced. Now, on the day before a Saturday slate, college
gets its two day-before pulls on top of Friday's own, at most a quarter more of that day's odds allowance, each
buying up to 12 games, the most-watched first. Next Friday night's heartbeat says how many of Saturday's games had
props (cfb `threes_short_why` `no_props_priced`). Switch: `QB_CFB_FRIDAY=off`. Still open from the list: (10) to
(14).

**AAF. An under's price was being lost, one thing that kept the one-book line quiet on football** (step 820; 21
November). Nothing to run. Step AAE's own count corrected me. On the first NFL board after it the count of posted
picks whose number no book lists any more (`unlisted`) read 0, and the same 35 of 165 legs still had no book at

number. A book quotes its main line both ways, and lists the same number again on its alternate ladder, mostly as
the over alone ("5+ receptions"). The ladder was filed last and replaced the main line, so the under's price was
gone. Two places read that list: the parlays' one-book line, which said nothing for a ticket with an under unless
its legs' own books happened to match, and a bet slip's live prices, which showed no current price for an under at
such a number. Both quotes are kept now: an under reads the main line's price, an over the better of the two, and
the fair chance still comes from one book's own pair. The next NFL board's `no_quote` says how many of the 35 this
was. Step AAE's rules stay, for the case they were written for, and its count stays on the heartbeat. I withdrew the
decision I had listed with it (decision 6 in docs/NFL_BET_CHECKING_METHOD.md), since there is nothing to decide
while the count is 0. One more change: the line saying where to place a ticket no longer shows on a game that has
started or finished.

below says how many of the 35 that explains. Six changes. A posted price no longer counts as a quote today: step AAD

can bet (Pinnacle) is never named as the one book. Report Picks does not lead with a ticket that can't be placed,
and Ask is told which those are. The heartbeat counts them: `one_book` has `gone` (tickets with such a leg) and
`one_book_legs` has `unlisted` (the legs). Its count of what became of each report pick (`pick_fates`) has
`unlisted` too, where such a pick had counted as `strong`. One decision is new (decision 6 in
docs/NFL_BET_CHECKING_METHOD.md): when the books move off a posted pick's number, should its parlay legs follow them

**AAC. Why college basketball had no props on Friday** (step 817; 21 November). One read-only command, any time;
paste it back. College basketball posted no pick and no parlay on Friday 20 November (40 games, 7 reports,

that those were one-way quotes is my inference, the receipts do not keep it). Legs like that would lose parlays. The
command prints the pacer's college decisions over the last day (was the 6pm pull held, and why) and, for each of the
last eight cached college pulls, every player market with its count of over prices, under prices and books (are the
