**TH. An open section and your place on the page outlast leaving the app** (step 640; 16 November).
Nothing to run. You said that when you open a section, leave the app and come back, the section is closed
and your place on the page is gone. Three things did it:
- **Coming back redraws the page** with whatever changed while you were away, and a redrawn section
  starts closed.
- **A new version of the site reloads the page** when you put the app away or bring it back, and a reload
  opens at the top.
- **A phone can close a page it put away** and load it again when you come back.

Now every section you open or close is remembered for the page you're on, on every page. A redraw keeps
it open and keeps your scroll where it was. When you put the app away, it writes down the page, your
scroll and your open sections. If the page loads again within two hours, it opens the sections and goes
back to your spot, and stops the moment you touch the screen. Tapping a tab still opens that page at the
top, and Back still returns to where you were.

What isn't graded, and why: the pass rush against the pass protection (sacks aren't in our box scores), and

**SU. A finished UFC fight shows how it ended and how our bet did** (step
627; 16 November). Nothing to run. You asked for the finished-game results
"for all sports". UFC has no game page, since each fight's card on the UFC tab
is its page, so the results go on the cards:

The results come from the live fight card the UFC tab already reads. It
refreshes every 10 seconds while you're on the tab, and it's the same feed the
bet-slip checker settles fight legs from. The grading follows the checker's
rules exactly, and a test holds the two together on every market and every
way a bout can end. If the feed hasn't said how a fight ended yet, the card
shows who won and leaves a method, distance or round bet ungraded until it
does. A bout the card can't tell apart from another one is left alone rather
than guessed.

The card and the Record page always agree. The record journals each UFC pick
as the moneyline on our fighter at the moneyline's price. That's the only bet
a card can make today, because no method or round prices reach the model. A
test now fails if one ever does before the record learns to journal that bet,
so a card can never say "Our bet lost" while the record counts a win.

**SS. A written report for every UFC fight** (step 625; 16 November).
Nothing to run. You said "Yes" to a written UFC fight report. Every fight
card on the UFC tab now has "The fight report" folded under it, in the same

  picks the other fighter) and the chance our bet is priced at. Then the

  takedowns against a leaky takedown defense, submission attempts, age past

- **Our bet:** the pick with its price, edge and grade, or why there's none.
- **What kills the bet:** the card's void rule and each fighter's red flags.

A fight the model couldn't read (no stats, no price yet) still gets what
it has and the reason. The reports are part of the subscription, like the

**SR. The record sets the one-team bar on each game's parlays** (step 624;
16 November). Nothing to run. You said "idk whatever is best" about the bar
a parlay with all one team's players has to clear (4 points likelier than
the best ticket with both teams, or 3 research points for a touchdown
pair). What's best is what our record shows, so the record now sets it.

How it works:
- After each grading pass that settles a parlay, the box splits every
  graded game parlay into one-team and two-team tickets and compares how
  often each hit against the chance it was posted at.
- If one-team tickets hit short of their chance more than two-team ones do,
  the bar goes up. If they beat their chance, it comes down.
- It waits for 30 graded tickets of each kind before moving anything, and
  even then it moves only part of the way while the sample is small.
- It stays between 2 and 10 points, and between 2 and 6 research points.
- At most one of a game's tickets can be one team's, as before.

The build log says the bar in force on every board ("one-club bar 4 points,
3 research points (the defaults until 30 of each settle)"), and the box's
log says when the record moves it.

It's only for a touchdown you see happen. It doesn't flash:

- for a field goal, or for a score that came in while the tab was hidden;

If you watch on a TV delay, it flashes when your TV shows the score. With
your phone's "reduce motion" setting on, the score changes colour and the
tag fades in and out without moving.

**SO. Who we think wins, in every game report** (step 621; 16 November).
Nothing to run. You said "I also wanna add in the game report section who
we think will win based off the data and match up and our game report and
offense and defense and all that". Every league's game report now has a
"Who we think wins" section, right under our picks:
- The call: the team, its chance to win and how sure we are. That's "A
  clear favorite" at 75% or more, "Favored" at 62%, "A lean" at 55% and
  otherwise "A coin flip". A bar shows both teams' chances.
- The numbers behind it: where the chance comes from, our simulation's
  chance, the prediction markets' and the score the lines expect.
- "Why" the favorite and "The case for" the other team, from the report's
  own data, for both sides:
  - each offense against the other defense where the ranks are far apart;
  - the records, the last five games, and the home and road records;
  - who is out (in football a quarterback first; in basketball a player who
    plays 20 minutes or more);
  - the starting pitchers' expected ERAs and the goalies' goals saved above
    expected.
- When more of the report points to the underdog, it says so: "the case for
  an upset, against the price".

Where the chance comes from: the books' moneyline with their cut taken
out. Without one it's the spread, on the league's own win curve, and without
that our simulation. It's never our team ratings alone. Where our NFL
ratings disagree with the closing line, the disagreement has carried nothing
(docs/NFL_MONEYLINE_ARITHMETIC.md). Bets on our baseball ratings alone
against the price lost 12.4%. Picking the winner off them would be a guess

**SN. Parlays and touchdown pairs take both sides** (step 620; 16 November).
Nothing to run. You said "a lot of these parlays we are making are very one
sided ... for both td and player props ... I understand if all the data
points too one side so that's fine but we just need to make sure", about
the 49ers game.

Why it happened: each game's four three-leg parlays were picked by chance
alone. A game's likeliest legs are usually one team's busiest players, and
the rule that the tickets should win together kept the next tickets on that
same team's script. So a team whose legs were a point or two likelier
filled the game. The touchdown pairs had the same lean through their
research ranking.

The rule now:
- A ticket whose legs are all one team's is posted only when it's clearly
  the stronger read than the best ticket with both teams that could take
  its place: 4 points likelier for a three-leg parlay, 3 research points
  stronger for a touchdown pair.
- At most one of a game's tickets can be one team's while a two-team ticket
  is available.
- If the other team has nothing good enough, the game posts what it has.

Every one-team ticket says on its card which of those it was, so you can
check it. The build log counts them for each league ("one club's alone").

On a test game shaped like the 49ers one, the old way posted two
49ers-only tickets that were only 2 to 3 points likelier than the best mixed
one. Now all four tickets take both sides, and the top one gives up about
3 points of chance for it.

**Decision for you:** the 4 points (and 3 research points) is my call. Say
if you want it stricter or looser.

back. A bet graded on the box score the same night stands. If the play file
has no row for a box number (the name is spelled another way), the play
file's own row is left alone. Also fixed: a game's box copy now goes the
moment its official rows are on file, whether or not a prop is still open
that day. Before, it stayed beside the official rows once the night's props
had settled, and that's how your cleanup found 130,078 duplicate rows
(engine/boxsettle.provisional_games). The NFL still grades on nflverse's
file.

(engine/gamescan.LEAD_CARRY_SHARE, the share the audit already calls key).
He can still read tough, and one reason against him still leans him there,

Every other pick shows its tier. A read the data doesn't back gets no pick,
and its card and the report's player card say why: a coin flip, our number
against the read, or a number too far from the books.

**QW. Each game's touchdown pairs are chosen on our research** (step 577;
14 November). Nothing to run. You wrote: "make sure we are making the TD
parlays based off reaseerach we do and the breakout canidates and game
scripts and all of that and not just based off the player lines". The pairs
were the game's likeliest priced scorers, which reads like the shortest

(engine/gameparlays.research), built from:
- the matchup the matchup picks already use (engine/matchpicks.td_matchup):
  his team's expected points, the defence at his position (the run defence
  for a back or a quarterback), his red-zone chances and red-zone trips
  both ways;

  by 7 or more -1, and a receiver or tight end in a shootout total +1.

A scorer needs a red-zone role and 4 of the 13 points. Scorers and pairs are
ranked on research first and our chance second. Each leg shows its research
score and leads with its case: the read, the defence, the script, then its
own reasons. The chance a pair shows is still our model's. A game with fewer
than three pairs says how many of its priced scorers carry a research case.
Hockey's goal-scorer pairs have no read and still rank on the chance.

isn't reachable from this environment, so this was built from developers'
migration notes; if v2 refuses something, `money_census.why` on each board
names it on the next build. Not moved, because I couldn't confirm their v2

- **The same-night box settle never purged a college game's copies.** It

What they left is removed by one command: the official row stays, the copies

```
cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys nice -n 19 python3 -m engine.cfbdedupe
```

Then, if the counts look like the PU run, the removal:

```
cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys nice -n 19 python3 -m engine.cfbdedupe --apply
```

It also prints where a box copy's number differs from the kept official one

**QF. One reason against a workhorse no longer makes him unfavorable**
(step 560; 14 November). Nothing to run. You, with two won Duke–Miami
parlays (Mark Fletcher Jr. and Nate Sheppard to score, and Sheppard 60+
rushing yards, at 63 by the second quarter): "based off our game reports,
one of these players was unfavorable which was wrong". Sheppard's read had
one reason against him, Miami's run defense ranked 5th, and nothing for
him: Duke's expected 20.5 points sat between the bars, and his own
blocking (69th) was one short of counting. One reason was enough to read
"tough", and the report printed that as "UNFAVORABLE", for a back with
62% of the carries and 17 touchdowns. This morning's fix had only stopped
it reaching "avoid".

Two rule changes, the same in every league (engine/readlogic.ladder):
- **The same bar both ways.** A read leans tough on as many reasons as it
  needs to lean good. Football leans on one either way. The NBA, the NHL
  and MLB lean good on two but had leaned tough on one since each league's
  first read, so one reason against a player outweighed one for him; they
  now need two either way.
- **A featured player needs one more.** That's a back with most of the
  carries, a receiver with a fifth of the targets, a starting quarterback,
  a starter's minutes, a skater who shoots three times a night, or a bat
  at the top of the order. One reason against him reads neutral, with the
  reason shown; two read tough, and he is never "avoid".

Sheppard now reads neutral with "Miami's run defense ranks 5th" said. A
back without the volume, or the workhorse with two reasons against him
(the defense and a low expected score), still reads tough. Where a go-to
scorer does read tough, the report says "TOUGH FOR YARDS — STILL THE GO-TO
SCORER", not "UNFAVORABLE". Fewer tough reads also means fewer unders
seated by a read on the Most Likely board, and fewer plays listed to avoid.

**QC. The posted picks, read against the matchup reads, every league**
(step 557; 14 November). One read-only command; paste it back. You: "audit
all the picks and all that shit and remove and add anything we need to."
The reads were fixed at the rule (step PW): one vote per factor, a featured
player never "avoid", a go-to scorer's tough draw said as one. I checked
every rule that turns a read into a pick or pulls one: the matchup picks,
the Most Likely board's matchup check, the game plan's plays to avoid, the
touchdown scenarios and the long-shot warning. None lets one rank sink a
go-to scorer's touchdown. What the boards post is only on the box (the
public copy has the picks taken out), so this reads each league's private
board (engine/pickaudit) and prints three things: the self-check's count
by kind (a pick its read argues against, a play to avoid another board
posts); every could-struggle read on a key player, with its reasons on each
side, go-to scorers first; and every go-to scorer with no touchdown pick on
any board, with his chance, his price and why, when the board says (the
injury report, the -250 cap). Each finding becomes a rule change, never a
hand-edited pick:

```
cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys nice -n 19 python3 -m engine.pickaudit
```

**PU. Why a college football player's game is listed twice** (step 549; 14
November). One read-only command; paste it back. You, on the Miami–Duke
report: Cooper Barkate's "Last 3" showed Notre Dame on both 7 November and
8 November, with different numbers, and the public logs
(https://qellysbook.com/api/players/logs?sport=cfb&player=Cooper%20Barkate)
hold the same game under two dates — his 92-yard line sits under 11-07 and
11-08 both. One real game is stored under two `period` values, which
inflates his season totals, his form lines on the report, and can void a
bet whose two rows disagree (the settler's duplicate rule). It is almost
certainly the same-night box-score settle (engine/boxsettle) filing its
provisional rows under one date and the official backfill
(engine/sources/cfbstats) under another, so the provisional ones are never
purged. This dumps every stored row for him, the games rows for Miami, and
how many college players carry the same opponent under two game ids, so the
fix lands on the real cause rather than a guess:

```
cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys python3 - <<'PY'
from engine import db
from collections import defaultdict
c = db.connect()
print("== Cooper Barkate, every stored row (season, period, game_id, market, value):")
for r in c.execute("SELECT season, period, game_id, market, value FROM player_game_logs WHERE sport='cfb' AND player='Cooper Barkate' AND market IN ('rec_yds','receptions') ORDER BY period, game_id, market"):
    print("  ", tuple(r))
print("== games rows involving MIA since 2026-10-15:")
for r in c.execute("SELECT season, period, game_id, home, away, home_score, away_score, date FROM games WHERE sport='cfb' AND (home='MIA' OR away='MIA') AND COALESCE(date,period) >= '2026-10-15' ORDER BY COALESCE(date,period)"):
    print("  ", tuple(r))
dup = defaultdict(set)
for r in c.execute("SELECT player, market, opponent, game_id FROM player_game_logs WHERE sport='cfb' AND season=2026"):
    dup[(r["player"], r["market"], r["opponent"])].add(str(r["game_id"]).replace("-box", ""))
many = {k: v for k, v in dup.items() if len(v) > 1}
print("== cfb 2026 (player, market, opponent) under 2+ distinct game ids:", len(many), "of", len(dup))
for k, v in list(many.items())[:12]:
    print("  ", k, "->", sorted(v))
PY
```

Caddyfile is installed. The automatic update pulls code and restarts the
site but never installs a Caddyfile (letting a push reconfigure the web
server as root is the kind of power its audit took away), so it is this,
with Caddy checking the file first; one that does not validate stops here
and the running one stays:

```
cd /srv/qellys && sudo caddy validate --config deploy/Caddyfile --adapter caddyfile && sudo cp deploy/Caddyfile /etc/caddy/Caddyfile && sudo systemctl reload caddy
```

Then, read-only, the address answering with its own title (it prints
`<title>College basketball · Qellys Book</title>`; the plain site title
means Caddy still has the old file):

```
curl -s https://qellysbook.com/cbb | grep -o '<title>[^<]*</title>'
```


How a college night works. ESPN's Division I scoreboard (every game, 60 to
150 a night) is the slate. The game lines for all of it come in the same
three-credit request the NBA's do. Player props are bought on the five best
games still to tip: ranked teams first, then the power conferences, then

college props on those games and few others, so the credits go where a price
exists. Each school's code is ESPN's for Division I and `espn:{id}` for a
small school (ESPN reuses codes below Division I: CAL is California and
Calvary). Headshots come from each school's own roster on ESPN, read by team
id, so a namesake at another school never lends a face.

It starts on probation, like the WNBA and the NHL: every pick is journaled
and graded, nothing is staked, until the record earns it. Its tuning is the
WNBA's 40-minute numbers until college's own seasons are measured.

https://qellysbook.com/data/heartbeat.json, under `chores` → `settle` →

**OQ. Rain and wind reach completions and a kicker's points** (step 519; 12
November). Nothing to run. You said the weather isn't a factor for the
picks. For most of the board it has been since September: the kickoff
forecast moves passing yards and touchdowns, receivers' yards and catches,
a back's carries and a receiver's touchdown chance (tonight's Commanders at
the Giants, 74% rain and 12 mph: passing yards −11%, receivers' yards −14%,
catches −10%, a back's carries +5%). Two markets priced since October never
had it: a quarterback's completions and a kicker's points. Measured the same
way (ten seasons of games, the same rule): completions ×0.917 in rain,
×0.949 at 12-18 mph and ×0.935 at 18+; a kicker's points ×0.930 from 12 mph
(fewer extra points, no more field goals to make up for them). Both now move
with the forecast: tonight a quarterback's completions −8%, a 15 mph Sunday
a kicker's points −6%. Pass attempts, field goals made, and a kicker in rain
or cold measured nothing clear and stay untouched. And a pick's weather line
is marked with or against its side by what the weather did to that pick's own
market: a back's carries OVER in rain read "against this side" (the same line
names his catches' cut); it reads "with this side" now, and a market the
weather leaves alone (a back's or a quarterback's rushing yards) says "his
rushing yards left alone" instead of wearing the passing cut. The next
`python3 wxfit.py` you run (KU's) measures the two with everything else, and
`--scale` checks their forecast rows against the games.

Asked the same day, and left alone: does rain move WHO scores a team's
first touchdown toward the backs? No. Over every team's first touchdown
since 2021, the pass catchers scored their usual share in rain (×1.06 ± .11,
78 of them), and putting the anytime rain cut on the first-touchdown shares
made the predictions worse; 12+ mph wind, ×0.98 ± .05 over 349, nothing.
The first-touchdown picks keep reading the lines, which carry the forecast
(docs/FIRST_TD_RESEARCH.md, "Which player").

One thing it cannot fix from here: Sunday's Patriots–Lions game in Munich
reads "no forecast pulled". The NWS, which the boards read since step KY,
covers the US only, and nothing falls back to Open-Meteo (its free use is
non-commercial). A free source abroad that allows commercial use with a
credit line (MET Norway) is in RUN_NEXT's decisions.

**OK. A player's matchup card says what the matchup says** (step 513; 12
November). Nothing to run. Ethan, on the Commanders at the Giants: "We're
saying that the Giants defense ranked 30th, but then we're saying that
Commanders running back is an unfavorable matchup ... it's supposed to rain
this game as well." The short version said the Giants' run defense ranks
30th, so there is room to run, and the card under it read "Rachaad White vs
NYG's run defense: UNFAVORABLE" in a game forecast 74% rain. The one reason
against him was his own share, only 28% of the carries so far, which the card
hides because its role line already says it; nothing about the Giants or the
weather counted against him at all. Two changes (engine/gamescan):

* A player's share of the work no longer counts toward his matchup, either
  way. It is said (with what was noticed and not counted) and it still
  decides a breakout, the volume to use a good matchup, but the verdict is
  the defence he faces, the points the lines expect, a teammate out and the
  forecast. One counted reason leans a card (favorable or unfavorable), two
  make it strong, where a starter's share used to stand in for one of them.
* The weather counts, as the board already prices it (engine/weather). In
  rain teams run more and a back keeps his share, so a back's carries go up
  (about 5% on that 74% forecast, measured 2016-2025); receivers' and
  quarterbacks' yards come down (about 15% and 11% that night, with the 12
  mph wind). A step of 3% or more on his headline market is one reason. A
  card that leans on the weather alone points only at what the weather moves:
  rain backs a back's carries, never his rushing yards, which our rain study
  found do not reliably follow (docs/WEATHER_AND_QB_2026-11-06.md).

On that night the Commanders' backs read favorable, Diggs unfavorable and
Daniels (the third-fewest passing yards allowed, and the rain) the one to
avoid, which is what the short version and the forecast say. The same
verdicts feed Most Likely's matchup check, so a back's carries over in the
rain is now backed and his rushing yards over is not.

The heartbeat's `chores.settle.phases.grade_parts` now shows `snapshot_replay`
(seconds) and `snapshot_replay_groups`; `snapshot_lead` counts a read done
all over again from the lead, which only the each-reader path still does.

**NM. The play simulator counts its pairs in one step** (step 489; 9
November). Nothing to run. With every NFL team kept (NI: `kept 30, drawn 0`
at 11:54), the simulator's part of the readings was 3.5 seconds, and nearly

both went over, a thousand steps a pair. Each leg's overs are now one
number, a byte a trial, and a pair's count is one AND of two numbers: the
same counts (a test checks every pair against the trial-by-trial count), in

**NL. The play simulator stops reading college for nothing** (step 488; 9
November). Nothing to run, and one thing to know. The simulator's first build
on the new store (NI) said `playsim_sims.cfb: teams 0, drawn 0`: college's
game logs file each game under its date, which the simulator's reader drops
(it reads a week as a number), and keep no targets, which a receiver's share
is made of. So the college section has drawn no team since it was built, and
read two seasons of logs on every college build to draw none (2 to 6
seconds). It now skips college. Making college work would need receivers
built from their catches and a measurement of its own before anything could
use it: the parlay pricer takes the simulation's correlation for any
football pair once the NFL's verdict holds. Nothing on the site changes: the
college pick pages never had a simulated reading.

**NK. The readings' journals each say their seconds** (step 487; 9
November). Nothing to run. The NFL build's `ideas readings` stage had one
part, `journals + write`, at 8.2 to 8.7 seconds on every build for hours
after the attention journal's recheck went out, and one number could not
say whether that was the attention journal running out its own eight-second
budget, the curves' journal or the file. The heartbeat now shows
`attention journal`, `curve journal` and `write` apart.

**NJ. The seal step walks each chain once a cycle** (step 486; 9
November). Nothing to run. The loop's `forecast-seal` step took 9.8 to 13.5
seconds of every cycle. It walked the forecast chain end to end together
with a walk of the whole journal for drift that nothing in the step reads,
and the change log end to end; then the daily heads sealed and walked both
chains again before seeing today's were already written, which they are on
every cycle but the day's first. The heads now look for today's entry
first, and the step asks for the chain alone. Nothing about what is checked
changes: a broken chain still prints `FORECAST LOG BROKEN` on the cycle it
breaks, and the daily heads, the record export, the nightly report and the
doctor still count the drift.

**NI. The play simulator keeps each team's games between builds** (step
485; 9 November). Nothing to run. The NFL build's readings spent 11.7 to
13.2 seconds in the play simulator on every build and ran out its
ten-second budget, so the teams after the cutoff had no simulated reading on
the pick page. A team's thousand simulated games come only from its last
eight games and the fitted shocks, which move when it plays or the box
refits, never when a line moves. Each team now draws from its own seed (its
games no longer change when another team comes onto or off the board), and
its games are kept in `data/feedstate/logcache/playsim_sims-nfl-kept.pkl`
(and `-cfb-`) beside the kept game-log reads, a few megabytes; a build only
counts the lines against them, and the budget only bounds the teams it has
to draw. The pick page's simulated numbers move once, at the first build
after this deploy, because of the new seeds. The heartbeat's `logcache`
shows `playsim_sims.nfl` and `playsim_sims.cfb`: the teams kept, drawn and
left for the next build.

(step 484; 9 November). Nothing to run. With its stages on the heartbeat
(NC), the UFC build said where its time went: `line moves`, 8.0 of its 9

test compares them with a whole read).

**NG. College's touchdown board blends a returner toward last season, as
documented** (step 483; 9 November). Nothing to run. The blend that shrinks
a player's few games this season toward his last season (three games to
half weight) never ran once a season was under way: its "last season" was
read with a function that serves the current season after the first
Saturday, so every man was blended toward himself, and a returner with no
game yet was dropped. Replayed here on 2021-2025 college games (downloaded
from the same free mirror the box ingests), on the board's own touchdown
chain, scored on 2024-25: as written, the blend would have made the board
worse (0.1836 against 0.1765, three games in), because last season's
graduates stayed in each team's volume and diluted everybody's share. With
them left out once a team has played, and the touchdown rate blended too,
it is better for a man with one game (0.1505 against 0.1545) or two
(0.1698 against 0.1716), the same from three games on, and a returner in
his first game is priced again. The matchup scan stops listing last
season's departed men once a team has played.

**MY. The prediction-markets build stops recounting the whole Polymarket
tape** (step 475; 9 November). Nothing to run. MU put the build's steps on

and each build adds only what arrived since: the new rows by their position

The Kalshi step (`kalshi board`, 36 seconds) had the same two habits: it

**MW. The play simulator does each sum once** (step 473; 9 November). Nothing
to run. The NFL build's inventions spent 12.2 seconds in the play simulator
(`ideas readings` › `sim`) at 07:49: a thousand simulated games per team,
and then every priced leg compared with every other. Each trial re-read the
same player numbers and recomputed the same exponential on every throw, and
each pair of legs was compared twice, with the over-or-under of each leg and
the length of its scores worked out again for every partner. Now each is
worked out once. Every float is the same expression on the same numbers,
drawn in the same order, so the readings are identical to the digit (the
old loop is kept in the tests as the reference, and a 28-team, 420-leg
slate gave the same file before and after); here that slate went from 3.0 to
2.1 seconds. Most of what is left is the random draws themselves, which
cannot change without changing the readings.

**MV. College's reads and every board's comps are kept until their rows
change** (step 472; 9 November). Nothing to run. MS's parts named the time at
08:35: the college build read the same logs again on every build, the comps'
history 11.5 seconds (each market's whole past, one walk per market), the
props' two seasons of player games 6.4, the defense ratings 5.6, the usage
table 3.8 three times (props, touchdown board, matchup scan) and the
lineup's season 3.5, from logs that change when a night's box scores land.

- The comps' indexes are kept for every board that has them (NFL, college,
  NBA, WNBA, MLB), stored as columns of numbers: about 10 MB a market and a
  hundredth of a second to load, against 16.5 MB and 0.15 seconds stored
  as they were. On real hockey rows (a 1.9-million-row copy here) 3,000
  random records per market counted the same to the digit, a replay's
  cutoff included; a replay (the Lab, the backtest) still builds its own.
- A kept read nothing has asked for in ten days is dropped, so last
  season's tables and a market no board prices any more do not pile up. No

  and its note says `too big` or `folder full`.
- The touchdown board's own two reads go the same way: every scorer's
  touchdown games of the newest two seasons, and who played for which
  school this season (the props' slate reads that one too).
- On the heartbeat each shows under `logcache` (`comps_rec_yds.cfb`,

Likely board` 18 and `opponent-adjusted ratings + game lines` 12. Each now
prints its steps as parts, in the order the build runs them, and the

Outside a build nothing prints, and the slate builds the same props with the

**MR. The bet-slip links and the private copy, faster** (step 468; 9
November). Nothing to run. MP's parts named the publish's time at 03:20: the
bet-slip links took 7.1 of the NFL publish's 11.1 seconds, 8.4 of college's
and 6.5 of the NBA's (23 seconds a sweep), and writing the indented private
copy another 7.7 seconds a sweep across the boards.

- The links matched every pick row against every banked game by normalising
  the same few hundred team and player names afresh each time; each name is
  now normalised once a process. On the 22 October NFL board (1,024 pick
  rows, 30 games) the stamp went from 0.43 to 0.12 seconds, with exactly
  the same links on every row.
- The private copy (`data/built/`) is now written by the same fast encoder
  as the public one, compact: every reader of it parses JSON, none reads it
  by line, and it is a third smaller. The NFL's took 2.5 seconds.
- The links' part is now two on the heartbeat, `bet link files` (reading the
  banked odds files) and `bet link rows` (the matching), so the next
  heartbeat says whether the files are worth keeping between builds too.

**MQ. The history file counts its own game-log changes** (step 467; 9
November). Nothing to run. MO's note on the heartbeat answered the question
it was put there for: at 03:05 the NHL player games were served from the
cache (0.23 seconds to load) and the NHL season means too (0.3 seconds for
the whole fantasy step, against 25.3 at 02:15), but deciding the player
games were still current took 4.65 seconds, counting the index entries of
all 556,969 rows they read.

- The history file now keeps, in a small table (`log_generations`), how
  many times each sport and season's game logs have changed, moved by
  triggers on the logs themselves in the same write, whoever does it: a new
  row, a corrected one, a deleted one, a relabelled one (both seasons). The
  kept reads key on those counts, one small query instead of the count. The
  table and its triggers are made by the first build after this lands; a
  night of new rows costs about 0.02 seconds more to write.
- Two traps built around: SQLite runs a trigger's statements under the
  conflict policy of the write that fired it, so under the logs' own
  insert-or-replace an "insert or ignore" would have reset a count to one
  on every write (measured: five writes left it at 1), and a column that
  must not be empty would have aborted a box score with no season. Neither
  is in it, and both are tested.
- A file the schema has not reached keys on the row count as before, and a
  fresh table draws a random epoch, so counts that start again never match
  a result kept before. The counts are trusted only while all three
  triggers are in place: a build killed between the schema's statements, or
  a dropped trigger, falls back to the row count (the read's note then shows
  `rows` instead of `gens`), never to counts that stop moving.
- On the box at 03:48: all three kept reads served, each key read in 0.0
  seconds; the NHL board stage 3 seconds (25 at 02:15) and its whole build
  about 9 (61).

**MP. A board's publish says where its seconds go** (step 466; 9 November).
Nothing to run. The NFL build's write stage ran 24 seconds at 02:11 on 9
November and 22.4 of them were the one call that writes the board's three
copies; the same steps take half a second on a ten-megabyte NFL board here,
so the time is in something the box has and this machine does not, most
likely the bet-slip links (stamped from the odds files the box banks, of
which this machine has none). Every publish inside a build now prints its
steps (prepare, bet links, downgrade check, served copy, private copy,
sidecar, public copy) as the parts of `publish <file>`, and the heartbeat
shows them under the board, e.g. `boards.nfl.parts["publish nfl.json"]`.
Outside a build nothing prints, and every file is written byte for byte as
before. The next heartbeat says which step, and I go after it from there.

**MO. The game-log cache holds between builds, and the heartbeat says whether
it did** (step 465; 9 November). Nothing to run. On the box after MN (02:15
on 9 November) the NHL build still read its player games (19.7 seconds) and
the fantasy file's season means (25.3) though nothing in them had changed.
The results pulls re-read days they already hold (the daily catch-up
re-reads each league's last final day; the settle pass re-reads every day
with an open pick, every pass), and every rewrite filed the same box score
under a new rowid, which the cache took for a change.

- A game-log row already stored exactly as given is now left where it is; a
  new or changed row goes in as before. A night of hockey written again
  costs 0.03 seconds and no writes instead of 0.12 seconds and 3,200 writes;
  a new night costs about 0.03 seconds more than it did.
- A delete can free a rowid that the next row takes back, and the season
  relabel updates rows in place, so the three paths that do either (the
  provisional box-score purge, the bet repair, the relabel) now drop that
  sport's kept reads.
- The heartbeat's new `logcache` field says, for each kept read, whether its
  last call was served (`kept`) or read again and why (`no copy`, `rows
  changed`, `code changed`, `unreadable`), with its seconds (`key_s`,
  `load_s`, `read_s`, `store_s`) and its size. By 02:22 the NHL season means
  were served (0.2 seconds against 25.3) while player games still took 8.7;
  the field says whether that is the key's count or a read, and I go after
  it from there.

**MN. Two game-log reads are kept until their rows change; the write stage
names its parts** (step 464; 9 November). Nothing to run. The first NBA and
NHL stage times (00:55 on 9 November) put 17 of the NHL board's 25 seconds
into reading every player's games of two seasons, about a million rows,
on every build, ten minutes apart, while those rows change about once a
day. The fantasy file's season means read the same seasons again for every
sport.

- Both results are now kept on the box (`data/feedstate/logcache/`) with
  the count and highest rowid of exactly the rows they read, and a hash of
  the code that computed them, and served while all three still match.
  Every write to the logs is an insert-or-replace, which moves the highest
  rowid, so a new or corrected box score is read the next build; a deleted
  row moves the count. Counting the key costs about a tenth of the read.
- Only the live history file is kept this way; the tests and the Lab read
  their own files fresh, as before. A cache file that cannot be read is a
  read from the table, never an error.
- The write stage now names its parts in the NHL, NBA and NFL builds
  (relock the Pick of the Day, freshness, publish, light board, fantasy
  tonight): it ran 36 seconds of the NHL build and 35 of the NFL's at
  00:51-00:56, and 9 of the NBA's, for the same few jobs. The next
  heartbeat says which part, and I go after it from there.

**MM. A bet logged in the evening keeps its day** (step 463; 9 November).
Nothing to run. The gate's browser check failed at 23:50 on Sunday 8
November: a member with a $100 weekly limit logged $110 in My Bets and saw
"This week: $0.00" and no warning. My Bets dated a new bet with the UTC
date, which turns over at 7pm Eastern (8pm in summer), so the Sunday-evening
bets were filed under Monday and fell outside the Monday-to-Sunday Eastern
week the limit counts. The same UTC date skipped tonight's game on the
fantasy desk after 7pm, took "Today" off the Record card in the evening and
cut a day off the countdown to a league's next slate. One page helper
(`etToday` in web/js/app.js) now gives all six places the Eastern date, and
a browser check logs two bets with the clock at Sunday 23:50 Eastern and
sees them dated Sunday, counted in the week, with the limit's one warning.
Bets already saved keep the date they were saved with; a member can change
one by deleting it and logging it again. The changelog says it on the
Methodology page.

**ML. The NBA and NHL builds say where their time goes** (step 462; 9
November). Nothing to run. The heartbeat at 23:26 on 8 November had the NBA
build at 78 seconds of every cycle and the NHL's at 61, beside the stage
tables the NFL and college builds keep, with nothing to say where either
one's time went. Each now prints a line as each stage ends, which the loop
already reads back into the heartbeat:

- the NBA build in sixteen stages, from the tuning fit and the schedule

  (`boards.nba.stages`; the WNBA's under `boards.wnba` when it plays);
- the NHL build in seven (`boards.nhl.stages`). Its board stage, where

The stage lines only report time; the boards come out the same. The build's
closing summary is still its last line, the one the loop reports. Once the

(577 seconds and killed at its limit, down to 139 to 187).

**MK. Which MLB bets are still open, and why** (step 461; 9 November).
The record's journal still counts 29 MLB bets as open (10 of them staked),
though the season is over. The nightly chores pull MLB results from where
they last stopped and then grade every open bet, so these are bets the
grader cannot settle. Two causes fit, and only the box can tell them apart:

- an "if necessary" postseason game that was never played. Its date has no
  other game on it, and the automatic void (`ledger.auto_void_unplayed`)
  only claims a bet when its day also holds a finished game, as proof the
  day's results came in;
- or older stragglers from earlier in the season.

Until they settle or void, they are missing from the MLB record.
Read-only: every open MLB bet with its date, section and stake, what the
history file holds for that date, and what the automatic void would claim.
Paste it back and I will fix whichever it is:

```
cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys python3 -c "
from engine import ledger, db
c, h = ledger.connect(), db.connect()
rows = c.execute(\"SELECT date, category, player, market, side, line, stake_units FROM bets WHERE sport='mlb' AND status='open' ORDER BY date\").fetchall()
print(len(rows), 'open MLB bets')
for r in rows: print(' ', tuple(r))
for d in sorted({r[0] for r in rows}):
    g = h.execute(\"SELECT game_id, home_score, away_score FROM games WHERE sport='mlb' AND period=?\", (d,)).fetchall()
    print(d, 'games on file:', [tuple(x) for x in g] or 'none')
print('the automatic void would claim:', len(ledger.unplayed_bets(c, h, sports=('mlb',))))
"
```

The check in one go:

```
cd /srv/qellys && nice -n 19 bash tools/catchup.sh MK 2>&1 | tee /tmp/mk.txt
```

  last two weeks, the build looks up the last line it saw before kickoff
  and writes it as that game's close. Each lookup scanned every college
  price ever stored before that game's kickoff, props and every book
  included, once per game. It now reads the tape once for the whole two
  weeks, and each game keeps its own lines from before its own kickoff.
  The closes written are the same.
- **Teams and re-key** (19.1 seconds). Every build searched the whole
  games and player-stats tables, twice each, for schools stored under
  ESPN's number instead of an abbreviation. Since the first repair it has
  found the same thing every time: visiting FCS schools that the FBS
  teams list can never name. Each table is now searched once, and the
  search runs at most once an hour, or at once whenever the teams list
  gains a school. A school that can be named is still renamed, now within
  the hour instead of within the build.

Nothing to run.

November). The new part timings from the 10:45 NFL build pointed straight

  each watched player's prices when they move: men on an injury report,
  or with an open pick. To know whether a price moved, it read every price
  the league had stored in ten days. That table also holds the game lines,
  and the line ledger writes every game's spread, total and moneylines at

- **The line-movement stamps** (15.0 of the pipeline's 15.5 seconds). Each

  and each pick gets its own. On 97,000 snapshots and 600 picks, 2.17
  seconds became 0.03, every chart the same. The NBA and MLB builds use

Nothing to run.

with its no-vig chance at the close (`closing_fair`): the honest version,
the market against itself rather than our best shopped price against it. On
8 November it covered 0 of the 145 graded NBA picks and 144 of 503 NFL picks.
Two causes, both fixed: the NBA board never wrote the market's fair price on
a pick (the NFL and MLB boards always have; it is now taken from every book
quoting the pick's number, three at least, as theirs is), and the settle
looked an NFL bet's closing price up in our own snapshots under its week's
label ("2026-W10"), which no close is ever filed under, instead of its game's
day; the closing line was always read by the day, and now the price is too.
A daily sport's bet reads exactly what it did. Nothing to run: NBA picks from
the next build on carry it, NFL bets graded from now on take it. Read-only,
any day after: how many of each sport's picks since 8 November carry each
half:

```

from engine import ledger
c = ledger.connect()
for sp in ('nba', 'nfl', 'cfb'):
    r = c.execute(\"SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(fair_consensus IS NOT NULL), SUM(closing_fair IS NOT NULL) FROM bets WHERE sport=? AND category='main' AND ts >= '2026-11-08'\", (sp,)).fetchone()

"
```

**LL. Sunday's NFL picks on Saturday: the day before** (step 440; 7
November). You, that Saturday evening: "its saturday and we are not showing
any nfl picks for sunday ... we need to be show picks a day before games."
The board had the week's fifteen games and no price it would show on

old. The cause was the tonight rule (IP, 30 October): a league bought prices
only on a night it played, so on a Saturday the NFL bought nothing, and
Sunday's picks could not post until Sunday's first pull. A second rule
finished the job: an allowed background pull, for a league whose share of
the day was small, priced only the next six hours, and on a Saturday those
hold none of Sunday's games.

also buy tomorrow's slate, the day before: Saturday prices Sunday's games
and Sunday night's, Sunday prices Monday night's, Wednesday Thursday
night's, Friday college's Saturday. Tonight's games still come first (the
month's plan funds tonight's leagues as before); a day with nothing tonight
lets tomorrow's slate bring its own two pulls, never more than a quarter of
the day's credits; two days ahead is still nothing, and a day-before pull
is never narrowed to six hours. The daily leagues (NBA, NHL) keep tonight
alone: their props post on the day. Read-only, any time after it lands: the

boards' game-day forecast came from Open-Meteo, whose free API is for

scoreboard, which nobody licensed to us (docs/DATA_SOURCES.md keeps the

scores under a key ($39.99 a sport a month for the full plan, by the
paper's figures; check app.balldontlie.io for what each plan includes and

and asleep: with a key, while an NBA or NFL game is on, the box reads
both feeds each few seconds and writes down which showed each score
first. Nothing a member sees changes; moving a league onto the licensed
feed is a separate change, made only where it measures as fast or faster.

```
cd /srv/qellys && sudo systemctl restart qellys
```

**KO. The backup says why its offsite copy failed** (6 November: it said
`403 storage_cap_exceeded`; the sync now deletes first and says how full
the bucket is, KT) (step 408; one
read-only check, under a minute; the owner's desk, 5 November: "Last
night's backup did not reach the offsite copy"). The nightly backup made
its copies on this disk, then `rclone sync` to Backblaze failed, and the
desk could only say that it had. rclone's own reason went to the backup
log, where the JT check never printed it (it shows only the lines naming
history.db, `offsite copy updated` and `FAILED`). The script now keeps
rclone's last error line in its note beside the copies (`why`: one line,
at most 240 characters, any long run of letters and digits such as a key
blanked), the desk's Backups card shows it under **What it said**, and the
alert on your phone quotes it. The 04:00 UTC run after this push is the
first to keep it. Read-only, any time after that run:

```
cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys python3 -c "from engine import ownerdesk as o; print(o.backups().get('run'))"
sudo tac /var/log/qellys-backup.log | sed '/syncing to/q' | tac | tail -30
```

The first line is the note: `'offsite': 'ok'` means the copy landed, and
`'failed'` comes with its `'why'`. The second prints the offsite part of
the last run's log, the tool's own words included. What the usual reasons
mean:

- `Cap exceeded` or `storage_cap_exceeded`: Backblaze's cap is reached
  again. Leave the cap at the free 10 GB (nothing paid), and check that
  the bucket's lifecycle rule is "Keep only the last version": each
  night's sync hides the copies it replaces, and hidden copies count
  against the cap until that rule removes them, a day later. If the box
  itself keeps more than about 8 GB (the last lines say), keep fewer
  history copies (`cd /srv/qellys && sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh
  QB_BACKUP_KEEP_HISTORY 2`) instead of a bigger cap.
- `unauthorized`, `bad_auth_token` or `401`: the application key was
  deleted or has expired. Make a new one in the console and put it in with
  `sudo rclone config`.
- `no such bucket` or `404`: the bucket named in `QB_BACKUP_REMOTE` is not
  there.
- A timeout or `connection reset`: the network dropped during the upload,
  and the next night usually lands. Two nights in a row, paste it.

Paste back both lines either way. `./deploy/backup.sh --test-remote` tries
the round trip again by hand (it writes one small test file and deletes it).

**JZ. The NBA board reads the rotation, and a scout says what still goes
wrong** (steps 360 to 366; you, 2026-11-04: "I want to make sure we're all
ready to go for NBA. I don't know much about NBA, so I want to make sure
we're picking the right bets, reading the right scripts, picking the right
models").

- **Minutes, measured.** About 70% of a prop's outcome is the minutes he
  plays, and the board's minutes rules were a written spec's, never
  fitted. On two full seasons through the board's own code: a man who
  suits up on a back-to-back plays his usual minutes (the board was
  cutting 4-8%, a third of the schedule, leaning picks to the under), and
  a blowout costs a favourite's starters 1-5%, not 9-14%. Minutes error
  fell 3% on the season it never saw.
- **The rotation's news, three new rules.** Each written before its run,
  fitted on one season, judged on the other, kept only if minutes AND
  points both landed closer in both:
  - his **first game back** plays light, more so the longer he was out
    (x0.96 after one missed game, x0.92 after two to four, x0.84 after five
    or more), and his second game back after two or more a little (x0.96);
  - a **role that just jumped** (his last three games 20%+ over the seven
    before) mostly holds, so his base moves 40% of the way there (a role
    that dropped did not pass and moves nothing);
  - a **regular's return** (24+ minutes a game, back from missing two or
    more) takes a quarter of his minutes back from the men who covered.
  Together: minutes error 6.17 to 6.09 and 6.20 to 6.11 on the season each
  never saw; points 0.6% closer, points-rebounds-assists 0.9-1.0%, and the
  games they touch (about one in five) far more (a man back from five or
  more missed games: minutes error down 20-35%). The card says when one
  moved a man ("First game back after missing 3 games — minutes x0.92").
- **The scout.** Fourteen spots a basketball person checks before trusting
  a pick, every threshold written down before any was measured, then each
  measured on both seasons, before any model and after ours. Six still go
  wrong after our number, and they now show on the cards as "Scout:"
  lines, on the Edge card and in Most Likely's "Why?": an under while a
  regular teammate sits (3-7% under what we said), an over after his
  minutes dropped (4-5%), an over the night a regular returns (2-3%), an
  under in a game the books expect to be high-scoring (2-3%), a man whose
  games swing widely (about 1%), and a man barely into his season (about
  2%). The rest are already in our number (first games back, a role jump,
  a hot shooting run) or were measured not to be problems at all: a
  starter's over in a projected blowout hits more often than we say, and an
  over on a back-to-back as often as any other. A scout line moves no
  number; it is there so you can skip a pick the record says goes wrong.
- **Still off: the minutes a teammate's absence opens.** The board has had
  this rule since October (`engine/nba/vacancy`) and it switches on only
  once your box's own test holds. On the lab's two seasons it holds: k 0.30,
  minutes 5.3-5.8% closer and points 2.5-2.7% in those games. It is the

  games' makes. A 3P% over the hundred threes a starter takes in twenty
  games swings five points either way on luck alone. On the season it never
  saw, projections landed closer for threes (1.68%), points (0.99%) and the

**JG. The disk filled on Sunday morning: what did it, and what can never do
it again** (step 319; you, 2026-11-01: "the server is down and stale and
won't let me log into my account"). Already done, by you, that morning:
deleted the two leftover scratch files in /tmp, restarted the service (back
at 11:19 UTC, 5.0 GB free), and set the Backblaze bucket to keep only the
latest version of each file.

- **What happened.** The weekly backup check (Sundays, 04:30 UTC, the
  `backup.sh --check` line in root's crontab) restores each backup to prove
  it works. It restored history.db, 6.5 GB, into /tmp with 4.5 GB free,
  filled the disk at 04:32 UTC, died, and left its half-written copy behind
  (a second one, from an earlier Sunday, sat beside it). From then every
  write failed: the boards, the journal's housekeeping, and signing in,
  which writes a session. The API answered 502 for seven hours.
- **Why the disk was nearly full anyway.** data/backups held 16 GB, mostly
  copies of history.db taken before journal repairs (`--repair-*`,
  `--void-unplayed`, `--resize-unstaked`), uncompressed and never deleted;
  plus the weekly zips. And the offsite copy had stopped: Backblaze's cap.
- **What the code does now.** The weekly check measures the disk before
  each restore and skips one that wouldn't leave 15% free ("NOT CHECKED"),
  keeps its scratch copy beside the backups rather than in /tmp, and
  deletes it however it ends. A pre-repair copy measures first and is
  refused without room (the repair stops, as it always did without a
  backup). Old pre-repair copies are pruned every cycle: the newest two
  stay whole, older ones lose their history.db copy after 7 days and go
  entirely after 60. The low-disk warning now comes at 8 GB free, not 2.

After this is live, give it one cycle (about half an hour) for the prune to
run, then the read-only check: what's in data/backups now, the disk, and the
backup log's last lines:

```
cd /srv/qellys && nice -n 19 bash tools/catchup.sh JG 2>&1 | tee /tmp/jg.txt
```

Which runs, one at a time (the first line prints 1 and 1 once the fix is
on the box):

```
cd /srv/qellys && grep -c "prune_repair_copies()" engine/maintenance.py && grep -c "NOT CHECKED" deploy/backup.sh
df -h / | tail -1
sudo du -sh /srv/qellys/data/backups /srv/qellys/backups /var/backups/qellys 2>/dev/null
sudo ls -lt /srv/qellys/data/backups | head -12
sudo find /tmp -maxdepth 1 -name 'tmp.*' -type f -size +100M -ls
sudo tail -8 /var/log/qellys-backup.log
```

And 1.4 GB you can clear yourself: /var/backups/qellys is where the backups

  717, MLB 744, NBA 88, NFL 272): with JE's lift rule the board's pairs made
  +8.99u over 418 tickets (Edge −0.8% over 139, Most Likely +3.6% over 279);
  without it, +12.80u over 511 (Edge +2.1% over 164, Most Likely +2.7% over
  347). The rule kept the tightly linked same-game pairs, and they lost 15.9%
  over 120; it took away the NFL's Edge same-game pairs, which had made 15.7%
  over 22. Our modelled correlations don't show up in the results strongly
  enough to pick same-game pairs by.
- **What held in every run is the kind:** without the rule, same-game pairs
  lost 9.5% over 213 (MLB −24.4% over 85, its Edge ones 0 for 14; the other
  leagues +0.4% over 128) and two-game pairs made 11.1% over 298 (+20.3% over
  140 outside MLB; the Edge two-game pairs +10.9% over 128).
- **Now:** every same-game pair that makes sense posts again (one pick on
  each team included), shown, journaled and graded, but money rides only on
  a two-game parlay whose two legs are both picks we stake, at half a unit. A
  same-game parlay is always tracked. Two of each kind a day stays (one, two
  and three a day did about the same). The Record page's backtest refreshes

**JE. Same-game parlays have to earn back the book's cut; the study reads every
league's games** (step 317; your JD paste, 2026-10-31). Nothing to run for the
change itself:

- **What JD said** (two of each kind a day, since August): Edge parlays made
  +3.4% over 162 (the same picks as singles −1.8%), +15.2% since 10-15, and
  won in the NFL (+11.5%), college (+42.2%) and the NBA (+23.3%); MLB's lost
  (−7.3%). Most Likely parlays lost 2.5% over 375: MLB −12.1% over 170 and
  the NBA −12.0% over 34, against the NFL +17.1% and college +4.7%.
- **The finding:** football's Most Likely same-game pairs lost 11.7% over 86,
  while its two-game pairs made 29.6% over 85. A book pays a same-game parlay
  about 9.5% under its two prices multiplied, and two heavy favourites in one
  game, joined only by the shared pace (+0.10), lift the chance both hit by
  1–3%. The pair pays less and doesn't hit more.
- **Now:** a same-game pair posts only when the link between its legs lifts
  the chance both hit by at least 10.5%, enough to win back the cut. A
  quarterback and his own receiver (measured +0.64) lift it about 30% and
  still post. A pick on each team never carries more than the pace link, so
  those no longer post. Edge parlays, two of each kind, and the stake rule
  are unchanged.
- **A bug in the study:** it read only football's games (272). The NBA and
  MLB keep a game's day in a different column, so a pick on each team of one
  of their games was graded as two games. Fixed; the Record page's backtest
  refreshes on its next export.

**JD. Parlays: two legs from our picks, and what pairing the past would have
done** (step 316; you, 2026-10-31: "get rid of the parlay button and the
parlay feature ... make the parlay feature an actual button ... two-leg
parlays ... picked from the most likely bet and the edge bets ... see what
would have happened if we did parlay our past picks together and record
that and put those picks on the data page"; and "remove the high confidence
button ... because we have most likely picks that are ranked"). Nothing to
run for the change itself:

- **Gone:** Parlay Mode (the menu switch), the + Parlay button on every
  card, the do-it-yourself slip and its dock, Add to slip in Ask, and the
  old parlay screen's tickets. High Confidence (the switch and its filter)
  is gone too, and the Filters heading with it. A parlay a friend already
  sent you still reads in Messages.
- **New: Parlays**, a button in the menu after Long Shots (and in the
  phone's menu), on the NFL, college, the NBA and MLB. Two sections, Edge
  parlays and Most Likely parlays. Each night the board pairs its own
  picks: two from one game when they belong together (teammates who rise
  together, like a quarterback and his receiver, or one pick on each team),
  and two from different games. A pick is used once per section, two of
  each kind at most. Edge parlays rank by what they return at the price
  (only ones that return more than they cost post); Most Likely parlays
  rank by the chance both hit.
- **Prices:** two games at the two prices multiplied (3% under that when
  the picks sit at different books); a same-game pair at 9.5% under the
  product, the middle of what books take off a same-game parlay. No odds
  feed we pull quotes a parlay, so that is the price the record grades at,
  and every card says how its price was made.
- **Money:** a parlay rides half a unit only when both its picks are ones
  the stake rule stakes; the rest are tracked. In a drawdown every parlay
  is tracked.
- **Recorded:** every posted parlay is journaled and graded off its two
  picks' own results, Edge and Most Likely apart, never mixed into the main
  record. The Record page (All bets, By product) shows both records, the
  staked units, the newest tickets, and the backtest: every graded day
  since the record began, paired the way tonight's board pairs, next to the
  same picks bet singly. The old screen's tickets stay graded under it,
  marked retired.
- **What the public receipts say** (no teams in them, so two-game pairs
  only): the top three a day made Edge +7.2% over 190 parlays (the same
  picks as singles −0.7%) and Most Likely +4.0% over 297 (singles +1.5%).
  Two a day did better: Edge +16.1% over 135, Most Likely +10.2% over 200,
  and more units than three in both, which is why the board posts two of
  each kind. MLB's Most Likely pairs lost (−6.7%). Before 10-15 it was near
  even; most of the gain is the last two weeks, so it is a start, not a
  finding.
- **The honest math:** a two-leg parlay does what its legs do, about twice.
  Where the picks beat their price it wins about twice as fast; where they
  pay the juice it loses about twice as fast. A Most Likely pick at −250
  has to hit 71% just to break even. That is why only picks we stake carry
  money as parlays.

**IZ. The record leads with the picks we stake** (step 312; you,
2026-10-31: "we need to find what bets and what unit bets ... works best for

Nothing to run for the change itself. What the study found
(docs/STAKES.md; every number reruns from the public receipts):

- Most Likely wins bets and loses money: 4,582-2,953 (60.8%), −17.4 units
  (−1.4%), because it pays −162 on average where 61.8% breaks even. Our
  chance doesn't beat the price there: the picks we called 5%+ better than
  the price made −2.6% at flat stakes.
- Edge makes money on the price ladder: +13.9 units (+1.85%) over 1,414
  picks; NFL Edge +16.1 (+5.1%), positive in both halves of the season.
- Every "follow what's winning" rule, walked forward a day at a time, did
  worse than flat stakes.
- Edge picks past +130 lose in every league: they hit 37.6% where the
  price itself said 41.1% (293 picks, −9.6u). It's the favourite-longshot
  bias. The +100 to +130 picks made +23.8u.
- As forecasts, our chances beat the price's only on NFL Edge (and tie it
  on NBA Most Likely). A per-market correction toward the price was
  measured and scored no better, so it wasn't built.

The rule from today (`engine/stakeplan`): Edge picks are staked on the
price ladder (−110 is 1u), never past +130, unless a league's Edge book is
clearly losing (100 graded at z −2.0 or worse). Past +130 a pick is
tracked on paper and its card says "Tracked · no stake". Most Likely picks
are tracked for their hit rate, not staked, until a league's book beats the
price (200 graded at z +2.0 or better). The NBA's has, so it stays staked.
NFL, college and hockey Most Likely stop carrying money. The site's record
now leads with every graded pick at the stake that rule gave it on its
day: 1,406 staked, 770-636, +23.1u, +3.2% ROI (through Oct 15 +28.2u,
since −5.1u). Most Likely shows its hit rate, and the record as placed
(−3.5u) stays on the Record page.

17. **The slim record and the slow handshake** (2026-10-09). Nothing to
    run for the slim record to work: after the box pulls, the next settle
    pass writes `record_head.json` beside `record.json` — the same record
    without the sections only the Record page draws (about half the
    bytes) — and Home reads that instead. Two read-only checks; paste
    what they print:
    ```
    for f in record record_head; do curl -s -o /dev/null -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" -w "$f %{http_code} %{size_download} bytes\n" "https://qellysbook.com/data/$f.json"; done
    uptime; free -m; swapon --show; vmstat 1 5; cat /proc/pressure/cpu /proc/pressure/memory; ps -eo pid,ni,rss,pcpu,comm --sort=-rss | head -8; for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "tls %{time_appconnect}s first byte %{time_starttransfer}s\n" https://qellysbook.com/data/record_head.json; done
    ```
    The first line should show `record_head` well under `record`; a 404
    on it only means no settle pass has run since the pull. In the second
    check, `vmstat`'s `si`/`so` columns above zero mean the box is
    swapping (the handshake waits on memory read back from disk); `st`
    above 5 means DigitalOcean is lending our one CPU to a neighbour,
    which no code change fixes; the `some avg10` lines above 10 mean the
    box is short of memory or CPU. Five handshakes all near 0.15 s is a
    steady cost; one slow and four fast was a cold start.
    (Done 2026-10-09. The slim record is 31.8 KB on the wire against
    136.7 KB for the full one. No swapping (`si`/`so` 0), no steal (`st`
    0–1); the CPU is full of the builds and chores, all at nice 10, so
    Caddy and the server still go first. The handshake is NOT the server:
    curl itself spends 0.08 s of CPU per run on this box, and from here
    Cloudflare's own site and Google's take as long as ours —
    0.119 s, 0.128 s, ours 0.102 s. A browser keeps its certificates
    loaded, so a visitor pays one round trip to New York instead. Also
    learned: Cloudflare is NOT in front of the site any more — no `cf-ray`
    or `server: cloudflare` header — whatever "Behind Cloudflare" in
    DEPLOY.md says. Don't chase the handshake again from the box; time it
    from a computer that is not the box if it ever matters.)

    ```
    print('built:', collections.Counter(r['market'] for r in recs))
    print('book-priced:', collections.Counter(r['market'] for r in recs if r.get('has_market')))
    print('most likely:', collections.Counter(r['market'] for r in d.get('most_likely', []) if r.get('market') in new))"
    ```
    A market at zero under "book-priced" with the others filled means the
    API refused that key (the guard drops it and the rest keep working).
    Settling needs this season's box scores re-ingested once, so the
    kickers' and defenders' rows exist; the nightly ingest does it.

26. **Make "Forgot password?" email people** (2026-10-11, Ethan: "we
    have to have a forgot a password feture"). The Forgot page is built
    and the Gmail settings are on the box, but the test said **"Could not
    reach smtp.gmail.com on port 587"**: DigitalOcean blocks the mail
    ports (25, 465, 587) on newer accounts and often will not lift it. So
    the site now also sends through **Resend**, an email service the site
    talks to over normal HTTPS (port 443), which DigitalOcean does not
    block. Free for up to 100 emails a day. About 10 minutes:

    **A. The box has the new code.** The top line should read `Mail: send
    through Resend` or something newer; if older, wait five minutes:
    ```
    git -C /srv/qellys log --oneline -1
    ```

    **B. Make the Resend account and connect the domain:**
    1. Go to **https://resend.com**, sign up with qellysbook@gmail.com.
    2. **Domains → Add Domain**, type `qellysbook.com`, then click
       **Sign in to Cloudflare** and allow it. Resend adds its DNS records
       to Cloudflare for you. Wait until the domain says **Verified**
       (usually a few minutes; refresh the page).
       No Cloudflare button? Choose manual setup: Resend lists 3–4
       records. For each one, in Cloudflare → qellysbook.com → **DNS** →
       **Add record**, copy the Type, Name and Value exactly, and leave
       Proxy status as **DNS only** (grey cloud).
    3. **API Keys → Create API Key**, name `qellys site`, permission
       **Sending access**, then **Add**. Copy the key (it starts with
       `re_`); Resend shows it once. Don't send it to me.

    **C. Put it on the box** (`ssh` in), one line at a time:
    ```
    cd /srv/qellys
    sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh QB_RESEND_KEY
    sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh QB_MAIL_FROM noreply@qellysbook.com
    sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh QB_MAIL_REPLY_TO qellysbook@gmail.com
    sudo systemctl restart qellys
    ```
    The first one asks for the value and shows nothing while you type:
    paste the `re_...` key and press Enter. Emails come from "Qellys Book
    <noreply@qellysbook.com>", and anyone who hits Reply reaches
    qellysbook@gmail.com. (The Gmail settings you already set can stay;
    while QB_RESEND_KEY is set they are not used.)

    **D. Test it** (your own inbox):
    ```
    cd /srv/qellys && sudo python3 -m engine.mailer test you@example.com
    ```
    It should say `Sent to ...`. If it says the domain is not verified,
    wait for B2 to show Verified and run it again. Then on the site: Log in
    → **Forgot password?** → your account's email → **Email me a link**.
    To see the site knows mail is on (`"reset_by_email": true`):
    ```
    curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/account/me; echo
    ```
    Optional: an email when the site's service crashes:
    `sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh QB_ALERT_EMAIL qellysbook@gmail.com` then
    restart.

    **Rather send from the Gmail itself?** Ask DigitalOcean (Help →
    Support): "Please unblock outbound SMTP (port 587) on my droplet. It
    sends password-reset emails for my own site through my Gmail
    account." If they do, switch back with
    `sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh --unset QB_RESEND_KEY`,
    `sudo ./deploy/setenv.sh QB_MAIL_FROM qellysbook@gmail.com`, restart,
    and run the test in D.

    Notes: at most 90 reset emails go out a day (under Resend's free 100)
    and 3 an hour to one address. The morning/nightly digests stay off on
    Resend's free plan and on Gmail; a mailing list would use up the
    day's password resets. Until C is done, the Forgot page tells people
    to email qellysbook@gmail.com, and you can make a link by hand:
    ```
    cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys python3 -m engine.accounts reset-link someone@example.com
    ```
    Email that link only to the account's own address.

37. **A failed payment or a cancellation locks the account** (2026-10-12,
    Ethan: "It should lock them too the paywall screen"). What I found,
    then what changed:
    * **Cancelling already walled people, but only if Stripe's webhook got
      through.** If Bot Fight Mode ate it, the account stayed open for good.
    * **A failed payment never walled anyone.** `past_due` kept access
      "until the paid period ends". The date it read was the end of the
      new, unpaid month, so a failed card kept the whole month free.
    * **The page put the wall up only when it first loaded.** A tab left
      open kept working.

    Now:
    * **A failed payment walls at once.** The paywall says "Payment failed
      — your access is paused" and has an **Update card** button. That
      opens Stripe's billing page, where the customer changes the card
      and pays the open invoice. The payment that clears lets them back in.
    * **Buying a second plan over a failed one is refused.** The customer
      is told to update the card instead, so nobody is billed twice.
    * **A plan cancelled from the billing page keeps the days already paid
      for**, then walls the second its date passes. A plan cancelled
      straight away walls straight away.
    * **The site asks Stripe itself** when the webhook doesn't say:
      hourly for a paying account while it uses the site, each minute
      for a walled one, and every six hours for everyone.
    * **An open tab checks again** when you come back to it, and every
      five minutes.
    * **A late webhook can't undo a newer state.** A payment failure that
      arrives after the payment that fixed it is ignored.

    The box picks this up on its own (auto-pull and restart). The first
    re-read of every subscription runs at the restart. Three things to do:
    * **Check the webhook gets through:** Stripe → Developers → Webhooks →
      your endpoint → Send test webhook. It should say `200`. If it's
      blocked, Bot Fight Mode is on; docs/DEPLOY.md says how to turn it
      off.
    * **Check the Stripe settings this depends on:**
      * Settings → Billing → Customer portal: "Update payment methods" and
        "Invoice history" switched on. That's how a locked customer pays.
      * Settings → Billing → Subscriptions and emails: "Send emails when
        card payments fail" on, so Stripe emails them the fix as well.
    * **Your call: cancel at the end of the month, or at once?** It's the
      same portal page: Cancellations → "At the end of the billing period"
      (the default: they keep what they paid for) or "Immediately" (walled
      the moment they press it). The site handles either. Nothing to code.

    Read-only check that the re-read is running. It prints only statuses,
    counts and hours since the last read, no emails:
    ```
    cd /srv/qellys && sudo -u qellys python3 -c "import time; from engine import accounts as A, billing as B; c=A.connect(); B.init(c); n=time.time(); print([tuple(r) for r in c.execute('SELECT status, COUNT(*), SUM(checked_at IS NOT NULL), ROUND(MAX(?-checked_at)/3600.0,1) FROM subscriptions GROUP BY status', (n,))])"
    ```
    Each tuple is (status, accounts, accounts read from Stripe, hours since
    the oldest read). Within six hours of the restart, every status except
    `canceled` and `none` should have the third number equal to the second,

      season behind), so 2026 targets are drawn as the throw, from the
      pocket. We measured guessing the route from the public 2026 data:
      the likeliest route for a target's depth and side matched the
      league's charting 43% of the time, so we don't guess. When nflverse
      publishes 2026's file, the nightly picks the routes up by itself.
    * **Season, "where he's thrown to":** the field in thirds and depth
      bands (behind the line, 0-9, 10-19, 20+), each shaded by his share
      of targets and labelled with catches/targets, every target a dot.
      Tables by depth, by third, by route, against man and zone, by
      coverage shell (charted seasons) and by down; catch rate, yards a
      target, contested catches won and drops; the NGS season line
      (separation, cushion, intended air yards, share of the team's air
      yards, yards after the catch over expected).
    * **What it can't show, and says so on the page:** the league's
      tracked paths aren't published, so a route's stem and break are
      drawn, not tracked, and where inside a third a ball arrived is
      spread so no two overlap; the run after the catch is drawn straight
      upfield.
    * **Kept current:** the same nightly play-by-play read as the carry
      chart (and the same "a finished game has no chart" check), the
      receiving tracking file every night, last season once.


51. **Can the new chart data make better picks? Measured — no, not on
    its own** (2026-10-13, Ethan: "is there more features or tools we
    can add to get more accurate data and able to use this data to make
    better pics"). Nothing to run. Three matchups the charts make were
    added to the scan's measurement (`engine/scanfit`) and measured on
    2022-2025 the way every scan reason is — on top of the player's form
    and the defence-versus-position step the board already takes, each
    season held out in turn:
    * **run direction** — a back's inside/outside mix against where the
      defence gives up yards: t 0.2, held-out gain below zero;
    * **side of the field** — a receiver's left/middle/right mix against
      the side a defence gives up: t at most 0.9, below zero every way;
    * **yards after the catch** — a catch-and-run receiver against a
      defence that allows yards after the catch: t 0.9, below zero.
    The three that waited on the box (target depth, yards after contact,
    the pocket split) failed too, and the six measured on 2026-09-24
    re-ran to within noise. So the charts stay what they are: the picture
    of what happened, on the page, with no number reading them. Where our
    own record points instead is the closing line: since the closes were
    repaired, Most Likely picks lose about 2 points to their close and
    the Edge picks beat theirs by about 2½ (same-book check, 2026-10-04).
    L re-reads the picks that lost the close on the repaired closes; if
    the market had news we did not, a last look before kickoff is the fix.

52. **The charts fill the day they are empty, not the next day**
    (2026-10-13, Ethan: "Also the charts aren't working for any
    players"). Nothing to run; K shows it. The charts themselves were
    fine — their tables were empty. Every carry and target is read by the
    daily chores, which run once a calendar day, and the box had already
    run that day's when the charts landed (16:55 and 17:20 UTC), so every
    player's chart said "No carries on file" and would have until the
    next day's. Now:
    * **Every cycle** the box asks whether a chart table is empty for a
      season it has played (this one or last, NFL carries and targets,
      college carries) — a few lookups — and when one is, starts the
      fill in the background (`engine/chartfill`, its log in
      `data/cache/weekly_chartfill.log`). A failed read (GitHub down) is
      tried again two hours later, not every cycle. Measured here on the
      real files: both NFL seasons in about 6 seconds once downloaded.
    * **While it fills**, the chart says so — "Carry charts are still
      being filled… check back shortly" — instead of "No carries on
      file" for a player who has hundreds. That shows only while nobody
      in the league has a row yet.
    * **Lighter on memory:** the play-by-play reader now splits the file
      into lines instead of holding it in a text buffer; the same rows,
      checked identical on every season 2021-2026, at 214 MB a season
      instead of 490 MB. The nightly read uses it too, inside the 1600 MB
      the service is allowed.
